grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.parentage_note: Identified by John Bowers and Carole Meredith at UC Davis using microsatellite (SSR) DNA markers, published in Nature Genetics in 1997. The spontaneous crossing almost certainly happened in a Gironde vineyard in the 17th or 18th century; VIVC lists the pedigree as confirmed by markers.
grapes.hectares: 341,000 ha worldwide in 2015, the most planted wine grape on earth (OIV Focus 2017). Largest holdings: China c. 60,000 ha, France 48,000, Chile 43,000, USA 41,000.
grapes.profile: The most planted wine grape on earth began as a chance seedling in a Gironde vineyard where Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc grew side by side. Small, thick-skinned berries with a high ratio of pip and skin to juice give deep colour, firm tannin and the cassis, cedar and graphite notes that made the Left Bank famous. It buds and ripens late, so on cool clay it struggles; on the warm, free-draining gravel of Pauillac and Margaux it thrives, which is why the Médoc built its 1855 hierarchy on it. The variety travels well and keeps its identity in very different climates, the trait that made it the calling card of Napa, Coonawarra, Maipo and Ningxia. Methoxypyrazines give a green capsicum note when it is picked underripe.
grapes.trivia: Before the 1997 DNA result, the most popular theory held that the name meant a 'wild' Cabernet, from the French sauvage, rather than a child of Sauvignon Blanc.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.parentage_note: Parents not confirmed. VIVC records parent-offspring relationships between Cabernet Franc and the Basque varieties Morenoa and Hondarrabi Beltza, which points to Basque roots, but the direction of those links is not settled. Its own offspring are certain: Cabernet Sauvignon (Bowers & Meredith 1997), Merlot (Boursiquot et al. 2009) and Carmenère.
grapes.hectares: About 53,000 ha in 2016, roughly two thirds in France (Anderson and Nelgen 2020 database); VIVC lists 36,948 ha in France in 2009.
grapes.profile: The quiet parent of the Bordeaux family. Cabernet Franc fathered Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Carmenère, yet it is often the junior partner in their blends. It buds and ripens about a week before Cabernet Sauvignon, which makes it the safer bet on cooler clay and limestone: that is why it dominates Château Cheval Blanc on Saint-Émilion's gravel and clay, and the tuffeau hills of Chinon and Bourgueil in the Loire. Wines are lighter in body than Cabernet Sauvignon, with raspberry, violet, graphite and, when picked early, a leafy or pencil-shaving edge. Its fine, perfumed tannins have made it a cult grape for Loire natural-wine makers and for growers in Hungary's Villány, where it is the backbone of the Super Premium category.
grapes.trivia: Cardinal Richelieu is said to have sent cuttings to the Abbey of Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil via his steward, the Abbé Breton, which is why the Loire still calls the grape Breton.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.parentage_note: Cabernet Franc was identified as a parent at UC Davis in the late 1990s. The second parent, an unknown vine first sampled in 1996 in Brittany at Saint-Suliac and later found in the Charentes, was named Magdeleine Noire des Charentes by Jean-Michel Boursiquot and colleagues in a 2009 paper (Vitis). VIVC confirms the pedigree by markers.
grapes.hectares: 266,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017), the second most planted red wine grape after Cabernet Sauvignon. France alone had about 112,000 ha.
grapes.profile: Merlot is Bordeaux's most planted grape and the soul of the Right Bank. It ripens early and loves the cool, water-retentive clays that Cabernet Sauvignon hates, which is why it dominates Pomerol's blue clay and Saint-Émilion's limestone plateau: Pétrus is almost pure Merlot. Fleshy, round, plum-and-chocolate fruit and soft tannins made it the easy entry red of the 1990s, and its fortunes then crashed after the 2004 film Sideways mocked it. Its early ripening is now a liability in warming Bordeaux, where alcohol creeps past 15 percent in hot years, and the 2021 AOC rule change allowing Touriga Nacional, Marselan and other heat-tolerant varieties was a direct response. In Ticino, Friuli and Washington State it makes some of its most precise wines.
grapes.trivia: The name was first recorded in 1784 by a Libourne official, who called it 'Merlau' and noted it made one of the best wines of the area; the word probably comes from merle, the blackbird that loves the ripe grapes.

grapes.name: Carmenère
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC lists 'different propositions' for Carmenère's pedigree. The parentage Cabernet Franc × Gros Cabernet was published by Boursiquot and colleagues (2009); Gros Cabernet itself appears to descend from the Basque variety Hondarrabi Beltza (VIVC). In 1994 Boursiquot also identified Chile's 'Merlot' vines as Carmenère by ampelography, later confirmed by DNA.
grapes.hectares: About 10,000 ha in Chile (2016, SAG cadastre via Anderson and Nelgen); VIVC lists 7,054 ha in Chile (2008) and 1,218 ha in China as Cabernet Gernischt (2009).
grapes.profile: One of the great comebacks in wine. Carmenère was a respected Médoc grape in the 18th century, but it set fruit poorly (coulure) and was almost abandoned when Bordeaux replanted after phylloxera. Cuttings had already crossed to Chile in the 1850s mixed with Merlot, and for 140 years Chileans sold it as Merlot. In 1994 the French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot, visiting Chile, recognised that many of these late-ripening vines were not Merlot at all. Chile recognised the variety in 1998 and turned it into a national signature. It needs a long, warm season: picked early it reeks of green pepper (high methoxypyrazines), but fully ripe it gives soft tannins, dark plum, paprika and smoky spice.
grapes.trivia: China's widely planted 'Cabernet Gernischt', long thought to be a distinct grape brought by Changyu in 1892, turned out on DNA testing to be Carmenère.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.parentage_note: Parentage published by Boursiquot, Lacombe, Laucou and colleagues in Vitis (2009), the same study that named Magdeleine Noire des Charentes. It makes Malbec a half-sibling of Merlot through their shared mother. Confirmed by markers in VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 45,000 ha in Argentina in the early 2020s (INV), against roughly 6,000 ha in France (VIVC 2009: 6,155 ha); Argentina holds about three quarters of world plantings.
grapes.profile: Malbec was the black wine of Cahors, famous in medieval London and once widely planted across Bordeaux, where it was called Côt or Pressac. Frost in 1956 and its tendency to drop flowers pushed it out of the Gironde. Its new home came by way of Michel Aimé Pouget, the French agronomist who brought cuttings to Mendoza in 1853 for Domingo Sarmiento's agricultural school. At high altitude in Argentina's Uco Valley, intense sunlight and cold nights produce thick-skinned, violet-scented wines with plush tannins and fresh acidity, a very different animal from the firm, iron-edged reds of Cahors' limestone causses. Argentina celebrates Malbec World Day every 17 April, the date in 1853 on which the Mendoza school's founding law was approved.
grapes.trivia: In Cahors the grape is officially called Côt, and the region's growers use the name Malbec on labels mainly for export markets that learned the name from Argentina.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. VIVC records it as a parent of Tressot's other parentage line and of several local crosses; some writers suggest Pyrenean origins, but no DNA study has identified its parents.
grapes.hectares: Under 10,000 ha worldwide (2016, Anderson and Nelgen); Spain and Australia each hold more than France's c. 730 ha (VIVC 2006).
grapes.profile: A seasoning grape in Bordeaux, where it rarely makes up more than a few percent of a Médoc blend, but a few percent go a long way: inky colour, violet and spice aromas, and tannin that stiffens a blend. It ripens even later than Cabernet Sauvignon, so in the Gironde it only fully ripens in hot years, which made it a gamble before climate change. Warm regions have turned that weakness into a strength. Spain, Australia's Riverland, Virginia and Chile make varietal Petit Verdot that is dark, floral and firm. Many top Médoc estates, Château Margaux among them, have kept or expanded small plots as summers have warmed.
grapes.trivia: The name means 'little green one', a reference to how often the berries stayed unripe in old Bordeaux autumns.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.parentage_note: DNA studies by Regner and others (late 1990s to 2000s) established a parent-offspring relationship with Savagnin (Traminer); VIVC records the pedigree as 'Savagnin × ?'. It is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon (Bowers & Meredith 1997) and is likely a sibling of Chenin Blanc.
grapes.hectares: 123,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017); France c. 30,000 ha and New Zealand about 20,500 ha, rising to roughly 27,000 ha by the mid-2020s (NZ Winegrowers).
grapes.profile: Few grapes are so tied to one aroma family: cut grass, gooseberry, elderflower, passion fruit and, from the thiol 3MH, grapefruit. Those smells come from methoxypyrazines in cool sites and from thiols released during fermentation. In the Loire, on the flint and Kimmeridgian marl of Sancerre and Pouilly, it gives taut, smoky wines. In Bordeaux it is blended with Sémillon, both dry in Pessac-Léognan and sweet in Sauternes. Marlborough's explosive style, first made famous by Montana in 1980 and Cloudy Bay in 1985, created a whole national industry: Sauvignon Blanc now makes up roughly 85 percent of New Zealand's wine exports. Styria in Austria and Friuli make dense, mineral versions.
grapes.trivia: Robert Mondavi rebranded his oaked Sauvignon Blanc as 'Fumé Blanc' in 1968 because American drinkers found the original name unsellable; he never trademarked it, so anyone could copy it.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. No DNA study has identified them; VIVC lists no pedigree.
grapes.hectares: About 20,000 ha worldwide (2016, Anderson and Nelgen), down sharply from the 1950s; France has about 11,000 ha (VIVC 2009 figure 11,693 ha).
grapes.profile: The golden grape of Sauternes. Its thin skin welcomes Botrytis cinerea in the autumn mists rising from the Ciron and Garonne, and the shrivelled berries give Château d'Yquem its honey, apricot and saffron. Blended dry with Sauvignon Blanc, it adds weight and a waxy, lanolin texture. Its most surprising expression is in Australia's Hunter Valley: picked early at 10 to 11 percent alcohol, unoaked, the wines taste of lemon and grass when young and turn toasty and honeyed after ten years without ever seeing a barrel. In the early 1800s Sémillon covered more than 90 percent of South Africa's vineyards, where it was simply called Groendruif, the green grape.
grapes.trivia: Hunter Valley growers sold Sémillon for decades as 'Hunter River Riesling' until EU wine agreements forced the name change.

grapes.name: Muscadelle
grapes.parentage_note: DNA analysis shows Muscadelle is an offspring of Gouais Blanc with an unidentified second parent (Vouillamoz and Boursiquot; VIVC pedigree '? × Heunisch Weiss'). Despite the name it is not a Muscat.
grapes.hectares: Under 2,000 ha in France (1,713 ha in 2006, VIVC), plus a few hundred in Australia.
grapes.profile: The third grape of white Bordeaux and Sauternes, used in small doses for its floral, grapey perfume. It is prone to rot and easily over-cropped, so most Bordeaux growers have pulled it out. Its finest role is far from home: in Rutherglen, northeast Victoria, it makes the fortified wines once called Tokay and since 2010 sold as Topaque, aged for decades in hot tin sheds until they taste of tea leaves, butterscotch and malt. Monbazillac and Bergerac still use it in their sweet blends.
grapes.trivia: Australia agreed to phase out the name 'Tokay' in its 2008 wine agreement with the EU because Hungary owns the name Tokaj; Rutherglen makers coined 'Topaque' as the replacement.

grapes.name: Magdeleine Noire des Charentes

origin.place: Saint-Suliac, Brittany and the Charentes, France

grapes.parentage_note: Discovered in 1996 by Boursiquot's team in an abandoned garden at Saint-Suliac near Saint-Malo and later in the Charentes; named and shown by SSR markers to be the mother of Merlot and Malbec in Boursiquot et al., Vitis 48 (2009). VIVC also records a parent-offspring link to Abouriou.
grapes.hectares: Effectively zero: a few conservatory and garden vines.
grapes.profile: One of the great detective stories of grape genetics. Merlot's mother was unknown until researchers sampled an old vine on Mont Garrot above the Rance estuary in Brittany, a region with no wine trade to speak of. More vines turned up in the Charentes. Locally it was linked to Saint Mary Magdalene's feast on 22 July, because it ripened unusually early. The DNA showed it had mated with Cabernet Franc to produce Merlot and with Prunelard to produce Malbec, making it the grandmother of a good share of the world's red wine. It has no commercial plantings and is kept alive in collections, notably at the Domaine de Vassal.
grapes.trivia: Its name honours the Feast of Mary Magdalene (22 July), the date by which its grapes were said to be ripe.

grapes.name: Prunelard
grapes.parentage_note: Identified as Malbec's father by Boursiquot et al. (2009, Vitis) through microsatellite markers. VIVC also records a parent-offspring relationship with Dureza.
grapes.hectares: About 13 ha in France (2008, VIVC), revived by Gaillac growers such as Robert Plageoles.
grapes.profile: An old Gaillac variety saved from extinction by local growers, notably the Plageoles family, who replanted it in the 1990s. It makes deep-coloured, peppery red wine. Its fame comes from its children: DNA showed it to be the father of Malbec, and VIVC records a parent-offspring link with Dureza, the father of Syrah. That makes this obscure Tarn grape a node connecting two of the most important red families in France. In the glass it is dark and spicy with plum and black-pepper notes, rustic but lively, and a handful of Gaillac estates now bottle it alone to show where Malbec's paternal line came from.
grapes.trivia: Gaillac added Prunelard to its list of permitted varieties only in the 2010s, centuries after it was first grown there.

grapes.name: Gros Cabernet
grapes.parentage_note: A rare old variety identified in Boursiquot's 2009 work as a parent of Carmenère. VIVC gives its own pedigree as 'Txakoli × unknown', Txakoli being a Basque accession, which reinforces the Basque roots of the Cabernet family.
grapes.hectares: Collection vines only.
grapes.profile: A near-forgotten vine whose importance is entirely genealogical. Its DNA shows it to be a parent of Carmenère, and its own pedigree points back to a Basque vine catalogued as Txakoli. That gives the Cabernet family a coherent story: Basque grapes moving north along pilgrim and trade routes, crossing in Gironde vineyards, and producing the varieties that built Bordeaux. It is a reminder that the most famous grape families can rest on vines nobody would choose to drink, kept alive only because ampelographers once thought them worth saving.
grapes.trivia: It survives only in research collections, yet without it there would be no Chilean Carmenère industry.

grapes.name: Hondarrabi Beltza
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. VIVC records a parent-offspring relationship with Cabernet Franc; which is parent and which is offspring is not confirmed.
grapes.hectares: A few dozen hectares in the Basque Country.
grapes.profile: The red grape of Txakoli, used for light, tangy reds and the rosé called Txakoli Rosado. Small plantings around Getaria and Zarautz, sometimes on their own roots in sandy coastal soils, cling to green hills facing the Bay of Biscay. Its significance is far larger than its acreage: DNA links it to Cabernet Franc, supporting the idea that the Cabernet family was born on the Basque coast before moving to Bordeaux. Most Txakoli is bottled with a slight spritz and poured from a height in the Basque bars of San Sebastián and Bilbao, where the red and rosé versions are a local favourite.
grapes.trivia: The Basque word beltza means black; its white partner in Txakoli is Hondarrabi Zuri, 'white Hondarrabi'.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Pinot as '? × Savagnin', a parent-offspring relationship found in SSR studies (Regner 2000; Vouillamoz). The direction is not certain and some researchers consider Pinot the older of the two. Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Meunier are colour or chimera mutations of the same genotype.
grapes.hectares: 112,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017); France c. 32,000 ha, USA 25,000, Germany 12,000.
grapes.profile: The grape of the Côte d'Or and the most demanding of the noble reds. Its thin skins and tight bunches make it vulnerable to rot, and it mutates readily: Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Meunier are all the same genotype, and there are hundreds of clones. Over two millennia of propagation it became the hub of a vast family: crossed with the peasant grape Gouais Blanc, it fathered Chardonnay, Gamay, Aligoté and at least a dozen more. Grown on the limestone and marl of Burgundy, it shows red cherry, rose, earth and forest floor, and transmits differences between vineyards a few metres apart better than any other grape, which is the whole premise of Burgundy's climats. It is also a pillar of Champagne and the most planted red in Germany.
grapes.trivia: The Cistercian monks of Cîteaux are credited with selecting and mapping Pinot by vineyard, and the 1395 edict of Philip the Bold banning 'disloyal Gamay' was written to protect it.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris
grapes.parentage_note: A berry-colour mutation of Pinot: genetically the same variety, distinguished by a mutation affecting anthocyanin production in the skin's epidermal layer (VIVC: 'Pinot Noir mutation'; Vezzulli et al.).
grapes.hectares: About 54,000 ha (2016, Anderson and Nelgen); Italy's Pinot Grigio DOC delle Venezie (created 2017) alone covers more than 25,000 ha.
grapes.profile: A pink-grey skinned mutation of Pinot Noir that lives two lives. As Italian Pinot Grigio, picked early from high-yielding Veneto and Friuli vineyards, it became the world's best-selling light white in the 1990s and 2000s. As Alsace Pinot Gris, from low yields on volcanic, granitic and limestone grand crus, it is rich, smoky and spicy, often off-dry, and can be made as Vendanges Tardives or Sélection de Grains Nobles. Oregon adopted it in 1966 when David Lett planted it at The Eyrie Vineyards. Skin contact gives the coppery 'ramato' style traditional in Friuli.
grapes.trivia: In 1711 a merchant named Johann Seger Ruland found the grape growing in Speyer in the Palatinate and propagated it; Germans called it Ruländer for 250 years afterwards.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.parentage_note: A colour mutation of Pinot Gris and ultimately of Pinot Noir (VIVC: 'Pinot Noir mutation'). Recognised as distinct from Chardonnay only in the late 19th century.
grapes.hectares: Germany 5,540 ha in 2018, its stronghold; Italy, Austria and Alsace follow (DWI figures cited by Wikipedia).
grapes.profile: The white mutation of Pinot, gentle in aroma (apple, almond, a little cream) but with good texture and a talent for reflecting soil. In Alsace it is the workhorse of Crémant d'Alsace and often blended with Auxerrois. In Germany, as Weissburgunder, it has become one of the fashionable dry whites of Baden and the Pfalz, and the VDP allows it for Grosses Gewächs. Alto Adige growers make some of the most precise examples from high, cool sites. For centuries it was confused with Chardonnay, and many Italian 'Pinot Bianco' vineyards turned out to be Chardonnay when the two were separated.
grapes.trivia: In Alsace a wine labelled 'Pinot Blanc' may legally be made from Auxerrois, and many are.

grapes.name: Meunier

origin.place: Northern France (chimera of Pinot; Champagne shown)

grapes.parentage_note: A periclinal chimera of Pinot: the epidermal cell layer carries a mutation that makes the leaves hairy and floury, while the inner layer is ordinary Pinot (Boss and Thomas, Nature 2002). VIVC: 'Pinot Noir mutation'.
grapes.hectares: About 11,000 ha in France (VIVC 2009: 11,088 ha), almost all in Champagne where it covers about 30 percent of the vineyard; Germany c. 1,800 ha.
grapes.profile: Champagne's third grape, long dismissed as the filler behind Pinot Noir and Chardonnay but in fact the backbone of the Vallée de la Marne, where it buds late enough to dodge spring frost on the cold clay valley floors. It gives fruity, early-maturing base wine, which is why it suits non-vintage blends. A wave of growers, led by houses like Krug (always a strong user) and growers such as Jérôme Prévost and Laherte Frères, now bottle Meunier on its own. In Württemberg it is called Schwarzriesling and makes light reds. Its white, dusty leaf underside gave it the name 'miller'.
grapes.trivia: Scientists showed in 2002 that Meunier is a chimera: grow a plant from its inner cell layer alone and you get a vine indistinguishable from Pinot Noir.

grapes.name: Gouais Blanc

origin.place: Central and eastern Europe (probably Croatia or the western Balkans)

grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. Its prolific parenthood was revealed by Bowers, Meredith and colleagues at UC Davis (Science, 1999), who showed that 16 northeastern French varieties are full siblings from Pinot × Gouais Blanc. Later work by Boursiquot, Lacombe, Laucou and others (2009 to 2011) linked it to more than 80 varieties.
grapes.hectares: A few hectares in Switzerland and in collections; an old planting survives at Rutherglen, Victoria.
grapes.profile: The most important grape no one drinks. Medieval nobles banned it as a peasant variety, and Burgundy's dukes ordered it uprooted, yet because it grew everywhere, right beside the noble Pinot, it crossed with Pinot again and again. Its offspring include Chardonnay, Gamay, Aligoté and Melon, and in other crossings Riesling, Furmint and Blaufränkisch. Genetically it is a 'Hunnic' grape of eastern origin, valued for vigour and high yields of thin, acidic wine. A handful of Swiss growers in the Upper Valais still make it as Gwäss, and Chambers Rosewood in Rutherglen preserved old vines in Australia. Without it, the white wines of Burgundy, the Mosel and Tokaj would not exist.
grapes.trivia: Its French name comes from gou, an Old French term of contempt; Duke Philip the Bold's 1395 edict and later bans tried to wipe it out precisely because it was so common.

grapes.name: Chardonnay

origin.place: Burgundy, France (village of Chardonnay, Mâconnais, gives the name)

grapes.parentage_note: One of 16 siblings from Pinot × Gouais Blanc identified by John Bowers, Carole Meredith and colleagues at UC Davis with INRA Montpellier using 32 microsatellite markers (Science 285, 1999). Confirmed by markers in VIVC.
grapes.hectares: 210,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017); France c. 51,000 ha, USA 43,000, Australia 21,000, Italy 20,000.
grapes.profile: The world's most adaptable white grape and the most famous child of the Pinot by Gouais Blanc marriage. Chardonnay itself has a quiet aroma; what makes it great is how faithfully it reflects place and how well it absorbs winemaking. On the Kimmeridgian marl of Chablis it is lean, saline and steely; on the limestone slopes of Meursault and Puligny it is nutty and layered; in Champagne's chalk Côte des Blancs it makes the purest blanc de blancs. New World producers in the 1980s gave it new oak, malolactic fermentation and ripe tropical fruit, which created both a boom and a backlash ('ABC: anything but Chardonnay'). Today Margaret River, Sonoma Coast, Limarí and Tasmania make tense, mineral styles.
grapes.trivia: The Mâconnais village of Chardonnay gave the grape its name; in the Middle Ages the place was called Cardonacum, 'place of thistles'.

grapes.name: Gamay

origin.place: Burgundy, France (hamlet of Gamay near Saint-Aubin)

grapes.parentage_note: A full sibling of Chardonnay from Pinot × Gouais Blanc, shown by Bowers, Meredith et al. (Science, 1999). Confirmed by markers in VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 30,000 ha in France (VIVC 2009: 30,443 ha) and shrinking fast; Beaujolais itself has fallen to roughly 13,000 ha in the 2020s (Inter Beaujolais), from over 22,000 ha around 2000.
grapes.profile: Exiled from the Côte d'Or by Duke Philip the Bold in 1395, who called it a 'very bad and disloyal plant', Gamay found its home on the granite hills of Beaujolais. There it makes bright, juicy wines of raspberry, peony and pepper, often by whole-cluster or carbonic maceration, which preserves fruit and keeps tannin low. The ten crus, Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent above all, can age for a decade and drink like Burgundy. Beaujolais Nouveau, released on the third Thursday of November since 1985, made it famous and then made it a joke. A wave of natural winemakers led by Marcel Lapierre and the 'Gang of Four' restored its reputation from the 1980s on.
grapes.trivia: Philip the Bold's edict of 31 July 1395 ordering Gamay uprooted is one of the earliest pieces of wine-quality legislation in Europe.

grapes.name: Aligoté
grapes.parentage_note: Pinot × Gouais Blanc sibling of Chardonnay (Bowers, Meredith et al., Science 1999). Confirmed by markers in VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 35,000 ha worldwide (2016, Anderson and Nelgen); Moldova (15,790 ha in 2009) and Ukraine hold far more than France's c. 2,000 ha.
grapes.profile: Burgundy's other white grape, long consigned to sharp everyday wine and the Kir (crème de cassis plus Aligoté), but capable of much more. Its high acidity and citrus-and-hazelnut character shine in Bouzeron, promoted to its own village AOC in the late 1990s, and from old vines on the Côte d'Or tended by growers such as Domaine de Villaine and Domaine Ponsot. Surprisingly, most Aligoté grows in the former Soviet Union, where it was planted widely for its cold hardiness. A growers' association, Les Aligoteurs, campaigns to restore its prestige.
grapes.trivia: Canon Félix Kir, mayor of Dijon after 1945, popularised the blend of Aligoté and cassis that now bears his name to promote two struggling local products.

grapes.name: Melon de Bourgogne

origin.place: Burgundy, France; now the Pays Nantais

grapes.parentage_note: Pinot × Gouais Blanc sibling of Chardonnay (Bowers, Meredith et al., Science 1999). Confirmed by markers in VIVC.
grapes.hectares: 12,844 ha in France in 2006 (VIVC), shrinking to under 10,000 ha in the Pays Nantais by the 2020s.
grapes.profile: A Burgundian grape that made its name at the mouth of the Loire. After the brutal winter of 1709 killed most vines around Nantes, Dutch traders who bought wine there for distilling encouraged growers to replant with a hardy, early-ripening Burgundian variety, and Melon became Muscadet. Neutral on its own, it is transformed by ageing sur lie, on its fermentation lees through the winter, which adds texture and a faint yeasty prickle. Since 2011, when Clisson, Gorges and Le Pallet were approved, Muscadet has added crus communaux that age on lees for 18 months or more and reflect granite, gabbro and gneiss subsoils.
grapes.trivia: Oregon and Washington plantings sold as Pinot Blanc for decades turned out to be Melon de Bourgogne when tested in the 1980s.

grapes.name: Auxerrois
grapes.parentage_note: Pinot × Gouais Blanc sibling of Chardonnay (Bowers, Meredith et al., Science 1999). Not related to Malbec, which is also called Auxerrois in Cahors.
grapes.hectares: About 2,300 ha in France (VIVC 2008), mainly Alsace; also Luxembourg and Germany.
grapes.profile: A low-acid, softly fruity sibling of Chardonnay that does much of the work in wines sold as Alsace Pinot Blanc and Crémant d'Alsace. Its ripeness and gentle acidity suit cool, marginal climates, which is why it is common in Luxembourg's Moselle, Lorraine's Côtes de Toul and the Netherlands. In good hands, from old vines on clay-limestone, it gives honeyed, broad wines with a hint of spice. Because it is so close to Chardonnay genetically and in the glass, Alsace growers often use it as a softer counterpart to the sharper Pinot Blanc in their blends, and many bottles sold as Pinot Blanc are mostly Auxerrois.
grapes.trivia: The same name is used in Cahors for Malbec, a completely unrelated red grape.

grapes.name: Romorantin
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC gives Gouais Blanc × a Pinot form (Meunier or Pinot Teinturier), making it a Pinot × Gouais sibling of Chardonnay in the broad sense.
grapes.hectares: About 70 ha (VIVC 2008), almost all in Cour-Cheverny AOC.
grapes.profile: A survivor. Tradition says King Francis I ordered 80,000 vines brought from Burgundy to his château at Romorantin in 1519, and this grape kept the town's name. It now survives only around Cheverny, where Cour-Cheverny AOC (1993) requires it. Wines are taut, waxy and long-lived, tasting of quince, honey and lemon. Pre-phylloxera, own-rooted vines planted around 1850 still produce at Domaine Henry Marionnet, among the oldest productive vines in France. Its acidity is so high that young wines can seem austere, but cellar time rewards patience with wax, honey and a quince-paste richness that recalls old Chenin Blanc.
grapes.trivia: Henry Marionnet's 'Provignage' cuvée comes from Romorantin vines planted before phylloxera reached the Loire, propagated by layering rather than grafting.

grapes.name: Syrah

origin.place: Northern Rhône and Isère/Savoie border, France

grapes.parentage_note: Identified as Dureza (father, from the Ardèche) × Mondeuse Blanche (mother, from Savoie) by Carole Meredith's UC Davis lab with Jean-Michel Boursiquot and INRA Montpellier (Bowers et al., Vitis 2000; work announced 1998 to 1999). VIVC confirms by markers. A recent long-read genome study of Shiraz (Onetto et al.) suggests the relationship with Mondeuse Blanche may be more complex.
grapes.hectares: 190,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017); France c. 64,000 ha and Australia c. 40,000 ha, where Shiraz is the most planted grape.
grapes.profile: For centuries legend traced Syrah to Shiraz in Persia or to Syracuse; DNA ended both stories by showing it is a native of the northern Rhône, the child of two obscure local grapes. On the steep granite of Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie it gives black olive, violet, bacon fat, white pepper (from the compound rotundone) and a firm, savoury frame, sometimes lifted with a few percent of Viognier at Côte-Rôtie. James Busby took cuttings to Australia in 1832, and as Shiraz it became the country's flagship, from the dense, chocolatey Barossa reds to Penfolds Grange. It also anchors Southern Rhône and Languedoc blends with Grenache and Mourvèdre.
grapes.trivia: The 'Shiraz from Persia' story was so popular that some Australian producers still print it on back labels; the DNA says Isère and the Ardèche.

grapes.name: Dureza
grapes.parentage_note: Identified as Syrah's father by UC Davis and INRA Montpellier in 1998 (Bowers et al., Vitis 2000). Later work by Vouillamoz and Grando (2006) found that Dureza is a full sibling of Teroldego, and VIVC records a parent-offspring link with Prunelard.
grapes.hectares: Effectively extinct as a commercial vine (11 ha in the late 1970s, 1 ha by 1988).
grapes.profile: A dark, hard-skinned Ardèche grape whose name means 'hardness'. It nearly vanished in the 20th century, but DNA put it at the centre of the Rhône story: Dureza crossed with Mondeuse Blanche to produce Syrah, and it is a full sibling of Trentino's Teroldego. That sibling link means Syrah is, genetically, a nephew of Teroldego and that varieties moved across the Alps between France and Trentino long before records began. Its story shows how DNA can rescue a variety's reputation: a grape abandoned as rustic turned out to be the paternal ancestor of one of the most valuable reds in the world, and a handful of growers now replant it out of curiosity.
grapes.trivia: A single parcel of Dureza is preserved by a few Ardèche growers and in the Domaine de Vassal collection.

grapes.name: Mondeuse Blanche
grapes.parentage_note: Syrah's mother per Bowers et al. (Vitis 2000). VIVC also lists it as a parent of Mondeuse Noire (with Tressot), making Mondeuse Noire a half-sibling of Syrah, and records a parent-offspring relationship with Viognier.
grapes.hectares: About 5 ha (1999), used in Vin de Savoie and Bugey.
grapes.profile: A rare Savoie white with an outsized family tree. It is the mother of Syrah and a parent of Mondeuse Noire, and VIVC records a parent-offspring relationship with Viognier. That makes Viognier and Syrah, the classic Côte-Rôtie co-fermentation partners, close relatives, a neat genetic footnote to an old winemaking habit. The few wines made from it are delicate, floral and lightly honeyed. The DNA result transformed the way historians see the northern Rhône, because it showed that Syrah was born locally from Alpine and Ardèche grapes rather than imported from Persia or Sicily. A few Savoie growers have replanted it since.
grapes.trivia: Its synonym Dongine comes from a Savoyard dialect word; the grape was known locally long before anyone suspected it had fathered half of the northern Rhône.

grapes.name: Petite Sirah
grapes.parentage_note: Carole Meredith's lab at UC Davis showed in 1997 that Durif is Syrah × Peloursin, confirming the story of a chance seedling found around 1880 by François Durif in his Tullins nursery. VIVC confirms by markers. Many old California 'Petite Sirah' vineyards are field blends including Peloursin.
grapes.hectares: About 4,800 ha in California (2023 Grape Acreage Report, c. 11,900 acres), plus Australia, Israel and Mexico.
grapes.profile: A French nursery accident that found fame in California. François Durif propagated a mildew-resistant seedling around 1880, and it reached California within a few years. There it became 'Petite Sirah', a name that confused it with Syrah for a century. The tiny berries give black colour, tannin by the bucket and blueberry, black pepper and liquorice; old-vine examples from Napa, Lodi and Livermore are among the most age-worthy reds in the state. In Australia's Rutherglen, as Durif, it makes huge, dark reds.
grapes.trivia: California growers formed a lobby group in 2002 with the blunt name 'P.S. I Love You' to promote the variety.

grapes.name: Peloursin
grapes.parentage_note: Mother of Durif with Syrah (Meredith lab, 1997). Also a parent of Joubertin with Persan.
grapes.hectares: Negligible; scattered vines in old California field blends.
grapes.profile: An old Isère variety, almost lost in France, that survives mostly as a hidden component of century-old California Petite Sirah field blends. Carole Meredith's DNA work found it mixed into those vineyards and identified it as Durif's mother. Its interest is historical: it shows how 19th-century nursery practice in the Rhône Alps sent mixed cuttings around the world. A few curious growers now bottle it separately, producing dark, firm, peppery reds that show where some of Petite Sirah's structure came from, and the vine is a living record of how mixed nursery stock spread grapes around the world.
grapes.trivia: Several 'Petite Sirah' vineyards in Napa are part Peloursin, so drinkers have been tasting it for a century without knowing.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. UC Davis profiling in 2004 showed it closely related to Freisa and a genetic cousin of Nebbiolo; VIVC records a parent-offspring relationship with Mondeuse Blanche, which would make it a close relative of Syrah.
grapes.hectares: Roughly 15,000 ha worldwide by 2016 (Anderson and Nelgen), up from about 8 acres in the northern Rhône in 1965; France 4,395 ha in 2009 (VIVC).
grapes.profile: Viognier came close to extinction: in 1965 only about 8 acres survived in Condrieu and the tiny Château-Grillet monopole. Perfumed and low in acid, it gives apricot, peach, honeysuckle and a heady, oily texture, and on the granite terraces of Condrieu it can be thrilling. A craze among Californian Rhône Rangers and Languedoc growers in the 1980s and 1990s rescued it. At Côte-Rôtie up to 20 percent may be co-fermented with Syrah, which stabilises colour and adds a floral lift. In Australia, Yalumba in Eden Valley built its reputation partly on it.
grapes.trivia: Château-Grillet, an amphitheatre of terraces under 4 ha, has been a single-owner AOC since 1936, one of France's few monopole appellations.

grapes.name: Marsanne

origin.place: Northern Rhône, France (village of Marsanne, Drôme)

grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. Vouillamoz's DNA work shows a parent-offspring relationship with Roussanne.
grapes.hectares: About 1,300 to 1,800 ha in France (VIVC: 1,266 ha in 2006); Tahbilk in Victoria has the world's largest single planting, some vines dating from 1927.
grapes.profile: The main white grape of Hermitage, where it makes broad, almond-and-honeysuckle wines that close down in youth and re-emerge after a decade with notes of beeswax and quince. It is more vigorous and reliable than its partner Roussanne. Chapoutier's single-vineyard Ermitage whites from it are among the longest-lived whites in France. Tahbilk in Victoria, Australia, holds old plantings from 1927 and claims the largest single Marsanne vineyard in the world. In Switzerland's Valais it is called Ermitage.
grapes.trivia: In the Valais, Marsanne is sold as 'Ermitage', borrowing the name of the hill where it is most famous.

grapes.name: Roussanne
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown; parent-offspring relationship with Marsanne (Vouillamoz). Some California 'Roussanne' traced to Bonny Doon proved to be Viognier on DNA testing in the 1990s.
grapes.hectares: About 1,500 to 2,000 ha (VIVC: 1,352 ha in France, 2009).
grapes.profile: Named for the russet colour of its ripe berries, Roussanne is finer and more aromatic than Marsanne: herbal tea, pear and a hint of honey, with better acidity. It is prone to mildew and rot and irregular in yield, which explains its rarity. Château de Beaucastel's Châteauneuf-du-Pape Roussanne Vieilles Vignes made its modern reputation. In Savoie it grows as Bergeron in Chignin-Bergeron, on steep, stony scree slopes above the Isère. It is susceptible to powdery mildew and wind, and its yields vary wildly from year to year, which is why many growers who admire it still plant Marsanne. With age it gains notes of beeswax, roasted nuts and dried flowers.
grapes.trivia: Tablas Creek imported Beaucastel's Roussanne cuttings into Paso Robles, and some earlier California vines sold as Roussanne turned out to be Viognier.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. Most researchers favour an Aragonese origin based on genetic diversity and early documentation; Sardinian scholars argue for Sardinia (Cannonau). VIVC lists Spain. It is a parent of Alicante Bouschet (with Petit Bouschet) and Marselan (with Cabernet Sauvignon).
grapes.hectares: 163,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017); France 81,000 ha and Spain 62,000 ha hold 87 percent.
grapes.profile: A grape of heat and wind. Grenache thrives on poor, dry, stony ground, ripens to high sugar, and gives generous strawberry, raspberry, white pepper and garrigue flavours with modest colour and tannin. It is the backbone of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, the heart of Priorat's old bush vines on slate and of Sardinian Cannonau. For decades it was dismissed as bulk blending fodder in Spain and Australia, and much was pulled out; old-vine plantings in McLaren Vale, the Barossa, Gredos and Aragon now drive a revival of lighter, more transparent styles. It oxidises easily, which suits the sweet fortified Vins Doux Naturels of Banyuls and Maury.
grapes.trivia: Sardinian researchers claim Cannonau seeds found at Bronze Age Nuragic sites prove a Sardinian origin; most geneticists remain unconvinced.

grapes.name: Grenache Blanc
grapes.parentage_note: A berry-colour mutation of Grenache Noir (VIVC: 'Garnacha Tinta mutation').
grapes.hectares: About 7,000 ha (VIVC: France 4,976 ha in 2009, Spain 2,100 ha in 2008).
grapes.profile: The white mutation of Grenache, broad and full-bodied with green apple, fennel and a soft, glycerol texture. It is a pillar of white Châteauneuf-du-Pape and of the Roussillon, where it also goes into sweet fortified Rivesaltes. Catalonia's Terra Alta has made it its signature white, holding a large share of Spain's plantings. Its low acidity means blending partners such as Roussanne or Bourboulenc are often used to keep wines fresh. Old vines in the Roussillon's schist and the Terra Alta's limestone give the most concentrated examples, which age into nutty, honeyed wines. California's Rhône Rangers adopted it in the 1990s for blends and varietal bottlings.
grapes.trivia: Because it is a colour mutation, Grenache Blanc, Grenache Gris and Grenache Noir can sometimes be found as different-coloured bunches on the same old vine.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. VIVC lists its prime name as Monastrell and Spain as country of origin. The French name probably comes from Murviedro (Sagunto) and the Australian one from Mataró near Barcelona.
grapes.hectares: About 70,000 ha (VIVC: Spain 63,244 ha in 2008, France 9,363 ha in 2009).
grapes.profile: A grape that 'wants its face in the sun and its feet in the sea', as Provençal growers say. Mourvèdre needs heat and a long season to ripen its thick skins, and then gives gamey, meaty, leathery reds with blackberry and herbs. Bandol is its spiritual home: the AOC dates from 1941, its rules now require at least 50 percent Mourvèdre in red Bandol, and Lucien Peyraud of Domaine Tempier led the push to make it the region's signature. In Spain, as Monastrell, it covers Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante, much of it on its own roots in sandy soils that phylloxera could not penetrate. It was devastated by phylloxera in France because it grafted poorly onto early rootstocks.
grapes.trivia: Many Jumilla Monastrell vines are ungrafted because the region's limestone-rich, sandy soils slowed phylloxera, which arrived there only in 1989.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Carignan Noir as Castellana Blanca × unknown. Earlier DNA work (2006) found a parent-offspring relationship with Graciano.
grapes.hectares: About 50,000 ha in France (VIVC: 53,155 ha in 2009), down from 167,000 ha in 1988 when it was France's most planted grape.
grapes.profile: Once the workhorse of the Midi and of French Algeria, Carignan gave high yields of deeply coloured, tannic, acidic wine for the bulk trade. EU vine-pull schemes from the 1980s removed most of it. What survives is often very old bush vines on poor slopes, and those make some of the most characterful reds of Corbières, Priorat (as Samsó or Cariñena), Sardinia's Carignano del Sulcis and Chile's dry-farmed Maule, where the VIGNO association (2010) champions old-vine Carignan. Carbonic maceration is often used to soften its tannin.
grapes.trivia: In 1988 France had about 167,000 ha of Carignan, making it the country's most planted grape until Merlot overtook it.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. Father of Pinotage (with Pinot Noir), bred by Abraham Perold in 1925.
grapes.hectares: About 35,000 ha (2016, Anderson and Nelgen); France c. 20,000 ha, the rest across North Africa, Lebanon, South Africa and Chile.
grapes.profile: A heat-tolerant, generous grape with soft tannin and red-berry and rose-petal perfume, prized for rosé in Provence and the Languedoc. In the mid-20th century it was South Africa's most planted red, known as Hermitage, and Abraham Perold crossed it with Pinot Noir to create Pinotage. Lebanon's Château Musar uses it in its long-lived red blend. Old, dry-farmed bush vines in Chile's Itata Valley and South Africa's Swartland now make light, juicy reds that sell for serious prices.
grapes.trivia: Lodi's Bechthold Vineyard, planted in 1886, is often cited as the oldest Cinsault vineyard in the world.

grapes.name: Alicante Bouschet
grapes.parentage_note: A deliberate cross made by Henri Bouschet in 1866 (VIVC records 1855 for the family's breeding programme) of Petit Bouschet (itself Teinturier du Cher × Aramon, bred by his father Louis) and Grenache. A documented breeding record, confirmed by markers.
grapes.hectares: About 35,000 ha (VIVC: Spain 22,251 ha in 2008, France 5,680 ha, Portugal 2,203 ha).
grapes.profile: A teinturier, meaning its flesh as well as its skin is red, bred by the Bouschet family to deepen the colour of pale Aramon wines in the Languedoc. During American Prohibition it was the darling of home winemakers: its thick skins survived rail shipping east and a ton of grapes could be stretched with water and sugar. In Portugal's Alentejo it has become a respected variety for dark, structured reds, notably at Herdade do Mouchão, where it has been grown since the early 20th century.
grapes.trivia: During Prohibition, California growers shipped so much Alicante Bouschet east to home winemakers that acreage expanded while legal wine sales were zero.

grapes.name: Marselan

origin.place: Marseillan, Hérault, France (INRA Domaine de Vassal)

grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Paul Truel at INRA in 1961 (VIVC), released in 1990. A documented cross.
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 ha in France plus several thousand in China (2016 to 2020 estimates), growing.
grapes.profile: Paul Truel crossed Cabernet Sauvignon with Grenache in 1961 hoping for big berries and high yields; he got small berries and quality instead, so the grape sat unused until 1990. It combines Cabernet's structure with Grenache's warmth, resists mildew and grey rot, and tolerates heat. China adopted it eagerly after Domaine Sino-French planted it in Hebei in 2001, and it is now promoted as a Chinese signature grape. In 2021 Bordeaux approved it among six new climate-adaptation varieties for Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur.
grapes.trivia: It is named after Marseillan, the Hérault seaside village where INRA's Domaine de Vassal grape collection was then located.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC lists no pedigree).
grapes.hectares: About 1,800 ha in Uruguay (INAVI 2023) and 2,900 ha in France (VIVC 2009).
grapes.profile: One of the most tannic grapes in the world, as its name suggests. In Madiran, growers such as Alain Brumont tamed it in the 1980s, and the region pioneered micro-oxygenation in 1990 (Patrick Ducournau) to soften it. Basque immigrant Pascual Harriague planted it in Salto, Uruguay, in the 1870s, and it became Uruguay's national grape, giving plush, dark wines in the humid Atlantic climate. Its procyanidin content is among the highest of any red grape, a fact that earned it attention in studies on red wine and longevity.
grapes.trivia: In Uruguay the grape was long called Harriague after the Basque immigrant who planted it near Salto around 1870.

grapes.name: Petit Manseng
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Savagnin × unknown. Not the parent or offspring of Gros Manseng despite the name. CSIRO found in 2020 that Australia's 'Petit Manseng' imported in 1979 is actually Gros Manseng.
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 to 1,500 ha in France (VIVC: 1,019 ha in 2009).
grapes.profile: Tiny, thick-skinned berries that shrivel on the vine into November (passerillage) give the great sweet wines of Jurançon: tropical fruit, ginger and candied citrus balanced by fierce acidity. It does not need botrytis because the drying autumn foehn winds from the Pyrenees concentrate the sugar. Virginia has adopted it as a dry and off-dry white because its thick skins resist rot in humid summers. Dry Petit Manseng is gaining ground in Jurançon and in Uruguay too, and its sugar-to-acid balance lets producers make late-harvest wines with as much as 150 grams of residual sugar that still taste fresh.
grapes.trivia: Legend says the infant Henri IV was baptised in 1553 with a drop of Jurançon wine on his lips and a clove of garlic.

grapes.name: Gros Manseng
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown; VIVC lists no pedigree.
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 ha in France (VIVC: 2,834 ha in 2006), growing with Côtes de Gascogne IGP whites.
grapes.profile: Larger berries and higher yields than Petit Manseng make Gros Manseng the grape of dry Jurançon Sec and of many crisp, tropical Côtes de Gascogne whites. Its high natural acidity and aromatic thiols travel well, which has made it popular in Australia, where many vines sold as Petit Manseng proved on DNA testing in 2020 to be Gros Manseng. Its thick skins tolerate the damp Atlantic autumns of the Pyrenean foothills. Late-harvested, it also makes moelleux Jurançon, though the finest sweet wines rely on Petit Manseng. Its rise in Côtes de Gascogne helped turn a former brandy region into an exporter of fresh, aromatic whites, often blended with Colombard and Sauvignon Blanc.
grapes.trivia: CSIRO's 2020 DNA audit forced several Australian wineries to relabel their 'Petit Manseng' as Gros Manseng.

grapes.name: Colombard
grapes.parentage_note: Gouais Blanc × Chenin Blanc per Bowers, Meredith and colleagues (late 1990s); VIVC confirms by markers. A full sibling of Meslier Saint-François.
grapes.hectares: About 33,000 ha (2016): South Africa c. 12,000, France c. 8,000, California c. 7,000.
grapes.profile: A Charentes grape of high acidity, bred into the Cognac and Armagnac distilling tradition and later the base of Côtes de Gascogne's crisp, cheap whites. It found its biggest markets in California's Central Valley (as French Colombard, once the state's most planted white) and South Africa, where it is used for brandy and fresh whites. On its own it is fresh and fruity, with grapefruit and green apple. Its reputation for neutrality is unfair: grown for table wine in Gascony and the Western Cape, it can be fresh, zesty and aromatic, which is why it became one of the export success stories of Côtes de Gascogne IGP alongside Gros Manseng.
grapes.trivia: In 1980s California, French Colombard covered more acreage than Chardonnay, nearly all destined for jug wine.

grapes.name: Ugni Blanc
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown; VIVC records Italy as origin. A 2008 Italian study (Crespan et al.) showed a close relationship to Garganega, possibly parent-offspring.
grapes.hectares: 111,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017); France c. 82,000 ha (mostly for Cognac) and Italy c. 21,000 ha.
grapes.profile: One of the most planted whites in the world, and deliberately neutral. In Cognac its high acidity and low alcohol make it ideal for double distillation; nearly all of the region's 80,000-plus hectares grow it, having replaced Folle Blanche after phylloxera. In Italy, as Trebbiano Toscano, white grapes were once compulsory in Chianti, a rule widely blamed for dilute wines; Chianti Classico dropped the requirement in the 1990s and banned white grapes from 2006. It is thought to have reached France in the 14th century, possibly via the papal court at Avignon.
grapes.trivia: In Cognac the grape is often called 'Saint-Émilion des Charentes', a name with no link to the Bordeaux appellation.

grapes.name: Folle Blanche
grapes.parentage_note: An offspring of Gouais Blanc with an unidentified second parent (Bowers et al.). Mother of Baco Blanc and, via Baco 1, Baco Noir.
grapes.hectares: About 1,800 ha in France (2009).
grapes.profile: Before phylloxera, Folle Blanche was the great Cognac and Armagnac grape, giving delicate, floral brandy. It grafted poorly onto American rootstocks and rotted easily in tight bunches, so it was replaced by Ugni Blanc and, in Armagnac, partly by its own hybrid child Baco Blanc. It survives as Gros Plant du Pays Nantais, a bone-dry, sharp white for oysters, and in boutique Armagnacs. Its name means 'crazy white', said to describe its wild vigour. The grape's acidity is so high that Armagnac distillers still prize it for the most delicate eaux-de-vie, and a few houses, such as Domaine Tariquet, bottle single-variety Folle Blanche Armagnac. In Nantes, Gros Plant is the cheaper counterpart of Muscadet.
grapes.trivia: Gros Plant du Pays Nantais was promoted from VDQS to AOC only in 2011.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.parentage_note: A parent-offspring relationship with Savagnin was shown in 1999 (Regner) and confirmed by later SSR studies; VIVC: 'Savagnin × ?'. Chenin is a sibling of Sauvignon Blanc and Trousseau and a parent of Colombard and Meslier Saint-François.
grapes.hectares: About 35,000 ha (2016): South Africa c. 17,000 ha (SAWIS, the largest planting) and France c. 10,000 ha.
grapes.profile: The Loire's great white and perhaps the most versatile grape in wine: sparkling, bone dry, off-dry and lusciously sweet, all from the same vine. Its piercing acidity lets it age for decades, and its quince, honey, lanolin and chamomile notes gain depth with time. Vouvray and Montlouis sit on tuffeau limestone, Savennières on schist and volcanic rock, and the Layon's sweet wines depend on botrytis and shrivelling. South Africa has more Chenin than France, much of it from old bush vines in the Swartland that a new generation of growers turned into world-class dry whites from the 2000s.
grapes.trivia: Abbey records from Glanfeuil in Anjou mention the grape in 845, and Thomas Bohier, lord of Chenonceau, is credited with planting it in Touraine around 1520.

grapes.name: Savagnin

origin.place: Northeastern France or southern Germany (Jura shown; exact place debated)

grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. DNA studies (Regner 2000; Vouillamoz; Lacombe 2013) show Savagnin/Traminer in first-degree relationships with Pinot, Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Grüner Veltliner, Sylvaner, Verdejo, Godello, Trousseau, Petit Manseng and many others, making it one of the founder varieties of western European viticulture.
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 ha including Traminer forms (VIVC); about 500 to 600 ha in the Jura.
grapes.profile: An ancestral grape that sits at the centre of the European family tree, a parent or child of Pinot, Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Grüner Veltliner and Sylvaner. In the Jura it makes vin jaune: wine aged at least six years and three months under a film of flor-like yeast (the voile) in barrels that are never topped up, then bottled in the 62 cl clavelin. The result tastes of walnut, curry and green apple and can last a century. Topped-up (ouillé) versions are crisp and saline. Its aromatic pink mutation is Gewürztraminer; in Switzerland's Upper Valais it is Heida, grown at Visperterminen around 1,100 metres.
grapes.trivia: Australian growers who imported 'Albariño' in the 1990s discovered in 2008 that their vines were actually Savagnin.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer

origin.place: Tramin (Termeno), South Tyrol, Italy, by name; mutation of Savagnin Rose

grapes.parentage_note: An aromatic mutation of Savagnin Rose, itself a colour mutation of Savagnin Blanc (VIVC). The word 'Gewürz' (spice) was added in Germany in the 19th century to distinguish the musky clones.
grapes.hectares: About 14,000 ha (2016); Alsace c. 3,000 ha.
grapes.profile: The most recognisable nose in wine: lychee, rose petal, Turkish delight and ginger, from high levels of terpenes such as geraniol and cis-rose oxide. The skins are pink to light red, and the wines are deep gold, often low in acidity and high in alcohol. Alsace is its stronghold, with dry, off-dry and late-harvest (Vendanges Tardives, Sélection de Grains Nobles) styles from grand crus such as Kessler, Zinnkoepflé and Furstentum. The village of Tramin in Alto Adige gave the Traminer family its name and still grows it on steep slopes above the Adige.
grapes.trivia: Rose oxide, the compound that gives Gewürztraminer its lychee smell, is the same one that scents lychee fruit and Bulgarian roses.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.parentage_note: Ferdinand Regner (Klosterneuburg) showed in 1999 to 2000 that Gouais Blanc (Heunisch) is one parent; the other is a seedling of Traminer (Savagnin) crossed with a wild vine, so Riesling is a grandchild of Traminer. VIVC lists '? × Heunisch Weiss'. First recorded at Rüsselsheim in 1435.
grapes.hectares: About 64,000 ha worldwide (2016, Anderson and Nelgen); Germany 23,596 ha in 2015, 23 percent of its vineyard, and about 24,000 ha in the 2020s (DWI).
grapes.profile: For many professionals the greatest white grape. It holds acidity even when very ripe, ages for decades, and reflects soil with uncanny precision: smoky and slatey on the Mosel's Devonian slate, broader on the Rheingau's loess and quartzite, spicy on the Pfalz's sandstone, mineral and tense in the Wachau's gneiss. It can be bone dry (trocken, Grosses Gewächs), off-dry or sweet (Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese and Eiswein), and botrytis concentrates it without dulling it. With age it develops a petrol note from TDN (1,1,6-trimethyl-1,2-dihydronaphthalene), stronger in sunny climates such as Australia's Clare and Eden valleys.
grapes.trivia: The earliest written record is an invoice from the cellar of Count John IV of Katzenelnbogen at Rüsselsheim, dated 13 March 1435, for 'seczlinge riesslingen in die wingarten'.

grapes.name: Sylvaner
grapes.parentage_note: Traminer (Savagnin) × Österreichisch Weiss, identified by Ferdinand Regner and Erika Maul with SSR markers (2000s); VIVC confirms. Österreichisch Weiss is a Gouais Blanc offspring, making Sylvaner a grandchild of Gouais.
grapes.hectares: About 4,500 ha in Germany (2023, DWI), half in Rheinhessen; Franken c. 1,500 ha, about a quarter of its vineyard.
grapes.profile: Its name suggests Transylvania, but DNA shows Sylvaner is Austrian, a child of Traminer and a near-extinct Austrian white. In 1960s Germany it was the most planted grape, then lost ground to Müller-Thurgau and the Liebfraumilch slump. Franken saved its reputation: on the shell limestone (Muschelkalk) and Keuper of the Main valley, bottled in the flagon-shaped Bocksbeutel, it is earthy, herbal and taut. Alsace gave Zotzenberg grand cru status for Sylvaner in 2006, and Switzerland's Valais calls it Johannisberg.
grapes.trivia: The first documented Sylvaner planting in Germany was at Castell in Franken on 5 April 1659, an anniversary still celebrated there.

grapes.name: Chasselas
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. José Vouillamoz's DNA work (2009) points to an origin around Lake Geneva, refuting the old Egyptian or Levantine origin legends. VIVC records several offspring, including Muscat Ottonel.
grapes.hectares: About 4,000 ha in Switzerland (VIVC: 4,013 ha, 2009), its second most planted grape; Germany c. 1,100 ha.
grapes.profile: Switzerland's emblematic white. Delicate and low in acid, it soaks up the character of its site: chalky and smoky in the Dézaley grand cru, rounder in Valais as Fendant. The Lavaux terraces above Lake Geneva, built by Cistercian monks from the 12th century, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007. Elsewhere Chasselas is mostly a table grape. In Baden's Markgräflerland it is called Gutedel and makes easy, fresh wines. DNA work by José Vouillamoz traced its origin to the Lake Geneva area rather than the Middle East. Much Swiss Chasselas undergoes malolactic fermentation to soften its low acidity, and the best Dézaley and Calamin wines age for decades into honeyed, smoky whites.
grapes.trivia: Lavaux growers say the vines enjoy 'three suns': the sky, the reflection from Lake Geneva and the heat stored in the stone terrace walls.

grapes.name: Mondeuse Noire
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Mondeuse Blanche × Tressot, making Mondeuse Noire a half-sibling of Syrah through Mondeuse Blanche. DNA has shown it is unrelated to Refosco, despite a long-standing belief.
grapes.hectares: About 300 ha in France (2009).
grapes.profile: Savoie's red grape, a half-sibling of Syrah, with which it shares black pepper, violet and dark berries, carried by bright acidity and light body. The cru Arbin, on south-facing scree slopes of the Combe de Savoie, is its classic site. Growers such as Louis Magnin and Domaine des Ardoisières have shown it can age. Small plantings in Victoria, Australia, and Virginia show its appeal in cool, continental climates. It ripens late and needs warm, well-drained sites; on the limestone and marl scree of the Combe de Savoie it makes some of the most age-worthy reds of the Alps, gaining notes of game and dried violet after a decade.
grapes.trivia: For a century Mondeuse Noire was claimed to be the same as Friuli's Refosco; DNA profiling showed the two are unrelated.

grapes.name: Jacquère
grapes.parentage_note: Gouais Blanc × unknown (VIVC; Vouillamoz).
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 ha (2009), half of Savoie's vineyard.
grapes.profile: The everyday white of the Alps: low in alcohol, crisp, smelling of white flowers, pear and wet stone. It dominates the crus of Apremont and Abymes, planted on the rubble of a catastrophic landslide from Mont Granier in 1248 that buried villages and created a chaotic, stony terrain ideal for vines. It is the classic match for raclette and fondue. Its high yields once made it a symbol of ski-resort wine, but low-yield bottlings from Apremont's old vines show surprising depth, with almond, citrus and alpine-herb notes.
grapes.trivia: The Abymes vineyards literally grow on the 'abyss' of debris left by the 1248 collapse of Mont Granier, which killed thousands.

grapes.name: Trousseau
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Trousseau Noir as '? × Savagnin', a parent-offspring link found in 2000s SSR studies. It is a sibling of Chenin Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc through Savagnin. DNA profiling showed it is the same as Portugal's Bastardo and Galicia's Merenzao.
grapes.hectares: About 2,000 ha worldwide: Portugal c. 1,100 ha (as Bastardo), the Jura about 170 ha.
grapes.profile: The Jura's dark red, though it is still light by most standards: pale cherry colour, red fruit, pepper and a savoury, earthy edge. It thrives on the warmer gravelly sites around Arbois and Montigny-les-Arsures, often called the capital of Trousseau. Under the name Bastardo it was once a significant Port and Madeira grape; in Galicia it is Merenzao. California producers such as Arnot-Roberts have made it fashionable. Like other Jura grapes it is also used in vin jaune country for crémant and macvin, and its thick skins let it be picked later than Poulsard. Growers such as Stéphane Tissot and Jacques Puffeney (retired 2014) built international followings for Arbois Trousseau.
grapes.trivia: Montigny-les-Arsures, a village of a few hundred people near Arbois, calls itself the 'capital of Trousseau'.

grapes.name: Poulsard
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown; VIVC lists Poulsard Noir without pedigree.
grapes.hectares: About 300 ha (2009), almost all in the Jura.
grapes.profile: A thin-skinned, pale red grape that makes Jura reds so light they look like dark rosé, with redcurrant, rose and forest-floor flavours and very little tannin. Pupillin calls itself the world capital of Ploussard. It is a favourite of natural winemakers such as Pierre Overnoy and Jean-François Ganevat, whose low-sulphur wines made the Jura a cult region from the 2000s. The skins are so thin that a long maceration barely darkens the juice, which is why Jura reds often look like rosé. It is also used for Crémant du Jura and for vin de paille, the straw wine made from grapes dried for months before pressing.
grapes.trivia: Pupillin's road signs proclaim it the 'capitale mondiale du Ploussard'.

grapes.name: Fer
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown; DNA suggests links to the Basque varieties of the Cabernet family (Boursiquot).
grapes.profile: A Southwest French red known under a different name in almost every valley: Mansois in Marcillac, Braucol in Gaillac, Pinenc in Madiran. Its name, 'iron', refers to its hard wood. On the red iron-rich soils (the rougier) of Marcillac it gives peppery, blackcurrant-scented reds with a herbal, slightly rustic edge. Its tannins are grippy and its flavours of blackcurrant leaf and red pepper resemble Cabernet Franc, which fits DNA hints that link it to the Basque ancestors of the Cabernet family. Gaillac uses it in blends with Duras and Syrah.
grapes.trivia: Marcillac AOC requires at least 90 percent Mansois (Fer), one of the strictest varietal rules in France.

grapes.name: Négrette
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. The legend that Knights Hospitaller brought it from Cyprus is unsupported by DNA.
grapes.hectares: About 1,500 ha (2006), nearly all in Fronton.
grapes.profile: The grape of Fronton, the vineyard north of Toulouse, where it must make up at least half of red and rosé blends. It gives soft, violet-scented wines with liquorice and a distinctive floral lift, best drunk young. It is sensitive to mildew and rot and suited to the warm, dry terraces of the Tarn. California once grew it as 'Pinot Saint-George'. The grape is fragile in damp weather, so the dry Fronton terraces on the Tarn's old alluvial gravels and boulbènes suit it well. It has a small following in California, where it was misnamed Pinot Saint-George, and producers like Château Bellevue la Forêt have made it the face of Fronton.
grapes.trivia: A popular story holds that the Knights of St John brought it from Cyprus in the 12th century; DNA has found no Cypriot relatives.

grapes.name: Mauzac
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC lists no pedigree).
grapes.profile: A late-budding white with a distinctive smell of dried apple skin, and the base of Blanquette de Limoux and the ancestral sparkling method (méthode ancestrale), in which wine is bottled before the first fermentation finishes. Limoux claims that monks at the Abbey of Saint-Hilaire made sparkling wine this way in 1531, more than a century before Champagne's sparkling tradition was recorded. Mauzac has several colour forms (Mauzac Blanc, Mauzac Rose, Mauzac Noir), and Gaillac uses it for dry, sweet and sparkling wines, including the méthode gaillacoise, Gaillac's own version of the ancestral method.
grapes.trivia: The Saint-Hilaire claim rests on a 1531 document; historians debate whether the wine described was truly sparkling.

grapes.name: Piquepoul
grapes.parentage_note: Piquepoul Blanc is a colour mutation of Piquepoul Noir (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 1,500 ha (France), mostly for Picpoul de Pinet.
grapes.profile: Its name means 'lip-stinger', for its high acidity, unusual in the hot Languedoc. Grown on the shores of the Étang de Thau, Picpoul de Pinet became an AOC in 2013 and the default white with the lagoon's Bouzigues oysters. Its fresh lemon and saline character has made it an export success. It is one of the 13 permitted grapes of Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Piquepoul Noir and Piquepoul Gris also exist, and before phylloxera all three were widely planted across the Languedoc for blends and vermouth. The Thau lagoon tempers summer heat, helping the grape keep its freshness, and the AOC now covers about 1,500 hectares.
grapes.trivia: Picpoul de Pinet is usually sold in a tall green bottle embossed with the Languedoc cross and waves, called the Neptune bottle.

grapes.name: Clairette
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.profile: An old Mediterranean white with low acidity and a tendency to oxidise, which suits the Rhône's white blends but asks for careful handling. Its most distinctive role is in the Drôme, where Clairette de Die Tradition, blended with Muscat, is made by the ancestral method and keeps a fizzy, grapey sweetness. Clairette du Languedoc was one of France's first AOCs for white wine (1948). It is one of the oldest documented grapes of the Midi, and in Bellet near Nice it joins Rolle in mineral whites grown on poudingue conglomerate. Clairette Rosé and Clairette Blanche are colour variants of the same family.
grapes.trivia: Pliny the Elder praised a sparkling wine from the land of the Voconces around Die, often read as an ancestor of Clairette de Die.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. DNA typing confirmed that Vermentino, Pigato (Liguria), Favorita (Piedmont) and Rolle (Provence) are the same variety.
grapes.hectares: About 20,000 ha (2016): Italy and France, plus a growing Australian planting.
grapes.profile: The white of the Tyrrhenian coast: Sardinia, Corsica, Liguria, Tuscany and Provence. It loves sun and sea air, and gives lime, almond, bitter herbs and a saline finish. Vermentino di Gallura in northeast Sardinia, on decomposed granite, became the island's only DOCG in 1996. In Provence it is called Rolle and adds freshness to rosés and whites. Australian growers have embraced it as a heat-tolerant white. Its tolerance of drought and wind makes it a favourite for growers adapting to hotter summers, from Bolgheri to McLaren Vale, and Ligurian Pigato from the Riviera di Ponente is fuller and more herbal than the island versions.
grapes.trivia: In Piedmont's Roero the same grape goes by Favorita, a name said to come from its popularity as a table grape.

grapes.name: Sciaccarellu

origin.place: Tuscany, Italy (as Mammolo); Corsica's signature grape

grapes.parentage_note: DNA work by Vouillamoz and colleagues identified Corsica's Sciaccarellu as Tuscany's Mammolo (VIVC prime name Mammolo).
grapes.hectares: About 700 to 900 ha in Corsica.
grapes.profile: Corsica's most distinctive red. On the granite around Ajaccio and Sartène it gives pale, peppery reds and rosés with notes of myrrh, red berries and maquis herbs. Its name means 'crunchy' in Corsican, for the firm berries. In Tuscany, as Mammolo, it is a minor blending grape in Vino Nobile and Chianti, prized for violet perfume. Corsica's granite soils and sea breezes produce delicate reds that resemble Pinot Noir in weight. Producers such as Domaine Comte Abbatucci and Clos Capitoro have made it the calling card of the island's southwestern appellations.
grapes.trivia: The Italian name Mammolo comes from mammola, violet, while the Corsican name describes the snap of the berry.

grapes.name: Grolleau
grapes.parentage_note: Gouais Blanc × unknown (VIVC).
grapes.profile: The grape behind Rosé d'Anjou, a sweetish pink that was one of France's best-selling wines in the mid-20th century. Productive and low in alcohol, it was long scorned, but Loire natural-wine producers now make juicy, light reds from old Grolleau vines, often as vin de France. Grolleau Gris, a colour mutation, gives pale, crisp whites and rosés. In Anjou's sweetish rosé it is usually blended with Gamay and Cabernet Franc, and its high acidity and red-fruit freshness are prized by natural winemakers who make it into light, chillable reds sold as vin de France.
grapes.trivia: Its name probably comes from grolle, an old regional word for crow, for the black berries.

grapes.name: Pineau d'Aunis

origin.place: Saumur area, Loire Valley (Priory of Aunis)

grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. DNA in the early 2000s showed it is unrelated to Chenin Blanc or Pinot despite the name.
grapes.hectares: About 435 ha (2009), down from 1,741 ha in 1958.
grapes.profile: A pale red grape with a striking white-pepper and red-berry perfume, grown on the flinty tuffeau slopes of the Loir (a northern tributary of the Loire). The Coteaux du Vendômois makes a speciality of vin gris rosé from it. It was said to have been favoured by Henry III of England, a story now hard to verify. The wine is light in colour but strongly peppery, thanks to high levels of rotundone, the same compound that gives Syrah its white-pepper note. Growers in Jasnières and Coteaux du Loir have revived old plantings.
grapes.trivia: Its name refers to the Priory of Aunis near Saumur, where monks are said to have grown it in the Middle Ages.

grapes.name: Tibouren
grapes.parentage_note: Identical to Liguria's Rossese di Dolceacqua per DNA profiling (Schneider and colleagues).
grapes.hectares: About 450 ha in France (2009) and c. 270 ha in Italy as Rossese.
grapes.profile: A Provençal grape with an earthy, herbal character that makes some of the region's most distinctive rosés, notably Clos Cibonne's 'Tibouren Cuvée Spéciale'. Across the border in Liguria it is Rossese di Dolceacqua, a light red that Napoleon is said to have enjoyed. The grape is low-yielding and irregular, so many Provence growers replaced it with Grenache and Cinsault, but a few estates near Saint-Tropez and Toulon still value it for rosés with a distinct garrigue, earth and spice character that ages surprisingly well. Its Ligurian twin, Rossese, has its own DOC at Dolceacqua near the French border, where it is grown on steep terraces.
grapes.trivia: Clos Cibonne near Toulon still ages its Tibouren rosé under a thin film of yeast in old foudres, a technique more typical of sherry.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.parentage_note: José Vouillamoz and colleagues at San Michele all'Adige proposed Ciliegiolo × Calabrese di Montenuovo in 2004 (published 2007, Vitis). VIVC lists 'different propositions': its own data give Ciliegiolo as Sangiovese × Moscato Violetto, which would make Ciliegiolo a child rather than a parent, and the question remains disputed. Sangiovese is a parent of Nerello Mascalese, Gaglioppo, Frappato and several other southern grapes.
grapes.hectares: About 54,000 ha in Italy in 2015 (Anderson and Nelgen), Italy's most planted red; VIVC lists 69,746 ha in Italy (2000). Corsica grows c. 2,000 ha as Nielluccio.
grapes.profile: Italy's most planted red and the soul of Tuscany. Its name is often read as sanguis Jovis, 'blood of Jupiter'. Thin-skinned and late-ripening, it gives sour cherry, dried herbs, tea and leather, with high acidity and firm, dusty tannin. It is extremely sensitive to site and clone, which is why the Brunello clone of Montalcino, selected by Clemente Santi and his grandson Ferruccio Biondi-Santi in the 19th century, gives darker, longer-lived wines than the Chianti Classico hills. In the 1970s the Super Tuscans (Tignanello in 1971) broke DOC rules to blend it with Cabernet or age it in barriques; since 1996 Chianti Classico may be 100 percent Sangiovese. Corsica's Nielluccio is the same grape.
grapes.trivia: Brunello di Montalcino was the first Italian wine to be awarded DOCG status in 1980, sharing the honour with Vino Nobile di Montepulciano and Barolo.

grapes.name: Ciliegiolo
grapes.parentage_note: Proposed as a parent of Sangiovese by Vouillamoz et al. (2007). VIVC gives the reverse, Moscato Violetto × Sangiovese, so the direction of the link is disputed; either way the two are first-degree relatives.
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 ha in Italy (VIVC 2000: 3,078 ha), declining.
grapes.profile: A soft, cherry-scented Tuscan red (ciliegia means cherry) that was long used to round out Chianti. It is either a parent or a child of Sangiovese, depending on which DNA study you trust, which makes it a key piece of the Sangiovese puzzle. In the Maremma, growers such as Sassotondo near Pitigliano make juicy varietal versions from old vines planted on volcanic tufa. It ripens earlier than Sangiovese and has lower acidity, so it rounds out blends and makes generous, early-drinking wines that are best within a few years of the vintage.
grapes.trivia: Its synonym 'Aleatico di Spagna' reflects an old belief that pilgrims brought it back from Santiago de Compostela.

grapes.name: Calabrese di Montenuovo

origin.place: Monte Nuovo, Campi Flegrei, Campania, Italy

grapes.parentage_note: An almost extinct variety found in Campania and proposed in 2007 by Vouillamoz et al. as the second parent of Sangiovese. VIVC records it as Sangiovese × unknown, which would make it Sangiovese's child instead.
grapes.hectares: Collection vines only.
grapes.profile: A nearly extinct southern Italian vine, found near the volcanic Monte Nuovo west of Naples, whose name ties it to Calabria. It became famous when DNA suggested it was one parent of Sangiovese, implying that Tuscany's emblem might have southern roots. Later data in VIVC reverse the direction, making it Sangiovese's offspring. The controversy captures how DNA can tell us two grapes are parent and child but not always which is which, unless a third relative is available to settle it.
grapes.trivia: Monte Nuovo itself is one of Europe's youngest mountains, formed by a volcanic eruption in 1538.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. Schneider, Vouillamoz and colleagues (2004 to 2006) found first-degree relationships between Nebbiolo and Freisa, Vespolina, Nebbiolo Rosé, Bubbierasco, Neretto di Bairo and others; VIVC lists Freisa and Vespolina as its offspring. Nebbiolo Rosé, once considered a clone, is a distinct variety and a first-degree relative.
grapes.hectares: About 6,500 ha in Italy (2020s, Piedmont region and consorzi), more than 85 percent in Piedmont.
grapes.profile: The grape of Barolo and Barbaresco: pale garnet in colour, yet high in both acidity and tannin, with rose, tar, cherry, liquorice and dried herbs. It is the first variety to bud and the last to be picked, often under the autumn fogs (nebbia) that may give it its name. It is notoriously site-sensitive and almost never succeeds far from northern Italy, which is why Barolo's MGA map of 181 named vineyards (2010) matters so much: the sandstone and sand of Serralunga and Monforte give more power, the Tortonian marls of La Morra and Barolo more perfume. In Alto Piemonte's acidic volcanic and porphyry soils and on the terraces of Valtellina it makes lighter, more mineral wines.
grapes.trivia: A 1268 document from Rivoli records a 'nibiol' vine, and 1431 statutes in La Morra punished anyone who cut down a Nebbiolo vine with a fine, a hand amputation or hanging for repeat offenders.

grapes.name: Freisa
grapes.parentage_note: UC Davis and San Michele DNA profiling (Schneider et al. 2004; Vouillamoz) showed a parent-offspring relationship with Nebbiolo; VIVC records Freisa as Nebbiolo × unknown. Also closely related to Viognier.
grapes.hectares: About 1,400 ha (VIVC 2000: 1,453 ha).
grapes.profile: A child of Nebbiolo with its parent's rose-and-raspberry perfume and firm tannins, usually in a lighter, rustic frame. Traditionally it was made frizzante and slightly sweet for drinking with salami and bread in the Turin hills. Serious dry versions from Langhe producers such as G.D. Vajra and Brezza show it can age. Its relationship with Viognier is one of the odd links DNA revealed between Piedmont and the northern Rhône. Its tannins can be fierce, so growers who make it dry often give it long ageing in large casks, the way Barolo is traditionally made.
grapes.trivia: Freisa was one of the varieties Thomas Jefferson tasted in Turin in 1787; he described a red that was 'as astringent as Bordeaux and as brisk as Champagne'.

grapes.name: Barbera
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC lists Barbera Nera as unknown × Coccalona Nera. Earlier studies found it distant from other Piedmontese varieties, leading some to suggest an origin outside Piedmont.
grapes.hectares: About 21,000 ha in Italy (2015, Anderson and Nelgen); VIVC lists 28,337 ha in 2000.
grapes.profile: Piedmont's everyday red and its most planted, Barbera has high acidity, low tannin, deep colour and a sour-cherry, plum snap that makes it the region's food wine. It was long treated as the grape for sites too cool or too poor for Nebbiolo. In the 1980s Giacomo Bologna of Braida aged his Bricco dell'Uccellone in new barriques, and the softened, richer style turned Barbera into a premium wine. The top hills of Nizza (DOCG since 2014) south of Asti now show its range. Immigrants planted it widely in Argentina and California.
grapes.trivia: In 1985 Barbera became tragically famous when several producers adulterated wine with methanol, killing 23 people, a scandal that forced a reform of Italian wine law.

grapes.name: Dolcetto
