grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Dolcetto Bianco × Moissan, the latter a French variety, implying an exchange across the Alps. UC Davis showed that California's Charbono and France's Douce Noire are not Dolcetto.
grapes.hectares: About 6,000 ha (2015), declining as Langhe growers replant with Nebbiolo.
grapes.profile: The 'little sweet one' is not sweet: the name refers to the low acidity and soft fruit of its grapes. Dolcetto ripens early, which suited the higher, cooler hills of the Langhe where Nebbiolo would not ripen. Wines are deep purple, with black cherry, liquorice and a characteristic almond bitterness, best drunk young. Dogliani gained DOCG status in 2005 for its fuller, longer-lived wines. Rising land values in Barolo have pushed many growers to replace it with Nebbiolo. Its low acidity and early ripening make it a grape for drinking within a few years of the vintage.
grapes.trivia: In Liguria the same grape is called Ormeasco, after the hill town of Ormea, and a rosé version is called sciac-trà.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). Unrelated to Sangiovese, despite the name it shares with the Tuscan town that makes Vino Nobile from Sangiovese.
grapes.hectares: About 35,000 ha (2015), Italy's second most planted red; VIVC 29,828 ha in 2000.
grapes.profile: Abruzzo's grape, deep in colour with soft, ripe tannins, plum and black cherry, sometimes with a herbal edge. It gives cheap, generous reds and also some of Italy's longest-lived: Emidio Pepe and Valentini have aged their wines for decades. Its pale pink cerasuolo rosé, now its own DOC (Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo, 2010), is one of Italy's most distinctive rosés. Colline Teramane became a DOCG in 2003. In the Marche it anchors Rosso Conero and Conero DOCG. It needs warmth to ripen fully, which is why it rarely succeeds north of the Marche, and its generous yields made it a bulk-wine staple before quality producers reined it in.
grapes.trivia: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, from the Tuscan town, contains no Montepulciano grapes; the town and the grape share a name and nothing else.

grapes.name: Aglianico
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. DNA studies show little relation to Greek varieties, undermining the old belief that the name comes from 'Ellenico' (Hellenic).
grapes.hectares: About 9,000 ha in Italy (2015), mostly Campania and Basilicata.
grapes.profile: Southern Italy's great tannic red, sometimes called the Barolo of the south. Aglianico buds early and ripens very late, often into November in the hills of Irpinia, where Taurasi (DOCG 1993) is grown at 400 to 700 metres. On the slopes of Monte Vulture, an extinct volcano in Basilicata, it gives dark, smoky, mineral wines. Its high acidity and powerful tannin need years in bottle, rewarding patience with black cherry, tar, leather and dried herbs. Mastroberardino kept Taurasi alive through the mid-20th century.
grapes.trivia: Taurasi's ageing requirement is three years, including one in wood, and four for the Riserva, among the longest in southern Italy.

grapes.name: Nero d'Avola
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC prime name Calabrese). Its synonym Calabrese is now thought to derive from Calaulisi, a Sicilian dialect form ('grape from Avola'), not from Calabria.
grapes.hectares: About 15,000 ha in Sicily (2015), the island's most planted red.
grapes.profile: Sicily's flagship red. Once shipped north in tankers to beef up pale wines from Piedmont and France, it was bottled under its own name from the 1990s. Wines are dark, juicy and soft, with black cherry, plum and a hint of liquorice, fresher from the limestone of Noto and Pachino in the island's southeast tip. In Cerasuolo di Vittoria, Sicily's only DOCG (2005), it is blended with the perfumed Frappato. Producers such as Planeta, Donnafugata and Gulfi showed from the 1990s what single-vineyard versions from the southeast could do, and its heat tolerance has made it a candidate for warm regions abroad.
grapes.trivia: In the 1990s Nero d'Avola was the most frequently used 'improver' grape in Italian blends, often without appearing on any label.

grapes.name: Nerello Mascalese

origin.place: Mascali plain near Etna, Sicily, Italy

grapes.parentage_note: Sangiovese × Mantonico Bianco according to VIVC (marker data; Cipriani et al. 2010). It shares this parentage with Gaglioppo, making them full siblings.
grapes.profile: The red grape of Etna, now one of Italy's most sought-after. On the black volcanic soils of the north slope, at 400 to 1,000 metres, old bush vines (alberello), many ungrafted, give pale, translucent reds with red cherry, smoke, herbs and fine, firm tannin, often compared with Pinot Noir and Nebbiolo. A wave of outsiders from the early 2000s, including Andrea Franchetti (Passopisciaro), Frank Cornelissen and Marc de Grazia (Tenuta delle Terre Nere), brought world attention to the mountain's contrade, the named districts that now appear on labels. It is usually blended with a little Nerello Cappuccio.
grapes.trivia: DNA shows it is a child of Tuscany's Sangiovese and Calabria's Mantonico, a sign that southern Italian grapes were crossing with northern ones long before records.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.parentage_note: Primitivo and Zinfandel were shown to be identical by isozyme and DNA tests in the 1990s. Carole Meredith, with Ivan Pejić and Edi Maletić of the University of Zagreb, found the Croatian source vines, Crljenak Kaštelanski, at Kaštel Novi in 2001. Later work found 15th-century records under the name Tribidrag and confirmed Montenegro's Kratošija as the same variety. Parents unknown; it is a parent of Plavac Mali (with Dobričić).
grapes.hectares: About 18,000 ha in California (2023, c. 40,000 acres) and about 12,000 ha in Puglia as Primitivo.
grapes.profile: America's heritage grape turned out to be Croatian. Zinfandel arrived on the US East Coast from an Austrian imperial nursery around 1829 and reached California during the Gold Rush. By the 1880s it was the state's most planted red, and many 100-year-old, dry-farmed, head-trained vines still grow in Lodi, Sonoma and Amador. It ripens unevenly, so bunches can carry raisined and green berries together, which produces jammy, high-alcohol wines with bramble and pepper. In the 1970s Sutter Home's sweet White Zinfandel rosé created a mass market that saved many old vineyards from being uprooted.
grapes.trivia: The DNA hunt ended in December 2001 when Croatian researchers found nine old Crljenak Kaštelanski vines in a single vineyard at Kaštel Novi, near Split.

grapes.name: Plavac Mali
grapes.parentage_note: Crljenak Kaštelanski (Zinfandel) × Dobričić, shown by Pejić, Maletić and colleagues in 2005 to 2008. VIVC records the parent-offspring relationship with Primitivo. Plavac Mali is therefore Zinfandel's child, not its twin as once believed.
grapes.hectares: About 1,600 ha in Croatia (2020s estimates), the country's most important red.
grapes.profile: Croatia's great red, grown on the scorching south-facing coastal slopes of Pelješac. Dingač, recognised in 1961 as the first protected wine site in the former Yugoslavia, sits on near-vertical limestone and dolomite slopes above the Adriatic, where sun reflected off the sea and rock ripens the grapes to high sugar. Wines are dark, often above 15 percent alcohol, with dried fig, carob and pepper. Its parent Zinfandel gives it a family resemblance in jammy richness. Island versions from Hvar's south coast, such as Ivan Dolac and Sveta Nedjelja, are similarly sun-baked and powerful.
grapes.trivia: Until 2000s road tunnels were built, Dingač's grapes had to be carried over the hill by donkey; the cooperative still uses a donkey on its label.

grapes.name: Negroamaro
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records unknown × Maiolica. The name probably combines Latin niger and Greek mavro, both meaning black, rather than amaro (bitter).
grapes.hectares: About 11,000 ha (2015), mostly Salento; VIVC 16,760 ha in 2000.
grapes.profile: The grape of the Salento peninsula, Italy's heel, where flat limestone plains bake under sun and sea wind. It gives dark, earthy reds with black plum, tobacco and a bitter-almond finish, often softened with Malvasia Nera, and is the basis of Salice Salentino. It also makes one of Italy's historic rosés: Leone de Castris's Five Roses, first bottled in 1943, was the first Italian rosé bottled and sold commercially. Much Negroamaro once went north in bulk for blending. Its thick skins and resistance to drought suit Salento's scorching summers, and old bush vines (alberello) remain common.
grapes.trivia: Five Roses got its English name after American officers stationed in Puglia during the Second World War asked for it, according to the Leone de Castris family.

grapes.name: Corvina
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. Vantini et al. (2003) and later work showed it is the parent of Rondinella; it is genetically distinct from Corvinone, with which it was long confused.
grapes.hectares: About 7,500 ha in 2010, nearly all in the Veneto.
grapes.profile: The backbone of Valpolicella. Corvina's thick skins resist rot, which makes it ideal for appassimento, the drying of grapes on racks or in lofts (fruttai) for three to four months after harvest. Dried grapes lose up to 40 percent of their weight and become the dense, high-alcohol Amarone and sweet Recioto. Fresh, Corvina gives light, cherry-and-almond Valpolicella and Bardolino. Ripasso refermented on Amarone pomace sits in between. Its partner Rondinella is its own offspring. Its berries are naturally low in colour, which is why Valpolicella's light everyday wines look so pale next to Amarone.
grapes.trivia: Amarone was, in local legend, a Recioto that was forgotten in barrel and fermented dry; the word means 'great bitter one'.

grapes.name: Rondinella
grapes.parentage_note: Offspring of Corvina with an unknown second parent (Vantini et al. 2003; VIVC parent-offspring record).
grapes.profile: Valpolicella's second grape, a child of Corvina. It is valued more for reliability than flavour: it resists disease, yields well and dries well, so it is a steady partner in the appassimento lofts. On its own it is rarely bottled, but it adds colour and a herbal note to Valpolicella, Ripasso and Amarone blends. Regulations allow it up to 30 percent of the blend in most Valpolicella wines, and its thick skins make it one of the safest grapes to dry for months without rot.
grapes.trivia: The name is said to come from rondine, swallow, because birds love the ripe grapes.

grapes.name: Teroldego
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. Vouillamoz and Grando (2006, San Michele all'Adige) showed that Teroldego is a full sibling of Dureza and a parent of Lagrein (with Schiava Gentile) and of Marzemino, which makes it an uncle of Syrah.
grapes.hectares: About 700 ha (VIVC 2000: 690 ha).
grapes.profile: The 'prince of Trentino', grown almost exclusively on the Campo Rotaliano, a flat gravel plain where the Noce river meets the Adige, protected by limestone cliffs. It gives inky, juicy reds with black cherry, violet and a bitter-chocolate finish. Elisabetta Foradori's work with old clones and amphorae from the 1980s on raised it from co-op staple to a cult wine. Its DNA links run surprisingly far: sibling to the Ardèche's Dureza, parent of Lagrein and Marzemino, uncle of Syrah.
grapes.trivia: Teroldego Rotaliano was among Trentino's first DOCs, recognised in 1971, and the plain it grows on is one of the few great Italian vineyards on flat land.

grapes.name: Lagrein
grapes.parentage_note: Teroldego × Schiava Gentile per VIVC and Vouillamoz et al. (2006); a grandchild of the Dureza-Teroldego family, so a cousin of Syrah.
grapes.hectares: About 500 ha (2015).
grapes.profile: Alto Adige's dark red, at home on the warm alluvial soils of Gries, a suburb of Bolzano that funnels hot afternoon air up the Adige valley. It gives deep purple wines with black cherry, plum, violet and a slight bitterness, fresh acidity and moderate tannin. Its rosé form, Lagrein Kretzer, was once more common than the red. Cantina Bolzano and Muri-Gries abbey are reference producers. Its tannins can be rustic, so producers often age it in large casks or in barriques to round them off, and it ripens only in the warmest corners of the valley floor.
grapes.trivia: The Benedictine monks of Muri-Gries have grown Lagrein beside their monastery in Bolzano since the 19th century, and the abbey label is still a benchmark.

grapes.name: Schiava
grapes.parentage_note: Schiava is a group name for several distinct varieties; the most planted, Schiava Grossa, is the same as Germany's Trollinger (VIVC). Schiava Grossa is a parent of Kerner (with Riesling) and Madeleine Royale (with Pinot) according to VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 3,400 ha in Italy (1990) and about 2,000 ha as Trollinger in Württemberg.
grapes.profile: Once the most planted red in Alto Adige, Schiava makes pale, light reds with strawberry, almond and violet, low in tannin and best served cool. Santa Maddalena from the hills above Bolzano and Lago di Caldaro were among the most famous Italian wines in Austrian times. In Germany, as Trollinger, it is Württemberg's everyday red. As Black Hamburg, a famous vine of this variety planted in 1768 at Hampton Court Palace near London is still fruiting, one of the oldest and largest vines in the world.
grapes.trivia: The Great Vine at Hampton Court, planted by Capability Brown in 1768, is a Schiava Grossa and still produces several hundred kilograms of grapes a year.

grapes.name: Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. DNA shows a relationship with Marzemino and that it is distinct from Terrano/Teran, which VIVC records as an offspring of Refosco Nostrano. Unrelated to Mondeuse Noire.
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 to 1,200 ha in Italy (2015).
grapes.profile: The 'refosco with the red stalk' is Friuli's most important native red, giving dark, high-acid wines with blackberry, plum and a bitter-almond edge. It thrives on the gravelly Grave plain and the marl-and-sandstone ponca hills of Colli Orientali. Across the Slovenian border in Istria, related Refosk and Teran grow on red terra rossa, giving even sharper, iron-tinged wines. Its tannins and acidity make it a good match for the region's cured meats and game, and the best versions age for a decade. Several distinct Refosco varieties exist, of which dal Peduncolo Rosso is the most widely grown.
grapes.trivia: The Roman empress Livia was said to have attributed her long life to Pucinum wine from near Trieste, which some identify with the ancestors of Refosco.

grapes.name: Sagrantino
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 ha (2010), up from 351 ha in 2000.
grapes.profile: Possibly the most tannic grape in Italy, measured by polyphenol content. Grown almost only around Montefalco in Umbria, it was traditionally made as a sweet passito for Easter, which is why the name is often linked to sagra or sacristy. The dry version, DOCG since 1992, is dark and powerful, with blackberry, cinnamon and earth, and needs long ageing. Arnaldo Caprai's investment from the 1970s and his research with the University of Milan reshaped its image. Long ageing is required by law: at least 33 months for the DOCG, including 12 in wood, among the longest in Italy.
grapes.trivia: By the 1960s only a few hectares of Sagrantino survived; plantings grew almost threefold between 2000 and 2010.

grapes.name: Lambrusco
grapes.parentage_note: Lambrusco is a family of at least a dozen distinct varieties (Salamino, Sorbara, Grasparossa, Maestri, Marani and others), not one grape. VIVC records Lambrusco Grasparossa as Cornacchia × unknown. DNA studies by Boccacci and others show several descend from local wild vines.
grapes.hectares: About 10,000 ha across the varieties (2015).
grapes.profile: The sparkling red of Emilia, made for cutting through the region's mortadella, salami and Parmigiano. The family ranges from pale, tart Sorbara with its violet perfume to dark, tannic Grasparossa from the Castelvetro hills. Most is made by the Charmat (tank) method, but traditional rifermentation in bottle (metodo ancestrale) has made a comeback. Its 1970s export success as sweet, cheap 'Riunite on ice' gave it a lasting bad reputation that dry, artisan bottlings are reversing. Its high acidity and low alcohol, usually 10.5 to 11.5 percent, are designed for the rich, fatty food of Modena and Reggio Emilia, where it is poured slightly chilled.
grapes.trivia: Cato and Pliny wrote of a vitis labrusca, a wild vine growing at field edges; the name Lambrusco descends from it.

grapes.name: Frappato
grapes.parentage_note: Sangiovese × unknown, according to VIVC and an Italian 2008 DNA study showing first-degree links between Sangiovese and ten southern varieties.
grapes.hectares: About 800 ha (VIVC 2000: 785 ha).
grapes.profile: A pale, fragrant Sicilian red with strawberry, pomegranate and floral notes, often compared with Beaujolais. It grows on the red sandy soils over limestone around Vittoria and is blended with Nero d'Avola in Cerasuolo di Vittoria, Sicily's first and only DOCG (2005). Producers such as Arianna Occhipinti and COS made varietal Frappato a natural-wine favourite from the 2000s. Its low tannin and bright red fruit make it one of the few Italian reds commonly served chilled. Its paleness and perfume make it a good partner for Nero d'Avola's darker fruit, which is exactly what the Cerasuolo blend does.
grapes.trivia: COS, founded in 1980 by three friends whose initials form its name, revived ageing in buried clay amphorae for Frappato and Nero d'Avola.

grapes.name: Gaglioppo
grapes.parentage_note: Sangiovese × Mantonico Bianco per VIVC, the same parentage as Nerello Mascalese, making them full siblings. Earlier claims of Greek origin are not supported by DNA.
grapes.hectares: About 3,500 ha (VIVC 2000: 3,703 ha).
grapes.profile: Calabria's main red grape, especially around Cirò on the Ionian coast, where it makes pale but tannic reds with red cherry, dried herbs and earth. Local tradition links Cirò to Krimisa, a wine said to have been given to Olympic victors in ancient Greece, though the grape itself is native. A new generation, the 'Cirò Revolution' growers, now make fresh, unoaked versions that have revived interest. It is drought-tolerant and resistant to heat, ideal for Calabria's arid coastal hills. Cirò Rosso must contain at least 80 percent Gaglioppo, and the best come from old bush vines close to the sea.
grapes.trivia: As a full sibling of Nerello Mascalese, Gaglioppo shares the pale colour and fine tannin of Etna's famous red.

grapes.name: Garganega
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. Crespan et al. (2008) showed Garganega has first-degree relationships with at least eight Italian varieties, including Catarratto, Albana, Malvasia di Candia and Trebbiano Toscano. It is identical to Sicily's Grecanico Dorato.
grapes.profile: The grape of Soave, and a hub of Italian white-grape genetics: DNA links it to Catarratto, Albana, Trebbiano Toscano and more, so it may be one of the founders of the peninsula's white varieties. In the hills of Soave Classico, on black volcanic basalt (east) and limestone (west), low-yielding pergola-trained vines give almond, white flowers and citrus with a fine, chalky texture and real ageing potential. Pieropan and Anselmi led the quality revolution in the 1970s and 1980s. Dried grapes make sweet Recioto di Soave, Italy's first DOCG for a white sweet wine (1998).
grapes.trivia: Soave Classico's 33 named crus (UGA) were mapped in 2019, and the Soave terraces were recognised by the FAO as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System in 2018.

grapes.name: Verdicchio
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. DNA studies identified it with Trebbiano di Soave and Lugana's Turbiana (VIVC lists Turbiana and Trebbiano di Soave as Verdicchio Bianco).
grapes.hectares: About 3,500 ha in Marche plus the Lugana plantings (VIVC 2000: 3,561 ha).
grapes.profile: Marche's great white. Its name refers to the green tinge of its wines. In the hills of the Castelli di Jesi and the higher, landlocked Matelica valley, it gives tense, almond-scented whites that age remarkably, gaining honey and anise. For decades it was sold in a fish-shaped amphora bottle, designed in 1953 for Fazi Battaglia, which made it famous and then cheap. Lugana on the southern shore of Lake Garda grows the same grape as Turbiana on white clay.
grapes.trivia: The amphora bottle created by Antonio Maiocchi for Fazi Battaglia in 1953 became one of the best-known wine bottles in Italy.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 1,500 to 2,000 ha (2015), increasing.
grapes.profile: One of southern Italy's finest whites, revived in Irpinia by Mastroberardino in the mid-20th century when it had almost disappeared. At 350 to 600 metres around Lapio and Avellino it gives waxy, nutty wines with pear, hazelnut, honey and a smoky mineral edge that improve for a decade. Fiano di Avellino became a DOCG in 2003. Its tolerance of heat has made it popular in Australia's McLaren Vale and Riverland. Its thick skins and resistance to disease make it reliable in damp autumns, and producers such as Ciro Picariello and Villa Diamante show that it can age for 15 years or more.
grapes.trivia: Romans called a wine from Irpinia 'Vitis apiana' because bees (apis) loved the sweet grapes; Fiano is often linked to that name.

grapes.name: Greco
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. DNA profiling shows that Campania's Greco is identical to Asprinio Bianco and distinct from Calabria's Greco Bianco; the Greek origin implied by the name is not supported.
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 ha in Campania (2006).
grapes.profile: The grape of Greco di Tufo (DOCG 2003), grown on sulphur-rich volcanic and clay soils around the village of Tufo, where sulphur mines operated until the 1980s. It gives firm, mineral whites with peach, almond and a bitter, flinty finish, more structured than Fiano. As Asprinio it is trained up poplar trees to 15 metres in the alberata aversana system north of Naples, one of the most spectacular vine-training methods in Europe. Its acidity is high, so some producers age it on lees or in old wood to round it out. The wines can age for a decade.
grapes.trivia: Asprinio vines on tall living trees near Aversa are picked by workers on ladders up to 15 metres high.

grapes.name: Falanghina
grapes.parentage_note: Two distinct varieties share the name: Falanghina Flegrea and Falanghina Beneventana (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 ha across both varieties (2015), growing.
grapes.profile: A fresh, citrusy Campanian white that often gets linked to the ancient Falernian wine, though no one can prove the connection. Falanghina Flegrea grows on the sandy volcanic soils of the Campi Flegrei west of Naples, many vines ungrafted because phylloxera cannot survive in sand. Falanghina Beneventana, a separate variety, dominates the Sannio hills and the large Falanghina del Sannio DOC (2011). Wines are bright, with lemon, pear and a saline edge. Its popularity in Italian restaurants abroad helped make it one of the best-known southern white grape names of the 2010s.
grapes.trivia: The name may come from falanga, the wooden stakes that supported the vines, a Latin word borrowed from Greek phalanx.

grapes.name: Arneis
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). Unrelated to Nebbiolo despite the synonym Nebbiolo Bianco.
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 ha (2020s), up from a few hectares in the 1960s.
grapes.profile: Saved from near-extinction in the 1960s and 1970s by Alfredo Currado of Vietti and Bruno Giacosa, Arneis is the white of the Roero, the sandy hills on the left bank of the Tanaro across from the Langhe. It gives soft, pear-and-almond scented whites with a hint of camomile. It was traditionally planted among Nebbiolo rows to attract birds and wasps away from the reds, and added to soften Nebbiolo. Roero Arneis became a DOCG in 2004. Roero's soft, sandy soils give it its delicate, early-drinking style.
grapes.trivia: In Piedmontese dialect arneis means 'little rascal', a reference to the vine's difficult, unpredictable nature.

grapes.name: Cortese
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 ha (VIVC 2000: 3,135 ha).
grapes.profile: The grape of Gavi, Piedmont's best-known white, grown in hills close to Liguria where sea air cools the vineyards. It gives crisp, lime-and-green-apple whites with a gentle bitterness. Gavi became fashionable in Genoa's fish restaurants in the 1960s and 1970s and was promoted to DOCG in 1998. The best come from the red clay and white marl around Gavi and Rovereto, sometimes aged on lees. Its delicate aroma and crisp acidity make it a match for Ligurian seafood, which is why Gavi sold mostly in Genoa until export success in the 1980s. It is also grown in Lombardy's Oltrepò Pavese and in the Colli Tortonesi.
grapes.trivia: La Scolca's 'Gavi dei Gavi' with its black label made Gavi a luxury white in Italy in the 1970s and 1980s.

grapes.name: Glera

origin.place: Prosecco, near Trieste, Italy and Slovenian Karst

grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Vulpea × unknown. The grape was renamed Glera in 2009, when Italian law made 'Prosecco' a geographical name tied to the village of Prosecco near Trieste.
grapes.hectares: About 40,000 ha in the Prosecco DOC and DOCG zones (2023, consortia), up from c. 8,000 ha in 2000.
grapes.profile: The grape behind the fastest-growing sparkling wine in the world. Glera has thin skins, high yields and delicate pear, apple and white-flower aromas that are best preserved by the tank (Charmat-Martinotti) method. In 2009 Italy renamed the grape Glera and created a huge Prosecco DOC across Veneto and Friuli, so that growers in Australia or Brazil could no longer sell 'Prosecco' made from it. The steep hills of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, UNESCO World Heritage since 2019, make the finest, with the 107 ha Cartizze hill at the top.
grapes.trivia: The village of Prosecco, which gave its name to the wine, sits in the province of Trieste, well outside the historic Conegliano Valdobbiadene heartland.

grapes.name: Friulano
grapes.parentage_note: Identical to Sauvignonasse, a southwest French variety, per DNA profiling (VIVC). It is not related to Hungary's Tokaji grapes, and a 1993 EU-Hungary agreement required Italy to stop using 'Tocai' by 2007.
grapes.hectares: About 4,700 ha in Italy (VIVC 2000), plus large Chilean plantings once sold as Sauvignon Blanc.
grapes.profile: Friuli's emblematic white, long known as Tocai Friulano until the EU, defending Hungary's Tokaj, forced Italy to drop 'Tocai' from 2008. It gives round, almond-and-pear whites with a bitter, herbal finish, perfect with prosciutto di San Daniele. In the ponca (marl and sandstone) hills of Collio and Colli Orientali, Mario Schiopetto pioneered modern Friulian whites with it in the 1960s. Much of Chile's 'Sauvignon Blanc' turned out to be this grape, sold as Sauvignon Vert. Its signature bitter-almond finish distinguishes it from other Friulian whites.
grapes.trivia: Slovenian producers across the border invented the name 'Jakot', which is Tokaj spelled backwards, as a protest.

grapes.name: Ribolla Gialla
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records unknown × Gouais Blanc. DNA studies in 2007 and 2008 showed no relation to the Greek Robola, disproving the long-held Ionian origin story.
grapes.hectares: About 400 to 500 ha in Italy (2020s) plus Slovenian Brda.
grapes.profile: An ancient white of the hills straddling the Italian-Slovenian border, documented in Friuli since the 13th century. Fresh, it makes lean, lemony whites and sparkling wines. Its thick skins made it the centrepiece of the orange-wine revival: in Oslavia, Josko Gravner and Stanko Radikon began macerating it on skins for weeks or months in the late 1990s, Gravner in Georgian qvevri from 2001, producing amber, tannic, honeyed wines that inspired a global movement. It is also widely grown in Slovenia's Goriška Brda as Rebula, where growers such as Movia and Klinec make both fresh and skin-macerated styles.
grapes.trivia: The Oslavia producers founded an association in 2010 dedicated to skin-macerated Ribolla, sometimes called the capital of orange wine.

grapes.name: Carricante
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Strinto Porcino × Visparola, both obscure Sicilian varieties.
grapes.hectares: About 300 ha (2010s), rising with Etna's popularity.
grapes.profile: Etna's great white, grown highest on the mountain's cooler east side around Milo, where Etna Bianco Superiore requires at least 80 percent Carricante. Its piercing acidity and lemon, aniseed and salty flavours develop petrol-like notes with age that invite comparisons with Riesling. Benanti's Pietramarina, first made in 1991, proved its ageing potential. Malolactic fermentation is often blocked to keep it taut. Its late ripening on the cool east slope, often into October, and its tendency to high yields mean careful vineyard work matters. It is often blended with a little Catarratto or Minnella in Etna Bianco, and the best wines age for 15 years or more.
grapes.trivia: The name comes from caricare, to load, a nod to the vine's generous yields.

grapes.name: Catarratto
grapes.parentage_note: Garganega × Mantonico Bianco according to VIVC and Crespan et al. (2008). The Comune, Lucido and Extra Lucido forms are the same variety.
grapes.hectares: About 30,000 ha (2015), Sicily's most planted grape and Italy's second most planted white; VIVC 43,246 ha in 2000.
grapes.profile: Sicily's workhorse white, long distilled or shipped in bulk, now increasingly bottled as fresh, lemony varietal wine. It is a child of the Veneto's Garganega and Calabria's Mantonico, more evidence of grapes crossing the length of Italy. It is a parent of Grillo with Muscat of Alexandria. Alcamo DOC in the northwest is its traditional heartland, and it contributes to Marsala and to Etna Bianco blends. Its lucido form has shiny, less waxy berries and gives more aromatic wine, and growers in the Alcamo and Monreale hills now make fresh, mineral bottlings that show it is far more than a bulk grape.
grapes.trivia: Catarratto covered about a third of Sicily's vineyard as recently as the 1990s.

grapes.name: Grillo
grapes.parentage_note: Catarratto × Muscat of Alexandria per VIVC; consistent with records that Antonino Mendola crossed them at Favara in 1869 or 1874.
grapes.hectares: About 8,000 ha (2020s), rising fast.
grapes.profile: Likely bred in 1874 by the Sicilian agronomist Baron Antonino Mendola, Grillo became the finest base for Marsala after phylloxera: high in sugar, it gave the extra alcohol and body the fortified wine needed. As Marsala declined, growers turned it into a fresh, citrusy, lightly herbal dry white, one of Sicily's export successes since the 2000s. It tolerates heat and drought, ripens to high sugar while keeping decent acidity, and thrives on the sandy soils around Marsala and Trapani. Varietal Grillo shows lemon, green herbs and a salty finish, with a little tropical fruit when picked ripe.
grapes.trivia: Mendola corresponded with Charles Darwin's contemporaries in ampelography and kept a collection of about 4,000 grape varieties at Favara.

grapes.name: Vernaccia di San Gimignano
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. 'Vernaccia' is a name used for several unrelated Italian varieties; DNA shows this one is distinct.
grapes.hectares: About 700 to 800 ha (VIVC 2000: 784 ha).
grapes.profile: The white wine of the towered hill town of San Gimignano, documented there since 1276 and mentioned by Dante, who placed Pope Martin IV in Purgatory for overindulging in eels and Vernaccia. It became Italy's first DOC in 1966 and a DOCG in 1993. On sandy, fossil-rich soils of marine origin, it gives firm whites with almond, citrus and a bitter, saline finish. Its ripe golden grapes were once traded across medieval Europe, and the wine appears in Boccaccio's Decameron. Today producers such as Montenidoli, Panizzi and Il Colombaio di Santa Chiara make long-lived versions, and a Riserva requires 11 months of ageing.
grapes.trivia: Vernaccia di San Gimignano was the first wine to receive DOC status when the system began in 1966.

grapes.name: Timorasso
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 300 ha (2020s), up from 20 ha in 2000.
grapes.profile: A Piedmontese white that nearly vanished after phylloxera and was rescued in 1987 by Walter Massa in the Colli Tortonesi. Its thick skins and high extract give powerful, mineral wines with honey, citrus and a petrol note reminiscent of Riesling, built to age. Producers market it as Derthona, the Roman name for Tortona. Even Barolo houses such as Vietti and Borgogno have bought in. Producers usually hold it back for a year or more before release because young wines can seem closed. Its high natural alcohol, often above 14 percent, is balanced by firm acidity, and growers say it is the white that ages most like a red.
grapes.trivia: Walter Massa's first bottling in 1987 was a deliberate act of rescue; by 2000 only about 20 ha remained.

grapes.name: Pecorino
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 1,500 ha in Abruzzo and Marche (2020s), up from 87 ha in 2000.
grapes.profile: A white from the mountain pastures of the central Apennines, its name probably linked to sheep (pecora) that grazed the vineyards or ate the grapes. Rediscovered in the 1980s by Guido Cocci Grifoni, who found old vines near Arquata del Tronto, it gives fresh, high-acid whites with citrus, sage and a saline finish. Offida Pecorino became a DOCG in 2011. Its early ripening suits high, cool Apennine sites, where yields are naturally low. The best bottlings from Offida and from Abruzzo's Colline Pescaresi and Teramane combine richness with acidity and age for several years.
grapes.trivia: In 2000 there were just 87 ha planted in Italy; Abruzzo alone now has well over 1,000 ha.

grapes.name: Nero di Troia
grapes.parentage_note: Bombino Bianco × Bouteillan Noir per VIVC. The legend of Diomedes carrying it from Troy is folklore; the name comes from the town of Troia in Puglia.
regions: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva
grapes.profile: Northern Puglia's great red, dark and tannic with violet, black cherry and spice, often compared to a southern Nebbiolo in structure. It is the key grape of Castel del Monte, below the octagonal castle of Frederick II, where a Nero di Troia Riserva DOCG was created in 2011. Its late ripening and firm tannins make it age-worthy. Its tannins are tough when young, so it is often blended with Montepulciano or Aglianico, and growers such as Rivera and Torrevento have championed varietal bottlings. A small-berried form, Nero di Troia a acino piccolo, is considered the finest.
grapes.trivia: Local legend claims the Greek hero Diomedes brought the vine from Troy after the Trojan War; DNA says one parent was Bombino Bianco, a local white.

grapes.name: Piedirosso
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Tintora × unknown.
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 ha (VIVC 2000: 1,013 ha).
grapes.profile: Naples' everyday red, named 'red foot' (and per'e palummo, pigeon's foot, in dialect) for its red stems, which look like a pigeon's legs. It grows on the volcanic soils of Vesuvius and the Campi Flegrei, often ungrafted on sand, and gives light, juicy reds with red cherry, herbs and a smoky, volcanic edge. It is part of Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio. Its fragile skins and low yields make it hard to grow, so it often appears in blends with Aglianico. On Ischia, where it is called Per'e Palummo, it grows on volcanic terraces above the sea and makes light, perfumed reds.
grapes.trivia: Lacryma Christi takes its name from a legend that Christ wept over the Bay of Naples, and vines sprang up where his tears fell.

grapes.name: Marzemino
grapes.parentage_note: A parent-offspring relationship with Teroldego and with Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso was found at San Michele all'Adige (Grando and Vouillamoz); Teroldego is usually considered the parent.
grapes.hectares: About 300 ha (VIVC 2000: 268 ha).
grapes.profile: A soft, violet-scented red of the Vallagarina in southern Trentino, best around Isera on basalt-rich soils. It gives fruity, slightly bitter reds with plum and violet, meant for drinking young. Its fame is literary: in Mozart's Don Giovanni (1787), the Don calls for 'eccellente marzemino' at his last supper. It was once one of the most prestigious wines of the Venetian Republic, prized at the tables of Venice in the 16th century, and today a small group of Isera growers have formed a quality project to restore its reputation. Its light body and floral perfume make it an easy summer red.
grapes.trivia: Lorenzo Da Ponte, Mozart's librettist, came from the Veneto and wrote Marzemino into Don Giovanni's final banquet scene.

grapes.name: Vespolina
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Nebbiolo × Coccalona Nera (Rohrtraube Blaurot), confirmed by markers.
grapes.hectares: About 150 to 200 ha (VIVC 1990: 175 ha).
grapes.profile: A peppery, aromatic offspring of Nebbiolo grown in northern Piedmont, where it is blended into Gattinara, Ghemme and Boca to add spice and colour. It has high levels of rotundone, the compound behind white pepper aromas, which makes varietal versions surprisingly Syrah-like. In Lombardy's Oltrepò Pavese it is called Ughetta and blended with Croatina. It also contributes to Lombardy's Bonarda-dominated blends. It ripens earlier than Nebbiolo, which adds to its value as a blending partner on cooler northern slopes. A handful of Alto Piemonte producers, such as Le Piane in Boca, now bottle it alone.
grapes.trivia: Its name may come from vespa, wasp, because wasps adore its sweet ripe berries.

grapes.name: Croatina
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). It is a parent of Ruché with Malvasia Aromatica di Parma. Not the same as Argentina's Bonarda (Douce Noire).
grapes.hectares: About 3,300 ha (VIVC 2000: 3,280 ha).
grapes.profile: A dark, soft, fruity red from the hills south of Pavia and Piacenza, where it is confusingly sold as Bonarda, often lightly sparkling. It is blended with Barbera in Gutturnio. Its parentage of Ruché links it to one of Piedmont's most aromatic reds. Rovescala is considered its home village. It is easy to grow and productive, with deep colour and soft tannins, and in Oltrepò Pavese it accounts for the region's best-known red wine. Its plush fruit makes it a common blending partner for Barbera, adding body and colour to that grape's high acidity. Producers in the Colli Piacentini also make still and frizzante versions.
grapes.trivia: Italian 'Bonarda' from Oltrepò Pavese and Argentine 'Bonarda' from Mendoza are completely unrelated grapes.

grapes.name: Ruché
grapes.parentage_note: Croatina × Malvasia Aromatica di Parma per VIVC, which explains its unusual floral perfume.
grapes.hectares: About 150 ha (2020s).
grapes.profile: A rare, intensely aromatic red from seven villages around Castagnole Monferrato, rescued in the 1960s by the parish priest Don Giacomo Cauda, who found old vines on the church's land. It smells of rose petals, violets and pepper, a perfume inherited from its Malvasia parent, with moderate tannin. It became a DOCG in 2010. Its tannins are light to moderate, so it is usually drunk within five years. Production is tiny, but its aromatic profile has made it popular with sommeliers. Some producers age it in tonneaux to soften its spicy edges.
grapes.trivia: Don Cauda's 'Vigna del Parroco' (the priest's vineyard) is still bottled and is the reference wine of the appellation.

grapes.name: Grignolino
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.profile: A pale, tart, tannic red of the Monferrato hills with strawberry, white pepper and bitter herbs. The name probably derives from grignole, dialect for its many pips, which add tannin. Once served at the Savoy court, it has a cult following among Piedmontese for its contrarian lightness. Heitz Cellar in Napa has grown it since 1961. It is notoriously difficult to grow: uneven ripening and frequent fruit set problems mean yields vary greatly. Producers such as Braida and Crivelli bottle it as a light, food-friendly red, and the Monferrato Casalese zone has started promoting older-style, longer-aged versions.
grapes.trivia: Grignolino can contain three or more seeds per berry, which is why careful winemakers avoid long macerations.

grapes.name: Schioppettino
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records unknown × Vulpea.
grapes.hectares: About 100 ha (VIVC 2000: 96 ha).
grapes.profile: A peppery, medium-bodied red from the Judrio valley on the Slovenian border, nearly lost after phylloxera. In 1976 the Rapuzzi family of Ronchi di Cialla gathered surviving vines, and a 1978 regional decree authorised its planting. It tastes of raspberry, black pepper and green peppercorn, with fresh acidity. Prepotto is now a designated sub-zone. It needs a warm site to ripen fully, and producers such as Ronchi di Cialla, Ronco del Gnemiz and La Viarte show it can age. In Slovenia, just across the border, it is known as Pokalca.
grapes.trivia: The name probably means 'little gunshot', for the way its crunchy berries pop in the mouth or the old fizzy style of the wine.

grapes.name: Cesanese
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. Cesanese d'Affile and Cesanese Comune are distinct but related varieties.
grapes.hectares: About 600 ha for Cesanese d'Affile (VIVC 2000: 615 ha).
grapes.profile: The red of the hills southeast of Rome, where the volcanic and limestone soils of the Ciociaria give perfumed, spicy reds with cherry, pepper and rose. Cesanese del Piglio became Lazio's first red DOCG in 2008. Once sold sweet and fizzy to Roman trattorias, it is now made dry by a small group of growers such as Damiano Ciolli. Its wines are best around five to eight years old, when the cherry fruit has softened into dried flowers and spice. Producers in Piglio have worked to reduce the old sweet and fizzy styles in favour of dry, structured wines, and the grape's revival is part of a broader return to Lazio's native varieties.
grapes.trivia: Cesanese del Piglio was the first red DOCG in Lazio, a region better known for white Frascati.

grapes.name: Mantonico Bianco
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. VIVC lists it as a parent of Nerello Mascalese and Gaglioppo (with Sangiovese) and of Catarratto (with Garganega).
grapes.hectares: A few hundred ha in Calabria.
grapes.profile: A Calabrian white of great genetic importance: it is the mother or father of Gaglioppo, Nerello Mascalese and Catarratto, three of the most widely grown southern Italian grapes. Its own wine is fresh and herbal, sometimes made sweet from dried grapes. It points to Calabria as a crossroads where northern and southern Italian grape lineages met. Calabrian growers have begun bottling it as a dry white again, and a sweet passito version is a speciality of Bivongi. Its role as an ancestor shows that the toe of Italy was once an important centre of grape breeding, probably through chance crossings among the many varieties planted in mixed vineyards.
grapes.trivia: Its name may derive from the Greek mantonikos, 'prophetic', though no source confirms the connection.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.parentage_note: Albillo Mayor × Benedicto, published by José Miguel Martínez-Zapater, Javier Ibáñez and colleagues (CSIC and ICVV Logroño) in 2012 using SNP and SSR markers. The cross probably happened in the upper Ebro valley. VIVC confirms by markers. Tempranillo Blanco is a white mutation found in a Murillo de Río Leza vineyard in 1988.
grapes.hectares: 231,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017), fourth most planted wine grape; Spain about 203,000 ha, Portugal about 18,000 ha.
grapes.profile: Spain's noble red. Its name means 'little early one' because it ripens weeks before Garnacha, an advantage in the cool, high plateaus of northern Spain. It has moderate acidity, firm tannin and flavours of red cherry, plum, tobacco and leather. In Rioja it was traditionally blended with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo and aged for years in American oak, building the vanilla and dill notes of classic Reserva and Gran Reserva. In Ribera del Duero, as Tinto Fino, at 750 to 1,000 metres, it gives darker, firmer wines, the style made famous by Vega Sicilia and Pesquera. In Portugal, as Tinta Roriz or Aragonez, it is a Port grape and an Alentejo staple. The 2012 DNA study revealed its parents, two nearly forgotten Spanish varieties.
grapes.trivia: One parent, Benedicto, was found surviving only as a few vines in a single old Aragonese vineyard and in collections.

grapes.name: Albillo Mayor

origin.place: Ribera del Duero and Castilla y León, Spain

grapes.parentage_note: Hebén × unknown per VIVC, making it a half-sibling of Airén, Pedro Ximénez and other Iberian whites. Identified as Tempranillo's mother in 2012 (Ibáñez, Martínez-Zapater et al.).
grapes.hectares: About 1,400 ha (VIVC 2008: 1,443 ha).
grapes.profile: A white grape traditionally interplanted with Tempranillo in old Ribera del Duero vineyards, where up to 5 percent was co-fermented into the reds. Its role in the family tree is enormous: DNA showed it is Tempranillo's mother. Ribera del Duero's 2019 rules began allowing white wines from it, and a growing number of producers, such as Dominio del Águila and Bodegas Arzuaga, make varietal Albillo Mayor with stone-fruit flavours, low acidity and a creamy texture. In Gredos, near Madrid, granite slopes give it freshness. Its revival reflects Spanish growers' renewed interest in the overlooked varieties that once filled their field blends.
grapes.trivia: Ribera del Duero created the 'Ribera del Duero Blanco' category for Albillo Mayor wines with its 2019 rule change, after decades of making only reds and rosés.

grapes.name: Benedicto
grapes.parentage_note: Identified as Tempranillo's father in 2012 (Ibáñez, Martínez-Zapater et al.); VIVC lists no pedigree of its own.
grapes.hectares: A handful of vines; considered almost extinct.
grapes.profile: One of the most obscure grapes in Spain and one of the most important. Benedicto survives as scattered old vines in Aragón and in research collections, yet DNA shows it is the father of Tempranillo, the country's most planted red. The finding suggests that Tempranillo was born somewhere in the upper Ebro valley where Albillo Mayor from the Duero met this Aragonese red. Its name probably refers to the Benedictine monasteries that dotted the region and that spread vines along the Camino de Santiago. Conservationists have begun to propagate it so its genetic heritage is not lost.
grapes.trivia: No commercial wine is made from Benedicto, but every bottle of Rioja carries half its genes.

grapes.name: Garnacha Peluda
grapes.parentage_note: A mutation of Garnacha Tinta with hairy leaf undersides (VIVC: 'Garnacha Tinta mutation').
grapes.hectares: About 1,300 ha (VIVC: Spain 903 ha in 2008, France 433 ha).
grapes.profile: A downy-leaved form of Garnacha whose fuzzy leaf undersides reduce water loss and help protect grapes from rot and sunburn. It tends to give slightly lower alcohol and higher acidity than ordinary Garnacha, which makes it attractive to growers worried about heat and rising sugar levels. It is found in Terra Alta and other Catalan zones, and in the Roussillon and Languedoc as Lledoner Pelut. Some Catalan producers bottle it separately to show its fresher, more herbal character, and it has become a talking point in discussions of climate adaptation.
grapes.trivia: Pelut and peluda both mean 'hairy', a literal description of its leaves.

grapes.name: Mencía
grapes.parentage_note: Alfrocheiro × Patorra per VIVC (marker-confirmed), both Portuguese varieties, which argues for a Portuguese origin and shows that Mencía is identical to Portugal's Jaen. Once thought related to Cabernet Franc, a theory DNA rejected.
grapes.hectares: About 9,000 ha in Spain (VIVC 2008: 9,055 ha) and 2,400 ha in Portugal as Jaen.
grapes.profile: The red grape of northwest Spain's slate and granite country. In Bierzo, steep slopes around Villafranca and Corullón give fragrant, red-fruited, mineral reds with floral and herbal notes; in Ribeira Sacra, vines cling to vertiginous terraces above the Sil and Miño rivers that Romans and monks began cutting two millennia ago. Its modern revival began in the late 1990s, when Álvaro Palacios and his nephew Ricardo Pérez founded Descendientes de J. Palacios in Corullón in 1999 and showed that old-vine Mencía on slate could rival the best reds of Spain. In Portugal's Dão it is called Jaen and was long thought to be a separate variety.
grapes.trivia: Ribeira Sacra's terraced slopes are so steep that grape pickers use small monorail cars, or carry baskets down to boats on the river.

grapes.name: Alfrocheiro
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records unknown × Savagnin, which makes Alfrocheiro another member of the Traminer clan. It is in turn the parent of Mencía, Castelão, Moreto, Malvasia Fina and other Iberian grapes (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 1,500 ha in Portugal (VIVC 2010: 1,492 ha).
grapes.profile: A Dão red with deep colour, fresh acidity and blackberry and strawberry fruit, used to add brightness to Touriga Nacional blends. Its genetic importance far exceeds its acreage: VIVC records it as a parent of Mencía, Castelão, Moreto and Malvasia Fina, so it sits near the root of a large part of Portugal's red and white grape family. Its own parent, Savagnin, connects Portugal's grape genealogy to the Jura and to central Europe. In the Canary Islands it grows as Baboso Negro, and in Spain's Arribes it is Bruñal, where old vines give concentrated, spicy reds.
grapes.trivia: Canary Island Baboso Negro, with its bright acidity, was shown by DNA to be Alfrocheiro, carried there centuries ago by Portuguese sailors.

grapes.name: Graciano
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. A 2006 DNA study found a parent-offspring relationship with Carignan; VIVC records Garro (Mandón) as Hebén × Graciano.
grapes.hectares: About 2,000 to 2,500 ha in Spain (2015), rising.
grapes.profile: A low-yielding, late-ripening Rioja grape that adds acidity, colour and a perfumed, slightly spicy edge to Tempranillo blends. It nearly disappeared after phylloxera because it crops so poorly, but its value in long-aged Gran Reservas brought it back from the 1980s; Contino's varietal Graciano is a benchmark. In Sardinia it is called Bovale Sardo or Cagnulari, and in southern Spain it survives as Tintilla de Rota, once used for sweet wines. Rising temperatures have made it more attractive as a blending partner that keeps wines fresh.
grapes.trivia: Its name comes from gracia, grace, perhaps because it is gracious to the wine rather than to the grower.

grapes.name: Bobal
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 61,500 ha in 2015 (Spanish ministry data cited by Wikipedia), Spain's second most planted red.
grapes.profile: The grape of the high, windy plateau of Utiel-Requena inland from Valencia. Bobal keeps good acidity despite the heat, gives dark colour and is high in resveratrol and anthocyanins. For decades it was sold in bulk to beef up wines across Europe and to make rosado. Since the 2000s, producers such as Mustiguillo (whose El Terrerazo became Spain's first Vino de Pago in the region, 2010) and Bodega Sierra Norte have shown that old bush vines give fresh, blueberry-scented reds with real character.
grapes.trivia: Its name may come from bovale, Latin for bull, because its bunches are said to look like a bull's head.

grapes.name: Hebén
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. VIVC records it as a parent of Airén, Albillo Mayor, Cayetana Blanca, Macabeo, Parellada, Pedro Ximénez, Malvasia Fina, Monica, Sumoll and others, many with unknown second parents. Earlier work (Vargas 2007) found Pedro Ximénez descends from the Moorish table grape Gibi, now considered Hebén.
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 ha (VIVC lists 1,080 ha in Argentina in 2009); scattered vines in Spain.
grapes.profile: An ancient grape, probably from the Islamic period in Al-Andalus, that turns out to be the matriarch of Iberian whites. VIVC lists Hebén as a parent of Airén, Pedro Ximénez, Albillo Mayor, Cayetana Blanca, Macabeo and Parellada, which means most of Spain's white wine, from La Mancha's bulk to Jerez's sweet PX and Cava, descends from it. Through Albillo Mayor it is also a grandparent of Tempranillo. It was grown mainly as a table grape, which helps explain how it travelled so widely. Its significance shows how Moorish agriculture shaped Iberian vineyards.
grapes.trivia: Its synonym Mourisco Branco means 'white Moorish one', a reminder of its likely medieval Arab origins.

grapes.name: Airén
grapes.parentage_note: Hebén × unknown per VIVC.
grapes.hectares: 218,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017), once the world's most planted wine grape; about 200,000 ha by 2020s.
grapes.profile: For decades the most planted wine grape in the world, grown almost entirely on the flat, sun-baked plateau of La Mancha. Its drought tolerance suits the region's widely spaced bush vines (en vaso), low-density planting that maximises water per vine. Most of it has gone into brandy (Brandy de Jerez) and bulk white or neutral alcohol, and EU distillation subsidies kept it planted. Modern, cool-fermented versions are fresh and lightly fruity. Since the 1990s, irrigation and EU restructuring grants have replaced much of it with Tempranillo, Syrah and other reds.
grapes.trivia: Even at its peak, Airén's yields were so low per vine that its vast acreage produced less wine than much smaller plantings elsewhere.

grapes.name: Pedro Ximénez
grapes.parentage_note: Hebén × unknown per VIVC; Vargas et al. (2007) found a parent-offspring relationship with the Moorish table grape Gibi. The legend of a soldier named Peter Siemens bringing it from the Rhine is unsupported.
grapes.hectares: About 7,000 ha in Spain (2019), most in Montilla-Moriles; larger plantings in Argentina and Chile (for pisco).
grapes.profile: The grape of the treacle-dark, intensely sweet PX sherry. In Montilla-Moriles, the summer heat of Córdoba ripens it to very high sugar, and grapes are laid out on esparto mats to dry in the sun (soleo) for a week or more, concentrating sugars until the juice is syrupy. Fortified and aged in solera, it tastes of figs, raisins, molasses and coffee, sometimes with more than 400 grams of sugar per litre. Montilla's dry wines also use PX and often reach 15 percent alcohol naturally, so they need no fortification.
grapes.trivia: The story that a 16th-century soldier called Peter Siemens brought it from Germany is now discounted; DNA links it to Moorish table grapes.

grapes.name: Palomino
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). It is a parent of Listán Negro (with Negra Mole), according to VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 20,000 ha in Spain (2015), including Listán Blanco in the Canaries.
grapes.profile: The grape of sherry. On its own Palomino is neutral and low in acid, which is exactly why it suits a wine built on ageing: under a layer of flor yeast in the solera system it becomes fino and manzanilla, tasting of almonds, sea air and bread dough; aged oxidatively it becomes amontillado and oloroso. The chalky white albariza soils of the Jerez triangle hold moisture through the summer drought, so vines survive without irrigation. A new movement of unfortified white wines from single pagos, led by producers such as Equipo Navazos and Ramiro Ibáñez, shows the grape's response to albariza in its own right.
grapes.trivia: The name is said to honour Fernán Yáñez Palomino, a knight of Alfonso X in the 13th century.

grapes.name: Listán Prieto
grapes.parentage_note: In 2007 the Centro Nacional de Biotecnología (Madrid) found that California's Mission grape matched Listán Prieto from the Canary Islands; Milla-Tapia et al. (2007) and Aliquó et al. (2017) confirmed that Chile's País and Argentina's Criolla Chica are the same. It is a parent of Torrontés Riojano, Cereza and Criolla Grande (with Muscat of Alexandria) and of Quebranta (with Negra Mole).
grapes.hectares: About 10,000 to 11,000 ha in Chile as País (SAG 2020s), plus Mission in California and Mexico and Criolla in Argentina; under 30 ha left in Spain.
grapes.profile: The first European grape of the Americas. Spanish settlers carried it from Castile via the Canary Islands in the 16th century: it was planted in Mexico by the 1520s, Peru by the 1540s and Chile by the 1550s, then by Franciscan missionaries in California from the 1770s. For three centuries it made the sacramental and everyday wine of the New World. Displaced by French varieties, it has been rediscovered as old, dry-farmed vines in Chile's Maule and Itata, where natural winemakers make light, earthy reds and pipeño, the traditional rustic wine of Chilean farmers. Its crossings with Muscat of Alexandria gave Argentina its Criollas and Torrontés.
grapes.trivia: The Mission vine at the Avila Adobe in Los Angeles and the 'Trinity' vine at Mission San Gabriel are said to descend from Franciscan cuttings of the 1770s.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. VIVC lists Portugal as country of origin. It is a parent of Caíño Blanco (with Caíño Bravo). The old story that Cistercian monks of Cluny brought it in the 12th century is discounted.
grapes.hectares: About 12,000 ha in Spain and 6,000 ha in Portugal (2020s, consejo regulador and IVV estimates).
grapes.profile: The white of Spain's green Atlantic corner, where rain falls more than 1,500 millimetres a year and vines are trained on high granite-post pergolas (parras) to let air circulate and keep grapes from rot. Thick skins protect it from mildew. Wines are aromatic and saline, with peach, lemon zest and a briny finish that pairs with Galician shellfish. Rías Baixas DO, founded in 1988, has made it Spain's best-known white. Across the Minho river in Portugal, Monção e Melgaço is the heartland of Alvarinho Vinho Verde, which tends to be fuller and less fizzy than mass-market Vinho Verde.
grapes.trivia: In Australia, many 'Albariño' vineyards planted in the 1990s turned out to be Savagnin when a French ampelographer checked them in 2008.

grapes.name: Verdejo
grapes.parentage_note: Castellana Blanca × Savagnin per VIVC, marker-confirmed; this makes Verdejo a full sibling of Godello.
grapes.hectares: About 22,000 ha (2020s), mostly in Rueda.
grapes.profile: The white of Rueda, on the gravelly, stony terraces of the Duero at around 700 to 800 metres. Verdejo oxidises quickly, so traditionally it was made into nutty, sherry-like fortified wine, but in the 1970s Marqués de Riscal, advised by Bordeaux oenologist Émile Peynaud, made fresh, reductively handled whites, and the modern style took off. Today Verdejo is Spain's best-selling white, with fennel, citrus and a bitter, herbal finish. Night harvesting with machines preserves its aromatics. Its sibling Godello comes from the same parents.
grapes.trivia: Rueda became Castilla y León's first DO in 1980, and its whites are now among the most consumed in Spanish bars.

grapes.name: Godello
grapes.parentage_note: Castellana Blanca × Savagnin per VIVC (prime name Gouveio), the same parents as Verdejo.
grapes.hectares: About 2,500 to 3,500 ha (2020s); Spain 1,153 ha in 2008.
grapes.profile: A Galician white that nearly disappeared, down to a few hectares in the 1970s, before the Recuperación de Godello project in Valdeorras rescued it. On the slate and granite hills of Valdeorras and Bierzo it gives textured, mineral whites with pear, citrus and a saline finish, often compared to white Burgundy when barrel-fermented. Rafael Palacios's As Sortes and Louro have become benchmarks. In the Douro it is called Gouveio and is part of white Port and Douro whites. Its acidity and texture also suit lees ageing.
grapes.trivia: By the mid-1970s Godello was so rare that the Valdeorras project had to search house gardens for vines to propagate.

grapes.name: Castellana Blanca
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records it as a parent of Verdejo and Godello (with Savagnin) and of Carignan.
grapes.hectares: Collection vines only.
grapes.profile: An obscure Castilian white with an extraordinary family: VIVC records it as a parent of Verdejo and Godello, and of Carignan. Its crossings with Savagnin produced two of Spain's leading white grapes, and its link to Carignan connects it with the red grapes of the Mediterranean. It survives mostly in research collections such as Spain's El Encín. Its story shows how much of a country's wine heritage can depend on a vine almost nobody has heard of, and how Savagnin, a Jura grape, contributed to Spanish wine centuries ago.
grapes.trivia: Through Verdejo and Godello, it is the genetic grandmother of most of the white wine sold in Spain's bars today.

grapes.name: Macabeo
grapes.parentage_note: Hebén × Brustiano Faux per VIVC (prime name Viura), confirmed by markers.
grapes.hectares: About 45,000 ha in Spain (2015), its second most planted white, plus about 2,800 ha in France (2007).
grapes.profile: The main white grape of Rioja (as Viura) and a pillar of Cava, where it provides body and gentle fruit to blends with Xarel·lo and Parellada. It buds late, avoiding spring frosts, but is prone to rot. Traditional white Rioja, aged for years in American oak, becomes nutty and honeyed: López de Heredia's Viña Tondonia Gran Reserva Blanco shows how well it can age. In the Roussillon it is part of sweet Vins Doux Naturels. Its neutral, slightly floral character makes it a blank canvas for winemaking, which is why it shows so differently in fresh Cava, oaked Rioja and sweet Roussillon wines.
grapes.trivia: López de Heredia releases some white Rioja Gran Reservas more than 20 years after the vintage.

grapes.name: Xarel·lo
grapes.parentage_note: Gibi (a Hebén-like table grape) × Brustiano Faux per VIVC.
grapes.profile: The most characterful of the three Cava grapes, giving body, acidity and a herbal, slightly earthy character. Growers serious about long-aged sparkling wine favour it: it is the backbone of many Corpinnat wines, a group of Penedès producers that left the Cava DO in 2019 to set stricter rules, including organic farming and hand harvesting. Still Xarel·lo from old vines is a growing category. It is rich in resveratrol and antioxidants, which helps long lees ageing. Its thick skins make it suitable for skin-contact whites, too.
grapes.trivia: Corpinnat requires all grapes to be organic and hand-picked within the Penedès, rules stricter than the Cava DO's.

grapes.name: Parellada
grapes.parentage_note: Hebén × unknown per VIVC.
grapes.profile: The lightest and most delicate of the Cava trio, thriving in the higher, cooler vineyards of the Upper Penedès and Conca de Barberà. It gives floral, citrus aromas and fresh acidity at modest alcohol. On its own it makes pleasant, early-drinking whites. Its role in Cava is to add finesse and lift to the more structured Macabeo and Xarel·lo. Rising temperatures in the lowlands have pushed growers to plant it higher up. In Conca de Barberà, the medieval Cistercian monastery of Poblet planted vines nearby, and the region's cooperatives remain major Parellada growers.
grapes.trivia: Torres's popular Viña Sol white, launched in 1962, was for decades made mainly from Parellada.

grapes.name: Cayetana Blanca
grapes.parentage_note: Hebén × unknown per VIVC. It is a parent of Castelão (with Alfrocheiro), Antão Vaz, Rabigato and Moreto, so it links Spanish and Portuguese families.
grapes.hectares: About 12,000 ha in Spain (2008), mainly Extremadura.
grapes.profile: Extremadura's most planted white, mostly distilled or made into simple bulk wine, which hides its genealogical importance. Under various names (Pardina, Jaén Blanco), it parented several Portuguese grapes: Castelão with Alfrocheiro, and Antão Vaz and Rabigato. That makes this unremarkable Spanish white a grandparent of much of southern Portugal's wine. Its tolerance of drought and heat suits the dry plains on either side of the Guadiana. A few producers now make fresh varietal whites from old vines. Its high yields made it a mainstay of the Spanish brandy and bulk wine trade.
grapes.trivia: In Portugal's Alentejo it was known as Mourisco Arsello, another name pointing to Moorish-era origins.

grapes.name: Prieto Picudo
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records unknown × Savagnin.
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 ha (2010s).
grapes.profile: The native red of León, grown around Valdevimbre and the banks of the river Cea. Its compact, pointed (picudo) bunches of dark (prieto) grapes give deep-coloured, fresh reds with red fruit, spice and good acidity. It was traditionally made into aguja, a lightly sparkling rosé fermented with whole bunches, and into reds stored in caves dug into hillsides. The Tierra de León DO, created in 2007, has made it its flagship. Its thick skins and small berries give it colour and acidity, qualities that make it attractive to growers as climate change pushes alcohol levels up elsewhere in Spain.
grapes.trivia: Valdevimbre's old wine cellars are dug into the earth like small caves, called cuevas, used for centuries to keep wine cool.

grapes.name: Listán Negro
grapes.parentage_note: Negra Mole (Negramoll) × Listán Blanco (Palomino) per VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 5,000 ha in the Canary Islands.
grapes.profile: The Canary Islands' main red, grown on volcanic soils that phylloxera never reached, so most vines grow on their own roots. In the Orotava Valley on Tenerife, growers train it in the cordón trenzado, braided cordons up to 10 metres long that are lifted on stakes and moved each year. The wines are light, peppery and smoky with red fruit and a volcanic, saline edge, and carbonic maceration is often used for young reds. Its parents link it to mainland Spain's Palomino and the Canary Negramoll.
grapes.trivia: The cordón trenzado of La Orotava is unique in the world: growers braid long cane cordons together and can move them up and down the slope.

grapes.name: Hondarrabi Zuri
grapes.parentage_note: The name is used for at least three distinct varieties; the main one is identical to French Courbu Blanc (VIVC links Hondarrabi Zuri to Courbu Blanc).
grapes.hectares: About 600 to 800 ha across the three Txakoli DOs.
grapes.profile: The main white grape of Txakoli, the light, tart, slightly sparkling wine of the Basque coast. Grown on high pergolas or wires on hillsides overlooking the Bay of Biscay, in one of the wettest wine regions of Europe, it gives lemony, saline wines of 10.5 to 11.5 percent alcohol. Bars in San Sebastián and Bilbao pour it from a height into flat tumblers to release its spritz. Getariako Txakolina became a DO in 1989. Its thick-skinned berries resist rot in the humid Cantabrian climate, and the best producers, such as Ameztoi and Txomin Etxaniz, now make serious single-vineyard and lees-aged versions alongside the classic bar wine.
grapes.trivia: The traditional pour from arm's height (escanciado) is meant to aerate the wine and refresh its natural fizz.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. VIVC records a parent-offspring relationship with Amaral. It is a parent of Touriga Franca and Tinta Barroca (both with Marufo/Mourisco Tinto).
grapes.hectares: About 13,000 ha in Portugal (2020s), up from 2,760 ha in the late 1990s.
grapes.profile: Portugal's flagship red, small-berried and low-yielding, with intense violet and bergamot perfume, black fruit and firm tannin. In the 1970s and 1980s, research by José Ramos Pinto Rosas and João Nicolau de Almeida singled it out as the best of the Douro's dozens of varieties, and it became central to the replanting of Port vineyards in block plantings. It is equally important in Dão, its likely birthplace, where it gives elegant, floral reds from granite. Its tolerance of heat and drought prompted Bordeaux to approve it as a climate-adaptation grape in 2021.
grapes.trivia: In 2021 Touriga Nacional became the first Portuguese variety authorised, in small proportions, for Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur.

grapes.name: Touriga Franca
grapes.parentage_note: Touriga Nacional × Marufo (Mourisco Tinto) per VIVC, marker-confirmed; Tinta Barroca shares the same parents.
grapes.hectares: About 12,000 ha (VIVC 2010: 12,055 ha), the most planted red in the Douro.
grapes.profile: The Douro's most widely planted grape, more reliable and productive than its parent Touriga Nacional. It gives aromatic, rose-and-blackberry scented wines with firm, fine tannins. It does best on warmer, south-facing schist slopes and adds perfume and structure to both Port and dry Douro reds. Most Port houses blend it with Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão, the five grapes recommended in the 1980s replanting. Its thick skins resist disease and heat stress, and it is less prone than Touriga Nacional to the poor fruit set that can hurt yields, which is why growers rely on it.
grapes.trivia: Despite its old name Touriga Francesa ('French Touriga'), it is a purely Portuguese cross with no French parent.

grapes.name: Mourisco Tinto
grapes.parentage_note: Its VIVC prime name is Marufo. VIVC records Marufo as a parent of Touriga Franca and Tinta Barroca (with Touriga Nacional).
grapes.hectares: About 3,600 ha in Portugal (2010) and 2,200 ha in Spain (2002) (VIVC, as Marufo).
grapes.profile: A pale, large-berried Douro red long regarded as a minor Port grape, until DNA showed it is the parent, with Touriga Nacional, of both Touriga Franca and Tinta Barroca. Its own wines are light and fruity, but its genes underpin much of the Douro's modern vineyard. In Spain it grows as Moravia Dulce in La Mancha. The Portuguese name refers to the Moors, a common naming pattern for old Iberian varieties. Its large berries were once prized for table grapes as well as wine. Growers today keep a few old vines in field blends, and some producers make it as a light red or use it in Port blends.
grapes.trivia: Because the name Mourisco was used for several different grapes, DNA was needed to identify the true parent of Touriga Franca.

grapes.name: Tinta Barroca
grapes.parentage_note: Marufo × Touriga Nacional per VIVC, making it a full sibling of Touriga Franca.
grapes.hectares: About 4,500 ha in Portugal (2010).
grapes.profile: A thick-skinned, early-ripening Douro grape that accumulates sugar fast, which makes it useful for Port on cooler, north-facing or high slopes where other varieties struggle. It is soft, sweet-fruited and rustic, usually blended. In South Africa it is used for Cape port-style wines and occasionally bottled as a dry red. It is a full sibling of Touriga Franca through Touriga Nacional and Marufo. It is thought to have been widely planted after phylloxera because it was easy to graft and productive, and it still forms a large share of many Douro vineyards.
grapes.trivia: Its tendency to raisin in heat makes it valuable for Port but awkward for dry wines in hot years.

grapes.name: Tinto Cão
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). It is a parent of the American teinturier Rubired (with Alicante Ganzin).
grapes.hectares: About 330 ha (2007).
grapes.profile: One of the Douro's oldest documented grapes, nearly abandoned because of its very low yields, then chosen as one of the five recommended Port varieties in the 1980s. It gives fine, spicy, high-acid wine that ages well and adds freshness to blends. Research plantings at the University of California in the 1950s led to its use in breeding Rubired, a red-fleshed grape for colour concentrate. It is valued for its resistance to heat and its ability to keep acidity in Douro summers, and its late ripening gives a long hang time. Old vineyards often hold it scattered among dozens of other varieties.
grapes.trivia: Its name means 'red dog', perhaps because the vines were so hard to grow that they 'bit' the grower.

grapes.name: Baga
grapes.parentage_note: Arinto do Dão × unknown per VIVC.
grapes.profile: The grape of Bairrada, where clay-limestone soils and Atlantic rain make it a challenge: Baga is thick-skinned, high in acid and tannin and ripens late, so in wet years it rots before it ripens. In good vintages from old vines it gives Nebbiolo-like wines with sour cherry, tobacco and smoke that age for decades. Luís Pato, his daughter Filipa Pato and the Baga Friends group have championed it since the 1980s, and it is also made into crisp sparkling wine, a Bairrada speciality since the 1890s.
grapes.trivia: Bairrada's main sparkling-wine town, Anadia, has been making espumante since the 1890s, based on Baga and local whites.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.parentage_note: Cayetana Blanca × Alfrocheiro per VIVC, marker-confirmed.
grapes.hectares: About 18,500 ha (2010), once Portugal's most planted red.
grapes.profile: Southern Portugal's most planted red for much of the 20th century. On the sandy soils of the Setúbal peninsula around Palmela, it gives perfumed, juicy wines with red currant, plum and a gamey edge, which can age surprisingly well from old bush vines. It became widely known as Periquita, the name of a brand created in 1850 by José Maria da Fonseca from a vineyard called Cova da Periquita ('parakeet's hollow'). Many Alentejo and Tejo blends use it to soften Trincadeira and Aragonez.
grapes.trivia: Periquita, first produced in 1850, became so famous that the brand name was used for the grape across Portugal.

grapes.name: Trincadeira
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). It is a parent of Mourisco (the unidentified accession) with Marufo.
grapes.profile: A demanding but rewarding Portuguese red, called Tinta Amarela in the Douro. It needs heat and dry conditions to avoid rot, which makes it an Alentejo specialist, where it gives spicy, herbal, plum-scented wines with good acidity. Blended with Aragonez (Tempranillo) and Alicante Bouschet, it forms the backbone of many Alentejo reds. Its yields vary greatly from year to year, and producers say it is either excellent or disappointing. In the Douro it is part of the traditional field blends in old vineyards that can contain 30 or more varieties.
grapes.trivia: The name comes from trincar, to crunch, perhaps describing the berries or the brittle wood of the vine.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC prime name Arinto). Distinct from Arinto do Dão, a different variety that is a parent of Baga, Bical and Fernão Pires.
grapes.profile: Portugal's most valuable white for acidity: Arinto holds its lemon-sharp acidity even in the heat of the Alentejo, so it is blended into many southern whites for freshness. In Bucelas, a small DOC just north of Lisbon, it gives taut, mineral, long-lived whites that were exported to England as 'Lisbon Hock' in the 19th century. It also makes good sparkling wine and contributes to Vinho Verde as Pedernã. Its thick skins resist rot, and it ages for 10 to 20 years, gaining honey and wax notes while keeping its lemony bite. In Vinho Verde it adds structure to blends with Loureiro and Alvarinho.
grapes.trivia: Wellington's officers took a liking to Bucelas during the Peninsular War, and it became fashionable in Regency London.

grapes.name: Encruzado
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 300 ha (2010).
grapes.profile: Dão's great white, grown on granite at 400 to 700 metres where the mountain ranges of Caramulo and Estrela shield the vines from Atlantic rain and continental extremes. Encruzado combines texture and freshness, with citrus, pear and a nutty, smoky character when barrel-fermented, often compared to white Burgundy. It ages well and is resistant to oxidation. Quinta dos Roques and Quinta da Pellada (Álvaro Castro) are reference producers. Its name may derive from 'crossed', perhaps describing the way its shoots grow. Plantings are small but growing as Dão's reputation for whites rises.
grapes.trivia: Encruzado's ability to resist oxidation lets producers age it on lees in barrel without losing freshness.

grapes.name: Loureiro
grapes.parentage_note: Amaral (Caíño Longo) × Espadeiro Branco (Branco Escola) per VIVC.
grapes.profile: One of Vinho Verde's most aromatic grapes, smelling of laurel (loureiro means laurel), lime blossom and green apple. It thrives in the Lima and Cávado valleys, close to the Atlantic, on granite. Traditionally Minho vines were trained high on trees and pergolas so farmers could grow crops below, and Loureiro's vigour suited this. Varietal Loureiro has become fashionable, dry and fresh, often under 12 percent alcohol. Loureiro is also grown in Spain's Rías Baixas, especially in the Val do Salnés, where it is blended with Albariño. Its high yields and fresh aromatics make it ideal for the light, low-alcohol whites the region is known for.
grapes.trivia: Vinho Verde means 'green wine', referring to youth and freshness, not colour; much of it was once red.

grapes.name: Fernão Pires
grapes.parentage_note: Arinto do Dão × unknown per VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 17,000 ha (2010), Portugal's most planted white.
grapes.profile: Portugal's most planted white grape, early-ripening and aromatic, with notes of orange peel, rose and spice that recall Muscat. It is the workhorse of Tejo and Lisboa whites and is also used for sparkling wine in Bairrada, where it is called Maria Gomes. It is versatile, from fresh, aromatic whites to late-harvest and botrytis styles. South Africa grows a little. It ripens early, so in hot regions it can lose acidity if picked late, but in cooler Bairrada it keeps more freshness. It is also prone to spring frost and mildew, so careful site selection matters. It responds well to skin contact and some producers make orange versions.
grapes.trivia: Its two names come from two men, a Fernão Pires and a Maria Gomes, about whom little is known except that they gave their names to the same grape.

grapes.name: Antão Vaz
grapes.parentage_note: Pardina (Cayetana Blanca) × João Domingos per VIVC; a grandchild of Hebén.
grapes.profile: The Alentejo's signature white, at home around Vidigueira, where the Serra do Mendro ridge funnels cool air into the plains. It handles heat well, giving full-bodied whites with tropical fruit, citrus and a hint of mineral. It is often blended with Arinto for acidity. Vidigueira has a long tradition of fermenting it in talhas, large clay amphorae sealed with olive oil or wax, a technique dating back to the Romans that has been revived since the 2010s. It is also used in long-aged whites from Alentejo's top estates, where lees ageing and oak give it weight.
grapes.trivia: Vidigueira is the hometown of Vasco da Gama, who was named Count of Vidigueira in 1519.

grapes.name: Sercial
grapes.parentage_note: Identical to mainland Esgana Cão (VIVC prime name). Parents unknown.
grapes.hectares: Under 30 ha on Madeira; small mainland plantings as Esgana Cão.
grapes.profile: The driest and most acidic of Madeira's noble grapes, grown on the island's highest and coolest vineyards on the north coast. Sercial Madeira is fortified early to stay dry and then aged for years by estufagem or the canteiro method, giving searing acidity, almonds, citrus peel and walnut. On the mainland it is called Esgana Cão, 'dog strangler', for its sourness. Madeira's best Sercials can age for a century. It ripens late and thrives in cooler, higher sites on Madeira, where other varieties fail to ripen. Its acidity also makes it a valuable blending partner in Bucelas, and its rarity has made old Sercial vintages highly collectable.
grapes.trivia: Esgana Cão, the mainland name, means 'dog strangler', a reference to its sharp acidity.

grapes.name: Verdelho
