grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Savagnin × unknown. Distinct from the Douro grape locally called Verdelho, which is Godello.
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 ha worldwide (2010s), split between Portugal and Australia.
grapes.profile: One of the four noble Madeira grapes, giving medium-dry wines with smoky, nutty, tangy character and high acidity. Before phylloxera and oidium it was the island's most planted variety. On Pico in the Azores it grows in currais, small plots enclosed by black basalt walls, now part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape (2004). In Australia, particularly the Hunter and Swan valleys, it makes fresh, tropical dry whites. Its thick skins and naturally high acidity also make it resistant to disease. In Madeira, Verdelho is fortified after part of the sugar has fermented, leaving it off-dry, and it develops well over decades.
grapes.trivia: Pico Verdelho was once shipped to the Russian imperial court, according to Azorean tradition.

grapes.name: Bual
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC's prime name is Malvasia Fina, with pedigree Hebén × Alfrocheiro. Madeira's Boal Cachudo is generally considered this variety.
grapes.hectares: About 2,200 ha as Malvasia Fina (2010), mostly mainland.
grapes.profile: Madeira's medium-sweet noble grape, between Verdelho and Malmsey in sweetness. Bual Madeira, fortified partway through fermentation, is rich and smoky with raisin, caramel and coffee notes balanced by bright acidity. On the mainland the same grape, as Malvasia Fina, is used for white Port and Douro whites. Its parents tie it to the Hebén family of southern Spain and the Alfrocheiro family of Dão. Its thin skins make it sensitive to rot, so growers on Madeira's humid south coast plant it in the warmer, lower vineyards. Old vintage Buals from the 19th century still appear at auction and can taste remarkably fresh.
grapes.trivia: On Madeira, varietal names on labels were made compulsory for the noble grapes, so 'Bual' indicates at least 85 percent of the grape.

grapes.name: Tinta Negra

origin.place: Andalusia, Spain (likely); now Madeira and the Canaries

grapes.parentage_note: Identical to Spanish Negramoll (VIVC links to Negra Mole). It is a parent of Listán Negro (with Palomino) and Quebranta (with Listán Prieto).
grapes.hectares: About 300 to 350 ha on Madeira, roughly 80 to 85 percent of the island's vineyard.
grapes.profile: The workhorse of Madeira. After oidium (1852) and phylloxera (1872) destroyed the island's noble vines, growers replanted with American hybrids and with this productive red, which can make any style of Madeira from dry to sweet. For decades it hid behind generic labels or traditional grape names, but since 2015 producers may name Tinta Negra on the label, and single-vintage (colheita) bottlings have improved its reputation. Its genes also run through the Canary Islands' Listán Negro and Peru's Quebranta.
grapes.trivia: Tinta Negra was allowed on Madeira labels only from 2015, despite making most of the island's wine for over a century.

grapes.name: Ramisco
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 20 to 25 ha (VIVC 2010: 23 ha).
grapes.profile: The red grape of Colares, on the Atlantic coast near Sintra, where ungrafted vines grow in deep sand dunes over clay. Growers dig trenches several metres deep through the sand to plant the vines in the clay below, then let the shoots sprawl along the dunes behind cane windbreaks. Phylloxera cannot move through sand, so Colares escaped the plague. Young Ramisco is ferociously tannic and acidic; after 20 years it becomes fine and fragrant. Colares DOC was created in 1908, one of the first in Portugal.
grapes.trivia: Colares is one of the very few European vineyards that never needed grafting, because phylloxera cannot survive in pure sand.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.parentage_note: Bred in 1882 by the Swiss botanist Hermann Müller (from the canton of Thurgau) at Geisenheim. For a century it was believed to be Riesling × Sylvaner; DNA work by Dettweiler and colleagues at Geilweilerhof (2000) showed the second parent was Madeleine Royale. VIVC records Riesling × Madeleine Royale, crossed 1882/1883.
grapes.hectares: About 22,000 ha worldwide; Germany about 11,000 ha in the 2020s (DWI), down from 25,000 ha in the 1970s.
grapes.profile: The most successful vine crossing ever made. Hermann Müller wanted a grape with Riesling's quality that ripened early, and Müller-Thurgau delivers early ripening and big yields, but rarely Riesling's depth. After the Second World War it spread across Germany, overtaking Riesling as the most planted grape by 1970, and supplied much of the Liebfraumilch and Piesporter Michelsberg exported in the 1970s and 1980s. Its reputation followed those wines down. At low yields on good sites, such as Franken's Muschelkalk or the high vineyards of Alto Adige (Kofererhof, Tiefenbrunner's Feldmarschall), it gives fresh, floral, nutmeg-scented whites. Luxembourg calls it Rivaner.
grapes.trivia: Müller himself believed his cross was Riesling × Silvaner, and the error stood for 118 years until DNA identified the table grape Madeleine Royale as the other parent.

grapes.name: Madeleine Royale
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Pinot × Frankenthal (Schiava Grossa/Trollinger), bred around 1845 by the Moreau-Robert nursery in Angers. Once thought to be a Chasselas seedling.
grapes.hectares: A few hectares; mostly a collection and table grape.
grapes.profile: A 19th-century French table grape from the Loire nursery of Moreau-Robert, notable for ripening very early, around the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene. It was grown in the Geisenheim collection when Hermann Müller made his crossings, and pollen from it fertilised Riesling to produce Müller-Thurgau. DNA showed in 2000 that Madeleine Royale itself descends from Pinot and Schiava Grossa (Trollinger). That makes Müller-Thurgau a great-grandchild of Pinot on one side and a grandchild of Gouais Blanc through Riesling on the other.
grapes.trivia: It was probably a mislabelled vine in Geisenheim's collection that led Müller to record the wrong parent.

grapes.name: Kerner
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by August Herold at Weinsberg in 1929: Trollinger (Schiava Grossa) × Riesling, a red × white cross that produced a white grape. Released in 1969. VIVC confirms.
grapes.hectares: About 2,000 ha in Germany (2020s), down from about 8,000 ha around 1990; 357 ha in Japan (2009).
grapes.profile: A crossing named after Justinus Kerner, a Swabian poet and doctor who wrote drinking songs. Kerner is winter-hardy, ripens reliably and keeps acidity, giving Riesling-like wines with a slightly grassy, muscat-tinged aroma. It boomed in Germany in the 1970s and 1980s and has since declined. Its best home today may be Alto Adige's Valle Isarco, where the Abbazia di Novacella makes vibrant, mineral versions, and Hokkaido in northern Japan, where its cold tolerance is a big advantage.
grapes.trivia: Kerner is one of the few modern crosses to produce a white grape from a red parent: Trollinger.

grapes.name: Scheurebe
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Georg Scheu at Alzey in 1916, recorded as Silvaner × Riesling; DNA in the late 1990s and 2000s ruled out Silvaner and identified Riesling × Bukettrebe (Bouquet Blanc). VIVC confirms.
grapes.hectares: About 1,400 ha in Germany (2018).
grapes.profile: Perhaps the best German crossing for quality. Scheurebe has a wild, exotic nose of pink grapefruit, blackcurrant leaf and passion fruit, thanks partly to the thiol 4MMP, the same compound that gives Sauvignon Blanc its blackcurrant note. Dry versions are fresh and pungent; sweet Auslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, especially from the Pfalz and Burgenland, are among Germany's most exciting dessert wines. Austria calls it Sämling 88, its seedling number at Alzey. Its pungent aromatics need full ripeness to avoid catty, green notes, so producers pick it late. Austrian growers in Burgenland and Styria grow small amounts.
grapes.trivia: Georg Scheu's seedling number 88 was so good that Austrians still label it by that number.

grapes.name: Bacchus
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Peter Morio and Bernhard Husfeld at Geilweilerhof in 1933: (Silvaner × Riesling) × Müller-Thurgau (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 1,700 ha in Germany (2020s) and a few hundred hectares in England, where it is the leading white for still wine (WineGB).
grapes.profile: A German crossing that has found a second life in England. Bacchus ripens early, even in cool, damp summers, and gives aromatic whites with elderflower, nettle and grapefruit that recall Sauvignon Blanc. In Germany it is mostly used in Franken and in blends. In England it has become the leading still white, the closest thing to a national grape for still wine, with producers such as Chapel Down and Lyme Bay showing its fresh, hedgerow character. England's cool summers keep its acidity high, and producers often blend it with Seyval Blanc or Ortega.
grapes.trivia: England's Bacchus is so associated with elderflower that some producers have nicknamed it 'England's Sauvignon'.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by August Herold at Weinsberg in 1955: Helfensteiner (Frühburgunder × Trollinger) × Heroldrebe (Portugieser × Blaufränkisch). Released 1979. Named after Immanuel Dornfeld, founder of the Württemberg viticulture school.
grapes.hectares: About 7,000 ha in Germany (2020s), its second most planted red after Spätburgunder.
grapes.profile: Germany's answer to the 1980s demand for deeper-coloured red wine. Dornfelder gives dark, soft, fruity reds with plum and blackberry, and its thick skins and loose bunches resist rot. Plantings exploded in the 1990s, and it is now Germany's second most planted red. Most is made into easy, slightly sweet red, but barrique-aged versions from the Pfalz show more structure. Its pedigree combines Pinot (via Frühburgunder), Trollinger, Portugieser and Blaufränkisch. Its rise reflected a shift in German taste after reunification, when domestic demand for red wine grew quickly.
grapes.trivia: Dornfelder plantings went from about 100 ha in 1970 to over 8,000 ha by 2006.

grapes.name: Blauer Portugieser
grapes.parentage_note: Blaue Zimmettraube × Grüner Silvaner per VIVC and Maul et al. The name comes from a legend that Johann von Fries brought it from Portugal to Austria in 1772; DNA shows it is central European.
grapes.hectares: About 2,500 ha in Germany (2020s), down from 4,400 ha in the 1990s.
grapes.profile: A productive, early-ripening red that makes light, soft, low-acid wine for everyday drinking, especially in the Pfalz, where it was once the most planted red, and as Weissherbst rosé. It has nothing to do with Portugal: DNA shows it is a child of Sylvaner and Blaue Zimmettraube, a half-sibling of Blaufränkisch. In Hungary's Villány, called Kékoportó, it used to be a signature early-release red. Its early ripening once made it a useful filler in cool northern regions, and in Austria's Thermenregion and Weinviertel it still makes simple, fruity reds for the Heuriger taverns.
grapes.trivia: Hungary renamed it Kékoportó in 2000 to avoid the reference to Portugal, after an EU agreement.

grapes.name: Elbling
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records unknown × Heunisch Weiss (Gouais Blanc); Regner and others suggest the other parent is a Traminer seedling, giving Elbling the same pedigree pattern as Riesling.
grapes.hectares: About 500 ha in Germany (2020s), almost all on the Upper Mosel; about 120 ha in Luxembourg.
grapes.profile: Possibly the oldest cultivated grape in Germany, often linked to vines the Romans planted along the Mosel. Elbling grows on the shell limestone of the Upper Mosel, upstream of Trier, unlike the Riesling slate of the middle Mosel. It gives light, sharp, low-alcohol wines with green apple and lemon, often made into Sekt. Its genetic profile suggests it shares parentage with Riesling, making the two near relatives. Luxembourg's Moselle, just across the river, uses it for light everyday wines and for Crémant de Luxembourg, and a few German growers now make serious, low-yield versions from old vines.
grapes.trivia: Some writers trace the name to Latin albus, white, or to vitis alba, a Roman description of Mosel vines.

grapes.name: Frühburgunder
grapes.parentage_note: An early-ripening mutation of Pinot Noir (Pinot Noir Précoce), long known in Germany.
grapes.hectares: About 250 ha in Germany (2008), revived from 15 ha in the 1960s.
grapes.profile: An early-ripening Pinot mutation that ripens up to two weeks before Pinot Noir, with lower acidity, deeper colour and soft cherry fruit. It nearly died out in the 1960s because of virus problems and low yields, until the Geisenheim institute bred healthier clones in the 1970s. The Ahr valley, with its steep slate slopes, is its heartland. It is also planted in England, where its early ripening is an asset. Its early ripening helps it avoid autumn rain, and the Ahr's producers, such as Meyer-Näkel and Deutzerhof, bottle it as a distinct, fragrant alternative to Spätburgunder.
grapes.trivia: Frühburgunder is one parent of Helfensteiner, and through it a grandparent of Dornfelder.

grapes.name: Regent
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Gerhardt Alleweldt at Geilweilerhof in 1967: Diana (Silvaner × Müller-Thurgau) × Chambourcin. Released 1996 (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 1,750 ha in Germany (2019), declining.
grapes.profile: Germany's most planted fungus-resistant red, known as a PIWI (pilzwiderstandsfähig, fungus-resistant). Regent carries resistance genes from its American hybrid ancestor Chambourcin, which reduces fungicide sprays by up to 80 percent. Because its crossing is mostly vinifera, the EU classifies it as vinifera and it can be used in quality wines. It gives dark, soft reds with cherry and blackcurrant. Its success in the late 1990s paved the way for newer PIWIs such as Cabernet Cortis and Souvignier Gris.
grapes.trivia: Regent was released for general cultivation in 1996 and became the first fungus-resistant grape to win a real commercial foothold in Germany.

grapes.name: Solaris
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Norbert Becker at the Staatliches Weinbauinstitut Freiburg in 1975: Merzling × Geisenheim 6493 (a Zarya Severa × Muscat Ottonel seedling, bringing in Vitis amurensis). VIVC confirms.
grapes.hectares: About 200 ha in Germany (2020) and the leading grape in Denmark and Sweden.
grapes.profile: The grape that makes Scandinavian wine possible. Solaris ripens extremely early, reaching high sugar even in short, cool northern summers, and resists fungal disease. It gives aromatic whites with pineapple, honey and citrus, and is used for dry, sweet and sparkling wines. In Denmark, Sweden and Norway it is the dominant variety, and it has become a symbol of the northward shift of viticulture as summers warm. Its sugar can climb so fast that growers in warm German sites must pick in August to avoid flabby, high-alcohol wine, while in Scandinavia the same trait is what makes ripening possible at all.
grapes.trivia: Solaris is grown at Lerkekåsa in Norway, one of the northernmost commercial vineyards in the world, at about 59 degrees north.

grapes.name: Souvignier Gris
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Norbert Becker in Freiburg in 1983. Long recorded as Cabernet Sauvignon × Bronner; DNA showed Seyval Blanc × Zähringer (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 770 ha in Germany (2020s), the fastest-growing variety in the country.
grapes.profile: A fungus-resistant (PIWI) white with pink-grey skins, fast becoming one of Germany's most planted new varieties because organic growers can farm it with few sprays. It gives full, aromatic whites with pear, quince and a hint of grapefruit, and handles both dry and sparkling styles. Its success shows how climate change and organic farming have revived interest in disease-resistant grapes, which were once considered second-rate. It is also popular in Switzerland and northern Italy, and its thick skins make it suitable for skin-contact styles, which some natural winemakers now favour.
grapes.trivia: Souvignier Gris grew by 170 ha in a single year, more than Chardonnay's increase in Germany during the same period.

grapes.name: Cabernet Cortis
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Norbert Becker in Freiburg in 1982: Cabernet Sauvignon × Solaris (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 50 ha in Germany (2020).
grapes.profile: A fungus-resistant red from Freiburg's PIWI programme, combining Cabernet Sauvignon's dark fruit and herbal notes with resistance genes inherited through Solaris. It ripens early enough for cool climates such as Denmark and Belgium and gives deep-coloured, Cabernet-like reds with blackcurrant and green pepper. Like other Freiburg PIWIs, its main appeal is that it needs far fewer fungicide sprays. It is also used in blends with other PIWIs, such as Cabernet Cantor and Regent, and is popular in Denmark, where cool summers make vinifera reds hard to ripen. Its tannins are firm and its colour deep, so it often goes into oak-aged blends.
grapes.trivia: Its name recalls both its Cabernet parent and cortex, bark, a reference to its hardy wood.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.parentage_note: Traminer (Savagnin) was identified as one parent by Ferdinand Regner in the late 1990s. In 2007 the other parent was found as a single abandoned vine in a pasture at St. Georgen am Leithagebirge near Eisenstadt, named St. Georgener-Rebe. Despite the name, Grüner Veltliner is unrelated to Roter Veltliner.
grapes.hectares: About 14,500 ha in Austria (2020 vineyard survey, ÖWM), roughly a third of the national vineyard.
grapes.profile: Austria's national grape. On the loess terraces of the Weinviertel and Wagram it gives fresh, peppery whites with green apple, lentil and the famous 'Pfefferl', a white-pepper note from rotundone. On the steep gneiss and granite terraces of the Wachau and Kamptal, from low yields, it becomes rich and complex, with Smaragd versions ageing for 20 years or more. In the 2000s sommeliers in New York and London turned it into a fashionable food white. Its pedigree adds another child to the vast Savagnin family.
grapes.trivia: The second parent survived only as a single, nearly dead vine in a field near Eisenstadt; it is now propagated and protected, and the spot is marked with a commemorative plaque.

grapes.name: St. Georgener-Rebe

origin.place: St. Georgen am Leithagebirge, near Eisenstadt, Burgenland, Austria

grapes.parentage_note: Discovered in 2000 by local vintner Michael Leberl as an old, abandoned vine in a pasture; identified by Ferdinand Regner (Klosterneuburg) in 2007 as the missing parent of Grüner Veltliner with Traminer.
grapes.hectares: One original vine plus propagated plants in collections.
grapes.profile: One of the most famous single vines in the world. A local grower noticed an old, gnarled vine in a field at St. Georgen near Eisenstadt, and DNA analysis by Ferdinand Regner showed it was the long-sought second parent of Grüner Veltliner. The vine was estimated to be several hundred years old, though no one can be sure. The discovery confirmed Grüner Veltliner's Austrian origins and showed how much heritage survives in forgotten corners. Cuttings have been propagated, and a few hundred vines now grow so the variety will not disappear.
grapes.trivia: The Austrian wine industry fenced off the original vine and placed a memorial stone beside it.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Friedrich (Fritz) Zweigelt at Klosterneuburg in 1922: St. Laurent × Blaufränkisch (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 6,000 ha in Austria (2023), its most planted red.
grapes.profile: Austria's most planted red, fruity and approachable with cherry, raspberry and a little spice. It combines Blaufränkisch's backbone with St. Laurent's softness and ripens reliably, which made it popular from the 1960s. Around Lake Neusiedl and in Carnuntum it makes juicy wines and is blended with Blaufränkisch in serious cuvées. Its name has become controversial because Friedrich Zweigelt was a committed Nazi who denounced colleagues in the 1930s and 1940s; some producers now prefer the old name Rotburger. It also makes rosé, sparkling wine and sweet wines in Burgenland.
grapes.trivia: Since the late 2010s a campaign by Austrian writers and some winemakers has urged growers to drop the name Zweigelt because of its creator's Nazi past and return to Rotburger.

grapes.name: Saint Laurent
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Pinot Noir × unknown; DNA confirms the long-suspected link to Pinot.
grapes.hectares: About 650 to 800 ha in Austria (2008 to 2020 surveys), with larger plantings in the Czech Republic and Slovakia (VIVC: 1,482 ha and 1,408 ha).
grapes.profile: A Pinot child that ripens early, often by Saint Lawrence's Day on 10 August, which is said to give it its name. It has dark cherry, plum and a velvety texture, with more colour than Pinot Noir but similar delicacy. It is hard to grow, prone to frost and coulure, and was almost abandoned in Austria before growers in the Thermenregion and Burgenland revived it. Its genes live on in Zweigelt, its most famous offspring. In the Czech Republic it is called Svatovavřinecké and is one of Moravia's main reds, made in styles from fresh and fruity to oak-aged.
grapes.trivia: Austrian growers say it begins to change colour around the feast of Saint Lawrence (10 August), hence the name.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch

origin.place: Lower Styria (now Slovenia) or wider Pannonian region

grapes.parentage_note: Blaue Zimmettraube × Gouais Blanc (Heunisch) per Maul, Regner and colleagues (2000s) and VIVC. Through Gouais Blanc it is a half-sibling of Chardonnay and Riesling; through Blaue Zimmettraube a half-sibling of Blauer Portugieser.
grapes.hectares: About 8,000 ha in Hungary (as Kékfrankos), about 2,600 ha in Austria (2020 survey) and about 1,700 ha in Germany (as Lemberger).
grapes.profile: Central Europe's great red, now Austria's most prestigious. It buds early, ripens late and gives dark cherry, blackberry and pepper, with fresh acidity and firm tannin. On the limestone and schist of the Leithaberg and the iron-rich schist of Eisenberg it is mineral and fine; in Mittelburgenland's heavy clays, nicknamed Blaufränkischland, rich and dark. Producers such as Moric (Roland Velich), Uwe Schiefer and Prieler showed in the 2000s that it could rival Pinot Noir and Syrah. In Hungary, as Kékfrankos, it is the most planted red, central to Eger's Bikavér and Sopron.
grapes.trivia: Its name probably refers to 'Frankish' grapes, a medieval label for noble varieties, as opposed to 'Hunnic' ones such as Gouais Blanc, its own father.

grapes.name: Blaue Zimmettraube
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records unknown × Blauer Gänsfüsser. It is the mother of Blaufränkisch (with Gouais Blanc) and of Blauer Portugieser (with Sylvaner).
grapes.hectares: Collection vines only.
grapes.profile: An almost extinct Styrian grape, identified by DNA as the mother of Blaufränkisch and of Blauer Portugieser. That makes this obscure 'cinnamon grape' a matriarch of central European red wine. Its own parent, Blauer Gänsfüsser, is equally obscure. Researchers such as Erika Maul at Geilweilerhof traced these links in the 2000s. Its discovery supports the idea that Lower Styria was a cradle of central European red varieties. The story it tells is that many central European reds share a handful of ancestors that crossed with the vigorous Gouais Blanc and with Sylvaner in mixed medieval vineyards.
grapes.trivia: Zimmet is an old German word for cinnamon, perhaps a reference to the colour or flavour of its berries.

grapes.name: Welschriesling
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Coccalona Nera × unknown, suggesting an Italian (Piedmontese) connection. Unrelated to Riesling.
grapes.hectares: About 40,000 ha across central Europe (2016), with Croatia's Graševina its largest single area.
grapes.profile: Not related to Riesling, but the most planted white of central and southeastern Europe. In Croatia's Slavonia, as Graševina, it is the national white, especially around Kutjevo, where Cistercian monks planted vines from 1232. In Hungary (Olaszrizling) it gives bitter-almond whites around Lake Balaton. Its greatest moments come from Austria's Neusiedlersee, where botrytis concentrates it into Trockenbeerenauslese: Alois Kracher's sweet wines made its reputation. Dry, it is fresh, with green apple and a slightly bitter finish. In Croatia, Graševina accounts for roughly a quarter of the national vineyard.
grapes.trivia: Welsch means 'foreign' or 'Latin' in old German, implying it came from Italy or France; the EU now bans calling it simply Riesling.

grapes.name: Rotgipfler
grapes.parentage_note: Traminer × Roter Veltliner per VIVC and Regner. A full sibling of Zierfandler is suspected.
grapes.hectares: About 110 ha (1999).
grapes.profile: One of the two traditional whites of Gumpoldskirchen, the spa-town wine district south of Vienna, on warm, limestone-rich slopes facing the Pannonian plain. Named for its red shoot tips (rot, red; Gipfel, tip), it gives full-bodied, spicy whites with yellow fruit and almond. It is traditionally blended with Zierfandler as Spätrot-Rotgipfler. It inherited its aromatic character from its Traminer parent. Its high sugar levels make it powerful, often reaching 14 percent alcohol or more, and producers such as Stadlmann and Johanneshof Reinisch bottle it as a single-variety wine.
grapes.trivia: Spätrot-Rotgipfler blends from Gumpoldskirchen were among the most fashionable whites in 19th-century Vienna.

grapes.name: Zierfandler
grapes.parentage_note: Probably Roter Veltliner × a Traminer-like vine (Regner); VIVC lists no confirmed pedigree.
grapes.hectares: About 100 ha in Austria (1999).
grapes.profile: A rare, late-ripening Thermenregion grape with pink-tinged skins that turn red as they ripen, hence its synonym Spätrot (late red). It gives powerful, long-lived whites with high acidity and flavours of quince, orange peel and nuts. It is prone to botrytis, which makes it good for sweet wines too. Gumpoldskirchen growers, such as Stadlmann and Zierer, have kept it alive. It is a late-ripening, low-yielding grape, picked well into October, and its thick skins allow it to hang long. The best wines age for 20 years and more.
grapes.trivia: There are fewer than 100 ha of Zierfandler in the world, almost all within a few kilometres of Gumpoldskirchen.

grapes.name: Neuburger
grapes.parentage_note: Roter Veltliner × Silvaner per VIVC and Regner (1990s).
grapes.hectares: About 500 to 1,000 ha (2020s), declining.
grapes.profile: An Austrian white with a charming origin story: in 1850, legend says, a bundle of vine cuttings washed ashore from the Danube near Spitz in the Wachau, and growers planted it. The resulting wine is round, nutty and low in acid, with notes of almond, honey and bread. It is best after a few years in bottle. DNA shows it is a natural cross of Roter Veltliner and Sylvaner. It is not highly aromatic, but its soft texture suits food, and Wachau and Leithaberg producers have made a niche for it. Older bottles develop notes of walnut and toast.
grapes.trivia: Spitz still celebrates the riverbank where the mythical bundle of Neuburger cuttings is said to have landed.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.parentage_note: Alba Imputotato × Heunisch Weiss (Gouais Blanc) per VIVC; Gouais was first identified as a parent by Boursiquot and colleagues. It is a parent of Hárslevelű.
grapes.hectares: About 4,000 ha in Hungary (2006), more than 60 percent of Tokaj.
grapes.profile: The soul of Tokaj. Furmint's thin skins welcome botrytis, and its high acidity, sustained through the noble rot, gives Tokaji Aszú its electric balance of sugar and acid, with apricot, orange peel, honey and smoke. The volcanic soils of the Zemplén hills, with their rhyolite, andesite and zeolite, give the wines a mineral tension. Since the 1990s Tokaj producers such as István Szepsy, Royal Tokaji and Disznókő have made dry Furmint that is among the most exciting whites of central Europe. In Slovenia it is Šipon.
grapes.trivia: Some sources say Furmint came to Tokaj with Walloon settlers in the 13th century, but its parent Gouais Blanc and the local Alba Imputotato point to a regional origin.

grapes.name: Hárslevelű
grapes.parentage_note: Furmint × Tzimliansky Belyi per VIVC (marker-confirmed).
grapes.hectares: About 1,500 ha in Hungary (2010s), about a quarter of Tokaj.
grapes.profile: Tokaj's second grape, a child of Furmint. Its name means 'linden leaf', after the shape of its leaves. Hárslevelű is more aromatic and softer than Furmint, with linden-blossom, honey and spice notes, and it adds perfume to Aszú blends. It also makes fine dry and late-harvest wines. Debrő near Eger has a long tradition of sweet, aromatic Hárslevelű. Its thick skins resist rot less well than Furmint's, but it shrivels well, and in Tokaj it is often used to add a honeyed, floral note to Aszú and late-harvest wines. Its large, loose bunches help air flow in humid autumns.
grapes.trivia: Hárslevelű is also grown in South Africa, where a few producers bottle it as a varietal white.

grapes.name: Kadarka

origin.place: Balkans (Lake Skadar region or Ottoman Thrace)

grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. A recent study claims Papazkarası from Turkish Thrace as a parent; not yet confirmed in VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 700 ha in Hungary (2008) and about 3,000 ha in Bulgaria as Gamza (2009).
grapes.profile: Hungary's historic red, probably arriving with Serbian refugees fleeing the Ottomans in the 16th and 17th centuries. It was the main grape of Egri Bikavér (Bull's Blood) in its heyday and of Szekszárd's reds. Kadarka ripens late, rots easily and suffers from uneven ripening, so after phylloxera and under communism it was replaced with hardier grapes. A revival since the 2000s, led by producers such as Heimann in Szekszárd, has brought back its light, spicy, red-fruited style. It is still grown in Bulgaria as Gamza, in Serbia and in Romania.
grapes.trivia: Its name may derive from Skadar (Shkodër), the lake on the Albania-Montenegro border.

grapes.name: Juhfark
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 150 ha (2008), mostly on Somló.
grapes.profile: A rare white from Somló, a small, isolated extinct volcano in western Hungary with basalt-rich soils. Its name means 'sheep's tail', describing the long, curved bunches. The wine is austere, high in acidity, smoky and salty when young, needing years to open. A legend says Habsburg nobles drank Somló wine on their wedding night to ensure a male heir. Producers such as Fekete Béla and Kreinbacher make its reputation. Its high acidity and austere minerality give the wines an ability to age for decades, and producers increasingly ferment it in large wooden casks.
grapes.trivia: Somló wine was so prized at the Habsburg court that it was nicknamed 'the wine of wedding nights'.

grapes.name: Petite Arvine
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. José Vouillamoz's DNA studies (2000s) found no close relatives outside the Valais, supporting a local origin.
grapes.hectares: About 150 to 200 ha in Switzerland (2009 figure 154 ha), plus Valle d'Aosta.
grapes.profile: The noblest of the Valais's native whites. On dry, sunny terraces above the Rhône around Fully and Sion, it gives salty, intense whites with grapefruit, rhubarb and a distinctive saline finish. It is made dry and also as flétri, late-harvested and shrivelled on the vine. Valle d'Aosta across the Alps has adopted it too. The Valais has kept old indigenous grapes thanks to its isolation and steep terraces. Its yields are low and it ripens late, so it needs the warmest, sunniest sites of the Valais, often terraced slopes with dry-stone walls.
grapes.trivia: Valais growers often describe Petite Arvine's tell-tale finish as 'salty', a characteristic attributed to the grape rather than the soil.

grapes.name: Cornalin
grapes.parentage_note: Swiss Cornalin (Rouge du Pays) is Petit Rouge × Mayolet, two Aosta Valley grapes, per Vouillamoz (2003). Italy's Cornalin d'Aoste is a different variety, an offspring of Rouge du Pays.
grapes.hectares: About 120 ha (2009).
grapes.profile: A Valais red that was rare by the 1970s because of low yields and irregular ripening, and was rescued by a group of growers. It gives dark, spicy, cherry-scented reds with good acidity. DNA shows its parents both came over the Alps from the Aosta Valley, illustrating how varieties crossed mountain passes. Confusingly, Aosta's own Cornalin is a different variety, a child of Valais Cornalin. It needs warm, dry slopes and careful yield control to ripen fully, which the sunny, dry Valais can provide. Producers around Salgesch and Sierre make the best versions, which age for a decade or more.
grapes.trivia: The confusion of two Cornalins across the Alps was untangled by José Vouillamoz's DNA work.

grapes.name: Žametovka
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (not found in VIVC under this name).
grapes.hectares: About 1,000 ha (2010s), mainly Dolenjska.
grapes.profile: A light Slovenian red, the main grape of Cviček, a pale, low-alcohol red blend that mixes red and white grapes in the Dolenjska hills. Its world fame comes from a single vine: the Stara Trta, or Old Vine, on the façade of a house in Maribor's Lent district, recognised by Guinness World Records as the oldest vine still producing grapes, over 400 years old. The vine yields a few dozen litres of wine each year, bottled in small flasks given as diplomatic gifts.
grapes.trivia: Bottles from Maribor's Old Vine are given as official gifts, and cuttings have been planted in twin towns around the world.

grapes.name: Muscat Ottonel
grapes.parentage_note: Bred in 1839 by Jean-Pierre Vibert and the Moreau-Robert nursery in Angers: Chasselas × Muscat d'Eisenstadt (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 2,000 ha in Romania (2010s), plus Austria and Alsace.
grapes.profile: A delicate, early-ripening muscat bred in the Loire, gentler and less acidic than Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. Its floral, orange-blossom perfume suits cool climates, so it spread through Alsace, Austria, Hungary and Romania. In Burgenland's Neusiedlersee it makes some of the finest sweet botrytis wines, and in Romania it is a staple for off-dry whites. It ripens early and is sensitive to coulure, which can lower yields. Its gentle muscat perfume is easily lost if wines are made too sweet or aged too long, so most are drunk young. In Alsace it is blended with Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains in the region's dry muscat wines.
grapes.trivia: It was bred in Angers, the same nursery that produced Madeleine Royale, the parent of Müller-Thurgau.

grapes.name: Grasă de Cotnari
grapes.parentage_note: Gouais Blanc × unknown per VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 640 ha (2010).
grapes.profile: The 'fat grape' of Cotnari in Romanian Moldavia, whose sweet, botrytised wines were famous in the 15th century under Prince Stephen the Great and later compared with Tokaji. Its thin skins and high sugar welcome noble rot, giving rich, honeyed whites with high acidity. In Tokaj it was known as Kövérszőlő and was part of the Aszú blend before phylloxera. Cotnari's vineyards lie on gentle hills in northeast Romania where autumn fogs encourage botrytis. Today most Grasă de Cotnari is made off-dry or sweet, and a cooperative and several private estates continue the tradition. It is often blended with Fetească Albă, Tămâioasă Românească and Frâncușă.
grapes.trivia: Prince Dimitrie Cantemir, in his Descriptio Moldaviae (1716), ranked Cotnari wine above all others of Moldavia and even compared it favourably with Tokaji.

grapes.name: Fetească Neagră
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 ha in Romania (2020s) plus Moldova.
grapes.profile: Romania's 'black maiden', a native red increasingly used for premium wines. It gives deep colour, plum, blackcurrant and spice with moderate acidity, ageing well in oak. It nearly disappeared under communism, when international varieties dominated state plantations, but has expanded since 2000 in Dealu Mare and in Moldova. It is cold-hardy but sensitive to spring frost. Producers such as Davino, Crama Oprișor and Lacerta in Dealu Mare and Castel Mimi and Et Cetera in Moldova have built its modern reputation, often blending it with Cabernet or Merlot.
grapes.trivia: Its name, 'black maiden', has white and royal counterparts: Fetească Albă and Fetească Regală.

grapes.name: Fetească Albă
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). It is a parent of Fetească Regală (with Grasă de Cotnari, per Romanian studies).
grapes.hectares: About 13,000 ha in Romania (2010).
grapes.profile: The 'white maiden', one of Romania's most planted grapes, giving delicate, floral whites with peach and a light muscat touch. It thrives in Transylvania's Târnave plateau and Moldavia's hills. In Hungary it is called Leányka, used in Eger whites. It is often made off-dry. Romanian researchers consider it a parent, with Grasă de Cotnari, of Fetească Regală. It is also widely grown in Moldova and Ukraine, where it was planted under Soviet-era collective farms, and in Hungary as Leányka. It is often made sparkling.
grapes.trivia: Its offspring Fetească Regală, a natural cross found in Transylvania in the 1920s, is now one of Romania's most planted whites.

grapes.name: Băbească Neagră
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). Moldova's Rară Neagră is the same variety.
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 ha in Romania (2010), plus Moldova.
grapes.profile: A light, high-acid red from southern Moldavia, with sour cherry, cranberry and spice, often compared to Pinot Noir in weight. Its name means 'grandmother's black', perhaps from the old women who grew it. In Moldova, as Rară Neagră, it has become a signature of the Purcari region, blended with Saperavi and Cabernet in the historic Negru de Purcari. Its light colour and fresh acidity make it suitable for rosés and light reds. Moldova's Purcari estate has made it a flagship, and growers in Romania's Nicorești have revived old plantings.
grapes.trivia: The Purcari winery says its Negru de Purcari won a gold medal in Paris in 1878 and was served at the British royal table.

grapes.name: Mavrud
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). A proposed link to Mourvèdre is not supported by DNA.
grapes.profile: Bulgaria's flagship native red, grown in the Thracian lowlands around Asenovgrad and Plovdiv. Late-ripening and small-berried, it gives inky, tannic wines with blackberry, dried plum and spice that age well. Modern producers such as Zagreus and Villa Yustina make serious oak-aged versions. Its thick skins and high tannin mean it is often aged in oak for one to two years, and its fruit can turn raisined in hot years, so growers pick carefully. Plovdiv's wine trade, with roots in Thracian and Roman times, made it the region's emblem.
grapes.trivia: Bulgarian folklore says Khan Krum ordered every vine uprooted, and that a mother who kept one secretly fed her son Mavrud its wine, making him the bravest warrior in the land.

grapes.name: Shiroka Melnishka
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. It is a parent of Melnik 55 (Ranna Melnishka) with Valdiguié (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares around Melnik.
grapes.profile: A late-ripening, small-berried grape from Melnik, Bulgaria's smallest town, set among sandstone pyramids in the warm Struma valley near the Greek border. It gives light, spicy, tobacco-scented reds that develop well with age. In the 19th century Melnik's wine was exported to Venice and Vienna, and Winston Churchill is said to have ordered it regularly. Its early-ripening offspring, Melnik 55, was bred in the 1960s. It ripens late, often well into October, which suits the long, warm autumns of the Struma valley.
grapes.trivia: Melnik producers like to say Winston Churchill ordered their wine regularly; the story is proudly told but hard to document.

grapes.name: Vranac
grapes.parentage_note: Duljenga × Kratošija (Zinfandel/Tribidrag) per VIVC, making Vranac a child of Zinfandel.
grapes.hectares: About 2,000 ha in Montenegro and more in North Macedonia as Vranec (2020s).
grapes.profile: Montenegro's national grape and the main red of North Macedonia. Its name means 'black stallion'. It gives deep, plush reds with dark cherry, plum and chocolate. The state-founded Plantaže estate on the Ćemovsko Polje near Podgorica, one of the largest single vineyards in Europe at about 2,300 ha, grows it on a vast scale. DNA shows its father is Kratošija, Montenegro's name for Zinfandel. Its deep colour and generous fruit made it popular across Yugoslavia, and it remains the region's best-known red. In North Macedonia's Tikveš it covers large areas.
grapes.trivia: Plantaže's Šipčanik winery is set in a former Yugoslav military aircraft hangar dug into a hill.

grapes.name: Prokupac
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 3,000 to 4,000 ha (2020s estimates).
grapes.profile: Serbia's historic red, grown in Serbia since at least the Middle Ages. It gives medium-bodied, bright reds with sour cherry, red pepper and herbs. Once dominant in Serbian vineyards, it lost ground to international varieties after phylloxera and during the Yugoslav era. Small producers in Župa have revived it since the 2010s, and it is now promoted as Serbia's signature grape. It is often blended with international grapes but increasingly bottled alone. Its resistance to drought and cold winters suits Serbia's continental climate, and it shares its light colour and spice with Kadarka.
grapes.trivia: Aleksandrovac in the Župa district holds the Župska berba every September, one of the oldest harvest festivals in the Balkans.

grapes.name: Žilavka
grapes.parentage_note: Alba Imputotato × unknown per VIVC; a half-sibling of Furmint through Alba Imputotato.
grapes.hectares: Several hundred hectares around Mostar.
grapes.profile: Herzegovina's main white, grown on the stony, karstic soils around Mostar under hot Mediterranean summers. It gives full-bodied whites with apricot, almond and herbal notes, often with a distinctive bitterness and good acidity. It is usually blended with a little Bena and Krkošija. The region also grows the red Blatina, a child of Primitivo. Its relationship to Furmint, through their shared parent, connects Balkan and Pannonian grape families. Herzegovina's vineyards lie on rocky ground with strong sun and dry summers, and the wines are usually high in alcohol. Producers such as Vinarija Škegro and Andrija Čitluk make modern versions.
grapes.trivia: Its name probably comes from žila, vein, after the visible veins in its translucent ripe berries.

grapes.name: Pošip
grapes.parentage_note: Zlatarica Blatska Bijela × Bratkovina Bijela per VIVC, both Korčula varieties.
grapes.hectares: About 500 ha (2020s).
grapes.profile: Croatia's leading Dalmatian white, discovered on the island of Korčula in the late 19th century. Pošip ripens early, keeps acidity and gives full, aromatic whites with apricot, fig and Mediterranean herbs. It was the first Croatian white to receive protected status in 1967. Its parents, also from Korčula, show the island's role as a cradle of local grapes. It is now grown along the Dalmatian coast and islands, where it adapts well to heat. Producers such as Grgić on Pelješac and Toreta on Korčula make reference examples.
grapes.trivia: According to Korčula tradition, a farmer from Smokvica, Marin Tomasović, found the original vine growing wild in the woods.

grapes.name: Teran
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Terrano as unknown × Refosco Nostrano. It is distinct from Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso.
grapes.hectares: About 800 ha in Slovenia (2008).
grapes.profile: The red of the Karst plateau above Trieste, grown on iron-rich terra rossa over limestone. It gives sharp, deeply coloured reds with sour cherry, blackberry and a rustic, gamey edge, traditionally drunk with Karst prosciutto (pršut). Slovenia registered 'Teran' as a protected name in 2006, leading to a long dispute with Croatia, whose Istrian producers also use it. The EU allowed Croatian use in 2017 under specific conditions. Its acidity is so high that it pairs well with fatty cured meats and game.
grapes.trivia: Teran was long believed to be good for health because of its iron content, and Karst families gave it to new mothers.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records unknown × Heunisch Weiss (Gouais Blanc).
grapes.hectares: About 2,200 to 2,500 ha (2013), entirely in Greece.
grapes.profile: Greece's most tannic and long-lived red, the 'sour black' of Naoussa, on the slopes of Mount Vermio. Pale in colour but high in acidity and tannin, it gives tomato, olive, sour cherry and dried herb flavours that develop over decades, often compared to Nebbiolo. Naoussa became one of Greece's first protected appellations in 1971. In cooler Amyntaio it makes rosés and sparkling wine. Producers such as Thymiopoulos and Kir-Yianni have modernised its image. It also makes sparkling and rosé wines in Amyntaio.
grapes.trivia: Naoussa's Boutari winery, founded in 1879, released one of Greece's first bottled red wines from Xinomavro.

grapes.name: Assyrtiko
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 1,500 to 2,000 ha in Greece (2020s).
grapes.profile: One of the great white grapes of the Mediterranean, keeping fierce acidity in heat that would flatten most varieties. On Santorini's pumice and volcanic ash, with almost no rain, ungrafted vines are trained in the kouloura, a low basket shape that shelters the grapes from the island's strong winds. The wines are bone dry, saline and smoky, with lemon and flint, and can age for decades. Vinsanto, made from sun-dried grapes, is the island's historic sweet wine. Its heat tolerance has made it a climate-change candidate in Australia and South Africa.
grapes.trivia: Some of Santorini's kouloura vines are estimated to have root systems hundreds of years old, because the island's soils kept phylloxera away.

grapes.name: Agiorgitiko
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 5,000 to 6,000 ha (2012), Greece's most planted red.
grapes.profile: The grape of Nemea, the classical site of Hercules' lion. It is versatile: soft and fruity at low altitude, structured and age-worthy from the higher slopes around Koutsi and Asprokampos. It gives plush red fruit, sweet spice and smooth tannins. Nemea is Greece's largest red-wine appellation, and producers such as Gaia and Skouras raised its profile from the 1990s. It also makes rosé and sweet wines. Its name honours Saint George, and the Nemea zone, at altitudes from 250 to 850 metres, is divided informally into lower, middle and upper zones.
grapes.trivia: Nemea's wine was nicknamed the 'blood of Hercules', after the hero's first labour.

grapes.name: Moschofilero
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 500 ha (2008).
grapes.profile: A pink-skinned, highly aromatic Greek grape grown on the high plateau of Mantinia in the Peloponnese, at about 650 metres. It gives light, crisp whites with rose petal, lychee and citrus, sometimes compared to Gewürztraminer but drier and lighter. Mantinia, one of Greece's coolest wine regions, was granted protected status in 1971. Its skins can also make rosé and sparkling wines. Its pink skins give it a slight colour if left in contact with the juice, which some producers use to make rosé. It is often harvested early to keep its freshness and low alcohol, sometimes around 11 percent.
grapes.trivia: Mantinia's harvest can run into late October, among the latest in Greece.

grapes.name: Malagousia
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: Several hundred ha (2020s), up from a few vines in the 1970s.
grapes.profile: Saved from extinction by Professor Vassilis Logothetis of the University of Thessaloniki, who collected surviving vines in the 1970s, and by winemaker Evangelos Gerovassiliou, who planted it at Epanomi near Thessaloniki in the 1980s. It gives perfumed, full-bodied whites with peach, jasmine and mint. Its success made it a symbol of the Greek revival of native grapes. Its intense aroma comes from terpenes similar to those in Muscat. It is now grown widely across Greece and has inspired other revival projects, including those for Limniona and Vidiano.
grapes.trivia: Gerovassiliou's Malagousia was the first commercial bottling, released in the 1990s.

grapes.name: Mavrodaphne
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 550 ha (1999).
grapes.profile: The grape of Mavrodaphne of Patras, a sweet, fortified red aged oxidatively in solera-like systems, with raisin, coffee and chocolate notes. Its fame began with Gustav Clauss, a Bavarian who founded the Achaia Clauss winery near Patras in 1861 and, legend says, named the wine after his fiancée Daphne, who died young. Dry versions are now made on Cephalonia and in Achaia. Mavrodaphne of Patras must be blended with Korinthiaki (the Corinth currant grape), and the dry wines from Cephalonia show more fresh black fruit and violet.
grapes.trivia: Achaia Clauss still keeps casks of Mavrodaphne dating back to the 19th century in its hilltop cellars above Patras.

grapes.name: Savatiano
grapes.parentage_note: Rhoditis × Karystino per VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 12,700 ha (1999), Greece's most planted white.
grapes.profile: The base of retsina, the pine-resin-flavoured wine of Attica. Drought-tolerant, it grows on dry, unirrigated bush vines in the Mesogeia plain east of Athens. Long dismissed, it has been revived by producers such as Papagiannakos and Mylonas, who make dry, mineral, age-worthy whites from old vines. Retsina itself has had a quality revival with lighter resin and better base wine. Its drought tolerance makes it valuable in a warming Attica, and growers are reviving old bush vines planted decades ago. Its neutral flavour suits retsina because the resin dominates.
grapes.trivia: Retsina's resin tradition comes from the ancient practice of sealing amphorae with pine resin to protect the wine from air.

grapes.name: Xynisteri
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 2,200 ha (2010), Cyprus's main white.
grapes.profile: Cyprus's main white grape, grown in the Troodos Mountains at up to 1,500 metres, where altitude tempers the island's heat. Cyprus has never had phylloxera, so vines grow on their own roots. Xynisteri gives fresh, light whites with citrus and herbs, and is used with Mavro in Commandaria, the sweet sun-dried wine that claims to be the oldest named wine still in production, linked to the Knights of St John at Kolossi in the 12th century. It is increasingly made as a fresh varietal white.
grapes.trivia: Commandaria's name comes from the Grande Commanderie of the Knights Hospitaller at Kolossi Castle.

grapes.name: Limniona
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: Under 100 ha (2020s).
grapes.profile: A rare Thessalian red rescued from near extinction by Christos Zafeirakis of Tyrnavos, who propagated surviving vines in the 2000s. It gives fragrant, mid-weight reds with red fruit, herbs and spice, with good acidity and fine tannin. Its name may relate to Limnos, though no link is proven. It has become a favourite of Greek sommeliers. Its tolerance of heat and fresh acidity make it attractive as a climate-adapted red, and plantings are slowly increasing in Thessaly, Macedonia and the Peloponnese.
grapes.trivia: Domaine Zafeirakis's Limniona was one of the first to show the grape's potential and inspired other Thessalian growers.

grapes.name: Vidiano
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Albanello × unknown.
grapes.hectares: A few hundred ha (2020s), growing.
grapes.profile: A Cretan white revived from a handful of surviving vines from the 1990s onwards, with the Lyrarakis family among its first champions. It gives textured whites with apricot, peach and herbs, keeping acidity in Crete's heat. Its thick skins and resistance to drought suit Crete's hot, dry climate, and producers now make both fresh and oak-aged versions. Its ability to age has surprised many, and it is often called the Cretan answer to Viognier because of its apricot and floral notes.
grapes.trivia: Vidiano's parent Albanello is a Sicilian grape, an unexpected genetic bridge between two of the Mediterranean's great islands.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown; VIVC lists Greece as country of origin. It is one parent of Muscat of Alexandria (with Heptakilo) and of Moscato Giallo and many other Muscats, making it the founder of the Muscat family (Crespan and Milani, 2001).
grapes.hectares: About 30,000 to 35,000 ha worldwide (2016); Italy 13,279 ha (2000, VIVC), Spain 21,902 ha as Moscatel de Grano Menudo (2015).
grapes.profile: The oldest and finest of the Muscat family and the grape whose aroma most resembles fresh grapes, thanks to high levels of linalool, geraniol and nerol. Many historians identify it with the apiana grape that Roman writers said attracted bees. It makes the lightly fizzy, low-alcohol Moscato d'Asti and Asti, the fortified Vins Doux Naturels of Beaumes-de-Venise and Frontignan, the sweet wines of Samos and Rutherglen's dark Muscats, as well as dry, floral whites in Alsace and Styria. Berries can be white, pink or brown. Its offspring include Muscat of Alexandria, one of the oldest crosses in the vine world.
grapes.trivia: Its berries are so loved by bees and wasps that the Romans called it apiana, the bee grape, a name that some link to the Muscat family.

grapes.name: Muscat of Alexandria

origin.place: Eastern Mediterranean (Egypt by legend; Greece or southern Italy likely)

grapes.parentage_note: Muscat à Petits Grains × Heptakilo (a Greek table grape) per Crespan and Milani (2001) and VIVC. It is a parent of Grillo, Torrontés Riojano, Cereza, Criolla Grande and Italia table grape.
grapes.hectares: About 40,000 ha worldwide (VIVC sum c. 38,000 ha); Spain 10,318 ha (2015).
grapes.profile: A heat-loving, ancient Muscat grown for wine, raisins, table grapes and brandy. Its large berries have a heady, grapey, slightly coarse perfume. As Zibibbo, it makes Passito di Pantelleria, from grapes sun-dried on the volcanic island between Sicily and Tunisia, where its bush training (vite ad alberello) was inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2014. Portugal's Moscatel de Setúbal and Spain's sweet Málaga are classics. In South Africa it is Hanepoot, long used for sweet wines and table grapes. It parented Argentina's Torrontés and Criollas with Listán Prieto, a crucial link in New World grape history.
grapes.trivia: Pantelleria's head-trained vines are planted in hollows dug into volcanic soil to shelter them from the island's constant wind.

grapes.name: Saperavi
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 9,000 to 10,000 ha in Georgia (2020s National Wine Agency estimates).
grapes.profile: Georgia's great red, one of the few red-fleshed vinifera grapes in the world: its name means 'dye' or 'paint'. It gives inky, high-acid wines with blackberry, black cherry, liquorice and smoke, able to age for decades. It is made both in European style and in qvevri, buried clay vessels in which grapes ferment on their skins. Kakheti's Alazani valley holds the classic appellations: Mukuzani for dry reds, Kindzmarauli and Akhasheni for naturally semi-sweet ones. Its cold hardiness made it a Soviet staple and has brought it to New York's Finger Lakes.
grapes.trivia: Because its flesh is red, Saperavi can make deep-coloured wine without long skin contact, something only a handful of vinifera grapes can do.

grapes.name: Rkatsiteli
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records a reconstructed Georgian genotype × unknown, a parentage it shares with Mtsvane Kakhuri, suggesting the two are half-siblings.
grapes.hectares: About 50,000 to 60,000 ha worldwide (2016); Georgia's most planted grape.
grapes.profile: One of the oldest cultivated grapes in the world and the most planted variety of the Soviet Union, where by 1978 it supplied 18 percent of all wine. Its name means 'red stem'. Cold-hardy and high in acidity, it was used for everything from table wine to brandy and sherry-style wines. In Georgia it is the main white of Kakheti and, fermented in qvevri with skins and stems for months, produces amber wines with apricot, walnut, honey and firm tannin. Gorbachev's 1985 anti-alcohol campaign destroyed huge plantings across the USSR. It has followers in New York and Virginia.
grapes.trivia: Konstantin Frank, a Ukrainian-born viticulturist, planted Rkatsiteli in New York's Finger Lakes from the late 1950s, among the first serious vinifera plantings in the eastern United States.

grapes.name: Mtsvane Kakhuri
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records the same reconstructed Georgian parent as Rkatsiteli, making them likely half-siblings.
grapes.hectares: A few thousand ha in Georgia (estimates vary).
grapes.profile: The 'green' grape of Kakheti, more aromatic and delicate than Rkatsiteli, often blended with it in Tsinandali, Georgia's classic European-style white. Manavi, a village with its own protected appellation, is its best-known home. Fermented in qvevri on skins, it gives aromatic amber wines with citrus, tropical fruit and white flowers. Its relationship to Rkatsiteli shows the depth of Georgian grape diversity, which counts more than 500 native varieties. It has more natural acidity than Rkatsiteli and is often harvested a little earlier.
grapes.trivia: Georgia counts more than 500 native grape varieties, and its national collection at Jighaura preserves several hundred of them.

grapes.name: Kisi
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Zakatalis Tetri × unknown.
grapes.hectares: A few hundred ha (2020s), up from 50 ha in 2008.
grapes.profile: A Kakhetian white that nearly vanished and has become one of Georgia's most fashionable grapes. Grown around Akhmeta in the upper Alazani valley, it gives full, aromatic wines with pear, apricot, marigold and tobacco, and in qvevri a complex, tannic amber wine. Its revival owes much to small producers such as Pheasant's Tears and Our Wine. Kisi is now a symbol of Georgia's return to native grapes after Soviet standardisation. Its berries are prone to sunburn, so growers often leave more leaf cover than with Rkatsiteli.
grapes.trivia: VIVC recorded only about 50 ha of Kisi in 2008; plantings have grown several-fold since, as amber wine became fashionable abroad.

grapes.name: Chinuri
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Mskhviltvala Tetri × unknown.
grapes.hectares: About 900 ha (2004).
grapes.profile: The white grape of Kartli, the region around Gori and Mtskheta west of Tbilisi. It ripens late with high acidity and moderate sugar, which suits traditional sparkling wine (Atenuri) and fresh, light whites. In qvevri it gives restrained amber wines with herbs and green apple. Iago Bitarishvili's qvevri Chinuri from Chardakhi was one of the bottlings that brought Georgia's natural wines to international attention in the 2000s. Its late ripening and high acidity suit Kartli's cooler continental climate, and growers there often pick in October. Producers are now making it in qvevri, as orange wine, and as pét-nat.
grapes.trivia: Atenuri takes its name from the Ateni gorge near Gori, site of the 7th-century Ateni Sioni church.

grapes.name: Areni
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC prime name Areni Sev).
grapes.hectares: Several thousand hectares (2020s), Armenia's leading red.
grapes.profile: Armenia's signature red, named after the village beside the Areni-1 cave, where archaeologists found a winery dated to around 4000 BC. Grown at 1,000 to 1,700 metres on volcanic soils, often ungrafted because phylloxera never reached many high Armenian vineyards, it gives medium-bodied reds with sour cherry, black pepper and dried herbs, often compared with Pinot Noir. Producers such as Zorah and Trinity Canyon have brought it international attention since the 2010s, some fermenting it in karas, traditional clay jars.
grapes.trivia: The Areni-1 cave winery, published in 2011, held a grape press, fermentation vessels and grape seeds about 6,100 years old.

grapes.name: Voskehat
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC prime name Voskeat).
grapes.hectares: A few thousand hectares.
grapes.profile: Armenia's most important white grape; its name means 'golden berry'. It grows on volcanic soils at altitude, keeping acidity and giving apricot, honey and wildflower notes. It makes dry whites, sweet wines and amber wines fermented in karas. Its ability to retain freshness at high altitude has made it a focus of Armenia's post-Soviet wine revival. Armenian producers have planted it at more than 1,500 metres in Vayots Dzor, and it is also used for sparkling wine. It is often blended with Kangun or Garan Dmak.
grapes.trivia: In Soviet times most Voskehat went into fortified and dessert wines, part of an Armenian industry geared to brandy and sweet wine.

grapes.name: Krasnostop Zolotovsky
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: A few hundred ha (2020s).
grapes.profile: A Don Cossack red grape whose name means 'red foot' for its red stems. It gives deep-coloured, high-acid wines with dark cherry, plum and spice. Like other Don varieties it was traditionally buried in soil over winter to survive the cold. Russian producers such as Vedernikov have championed it as a national grape, and plantings are spreading into the Krasnodar region. It is often blended with Tsimlyansky Cherny and Sibirkovy, other Don natives. Its ability to hold acidity in hot summers makes it a promising grape as Russian viticulture expands.
grapes.trivia: Many Don valley growers still bury their vines under earth each autumn to protect them from severe winter cold.

grapes.name: Tsimlyansky Cherny
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. A white form, Tsimlyansky Bely, is a parent of Hárslevelű with Furmint (VIVC), linking the Don valley to Tokaj.
grapes.hectares: A few hundred ha.
grapes.profile: A Cossack grape famous for Tsimlyanskoe, a red sparkling wine made since the 18th century near Tsimlyansk on the Don. Its wines are dark, with red fruit and spice. The related white Tsimlyansky Bely appears in VIVC as a parent of Hárslevelű, a surprising link between the Don valley and Tokaj, probably through trade along the Danube and Black Sea. Pushkin mentions it in Eugene Onegin. Its sparkling wine tradition has been revived since the 2000s by producers along the Don.
grapes.trivia: Tsimlyanskoe sparkling red was fashionable in 19th-century Russia and appears in the literature of the period, Pushkin included.

grapes.name: Öküzgözü
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (not confirmed in VIVC).
grapes.hectares: A few thousand hectares (2010s).
grapes.profile: 'Ox eye' in Turkish, for its large, round dark berries. Grown in the Euphrates valley around Elazığ, it gives soft, juicy reds with red cherry, plum and fresh acidity, often blended with the tannic Boğazkere. Turkey is one of the world's largest grape producers, but most grapes are eaten or dried, and wine is a small, heavily taxed industry. Producers such as Kayra and Doluca have championed native grapes since the 1990s. Its soft tannins and juicy fruit make it suitable for early drinking and for rosé.
grapes.trivia: Turkey has one of the largest vineyard areas in the world, but only a small fraction of its grapes are made into wine.

grapes.name: Boğazkere
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.profile: Its name means 'throat burner', a fair warning about its fierce tannins. Grown in the hot, dry Tigris basin around Diyarbakır, it gives dark, powerful reds with black fruit, liquorice and spice. It is usually blended with Öküzgözü, which softens it, and the combination is Turkey's classic red blend. Modern oak-aged versions show its ageing potential. It ripens late in the scorching southeast, where temperatures often exceed 40 degrees in summer, and it needs careful handling to avoid harsh tannins. Some producers now give it longer oak ageing to soften it, and its ageing potential is drawing interest abroad.
grapes.trivia: The Öküzgözü-Boğazkere blend is often described as Turkey's answer to the Cabernet-Merlot partnership.

grapes.name: Kalecik Karası
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). A different local grape, Kalecik Siyahı, is a parent of Narince.
grapes.hectares: About 700 ha (2010).
grapes.profile: A central Anatolian red from the Kızılırmak river valley near Ankara, nearly extinct by the 1970s until researchers at Ankara University saved it. It gives pale, aromatic reds with strawberry, cherry and spice, often compared with Pinot Noir. Its revival coincided with growing interest in Turkish native grapes among producers such as Kavaklıdere, founded in Ankara in 1929. Its delicacy makes it one of Turkey's most food-friendly reds. Most plantings are still close to Kalecik, where the river valley gives a moderate microclimate. Several producers make it as rosé and sparkling wine too.
grapes.trivia: Ankara University's faculty of agriculture propagated surviving vines in the 1970s, saving the variety from extinction.

grapes.name: Narince
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC records Kalecik Siyahı × Dimrit.
grapes.hectares: Several thousand ha including use for stuffed vine leaves.
grapes.profile: Turkey's best-known white wine grape, from the Yeşilırmak valley around Tokat. Its name means 'delicate' or 'graceful'. It gives fresh whites with citrus, pear and floral notes, and oak-aged versions gain hazelnut. Its tender leaves are prized for sarma (stuffed vine leaves), so a large share of the crop is grown for leaves rather than grapes. Its fresh acidity and moderate alcohol make it versatile, and it is increasingly blended with Chardonnay or Emir. Some producers have planted it in Thrace and the Aegean.
grapes.trivia: Narince leaves are considered the best in Turkey for stuffed vine leaves, and some growers earn more from leaves than from grapes.

grapes.name: Obaideh
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). The claim that it is related to Chardonnay is not supported by DNA.
grapes.hectares: A few hundred ha.
grapes.profile: One of Lebanon's two traditional white grapes, used for centuries to make arak, the anise spirit. Château Musar blends it with Merwah in its long-lived white, aged in oak and released only after several years, which tastes of honey, nuts and beeswax. Lebanese wine traces its roots to the Phoenicians of Byblos and Tyre, and the Bekaa Valley at about 1,000 metres has been planted with vines since antiquity. Some producers now make it as a varietal wine, alongside the classic arak tradition.
grapes.trivia: Château Musar releases its white several years after the vintage, and old bottles last for decades.

grapes.name: Merwah
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC). Its old identification with Sémillon is not supported by DNA.
grapes.hectares: Small, scattered plantings at altitude.
grapes.profile: A high-altitude Lebanese white often grown ungrafted on Mount Lebanon at 1,300 to 1,700 metres. It was long said to be Sémillon, but DNA does not support that. It gives waxy, nutty whites that age well, especially in Château Musar's blend with Obaideh. Lebanese producers now bottle it alone as interest in native grapes grows. Château Musar and smaller estates such as Domaine des Tourelles have championed it, and some producers make it as orange wine. Its resistance to drought makes it well suited to Lebanon's dry summers, and it is one of the few native white grapes remaining in a country dominated by French varieties.
grapes.trivia: Many Merwah vines grow on their own roots in remote mountain villages, untouched by phylloxera.

grapes.name: Koshu
grapes.parentage_note: DNA work by Goto-Yamamoto and colleagues (2015, National Research Institute of Brewing) found Koshu is about 70 percent Vitis vinifera with the rest from East Asian wild species, notably Vitis davidii, through hybridisation along the Silk Road. It probably reached Japan via China. VIVC classifies it as an interspecific variety.
grapes.hectares: About 450 to 500 ha (2020s), mostly in Yamanashi.
grapes.profile: Japan's signature wine grape, grown in the Kōfu Basin of Yamanashi below Mount Fuji. Its pinkish-purple skins and thick berries resist the humid summers and typhoon rains, especially when trained on traditional overhead pergolas (tanazukuri). Koshu gives delicate, low-alcohol whites with yuzu, white peach and a gentle bitterness, sometimes aged on lees (sur lie, a technique popularised in Yamanashi from the 1980s). Legend dates the grape to 718 or 1186. In 2010 it became the first Japanese variety listed by the OIV, opening the way to EU exports with its name on the label.
grapes.trivia: Its DNA shows that the grape carries genes from Vitis davidii, a wild Chinese vine, evidence of hybridisation on its long journey east.

grapes.name: Muscat Bailey A
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Zenbei Kawakami at Iwanohara Vineyard in 1927: Bailey (an American hybrid) × Muscat Hamburg (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: Japan's most planted red wine grape (several hundred ha).
grapes.profile: Japan's most widely grown red wine grape, bred in Niigata by Zenbei Kawakami, the 'father of Japanese wine', who made more than 10,000 crosses to find grapes suited to Japan's wet, cold climate. It has a candied, strawberry-and-cotton-candy aroma from its American parent and soft tannins. Long used for sweet wines, it now appears in drier, oak-aged styles. It was registered with the OIV in 2013, three years after Koshu. It is also used for rosé and sparkling wine.
grapes.trivia: Kawakami founded Iwanohara Vineyard in 1890 and is said to have made more than 10,000 crossings in search of grapes suited to Japan.

grapes.name: Kyoho
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Yasushi Ōinoue in 1937: Ishihara Wase (a Campbell Early sport) × Centennial; a tetraploid labrusca-vinifera hybrid (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 365,000 ha in 2015, mostly in China, the most planted grape variety in the world by area (OIV Focus 2017).
grapes.profile: The most widely planted grape variety in the world, by OIV's 2015 figures, but almost entirely as a table grape. Kyoho's large, dark, slip-skinned berries have a foxy, grapey sweetness from its labrusca ancestry, and they dominate fresh-grape markets in China, Japan and Taiwan. It is occasionally made into sweet wine or fermented in Taiwan and China. Its success shows how much of the world's vineyard area is not devoted to wine at all. In China, Kyoho covers much of the country's grape area, particularly in the east.
grapes.trivia: Its name means 'giant peak', after Mount Fuji, visible from the breeding site in Shizuoka.

grapes.name: Sultana
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown. VIVC lists Central Asia as origin. A seedless variety propagated vegetatively for centuries.
grapes.hectares: 273,000 ha in 2015 (OIV Focus 2017), mainly for raisins and table grapes.
grapes.profile: The world's leading raisin and seedless table grape, known in the US as Thompson Seedless after William Thompson, who grew it in California in 1872. In the 20th century, especially in California's Central Valley and Australia's Riverland, much Sultana was crushed for cheap wine and brandy, particularly during shortages. It gives neutral, low-acid wine. Its history stretches back to Persian and Ottoman vineyards, and Turkey's Manisa region near Izmir remains a raisin capital. Its seedlessness comes from a mutation called stenospermocarpy, in which seeds stop developing early.
grapes.trivia: In the 1970s so much Thompson Seedless went into California jug wine that it was among the most crushed grapes in the state, though it was grown mainly for raisins.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.parentage_note: Bred in 1925 by Abraham Izak Perold, first professor of viticulture at Stellenbosch University: Pinot Noir × Cinsaut (then called Hermitage in South Africa, hence the name). A documented cross, confirmed by markers in VIVC.
grapes.hectares: About 7,000 ha in South Africa (SAWIS 2017: 6,979 ha), about 7 percent of the national vineyard.
grapes.profile: South Africa's own grape. Perold planted four seeds in his garden at the Welgevallen farm in 1925 and left for a job at the KWV; the seedlings were rescued by Charlie Niehaus, a colleague, when the garden was being cleared. The first commercial plantings came in 1943, and a Pinotage from Bellevue won the General Smuts Trophy in 1959. It gives deep, fruity reds with plum, banana and smoke, sometimes with an acetone note when poorly made. Producers such as Kanonkop, Beyerskloof and young Swartland growers have made it more refined. 'Coffee Pinotage', with mocha oak, became a popular style from the 2000s.
grapes.trivia: The seedlings survived only because Charlie Niehaus happened to pass by as Perold's old garden was being cleaned up and rescued them.

grapes.name: Torrontés
grapes.parentage_note: Torrontés Riojano is Criolla Chica (Listán Prieto) × Muscat of Alexandria per Agüero, Rodríguez et al. (2003) and VIVC. Torrontés Sanjuanino has the same parents; Torrontés Mendocino has Muscat of Alexandria and an unknown parent. Unrelated to Spain's Torrontés.
grapes.hectares: About 8,000 ha of Torrontés Riojano in Argentina (2020s INV), plus Sanjuanino and Mendocino.
grapes.profile: Argentina's signature white and a genuine New World native, born when the Spanish settlers' Criolla Chica (Listán Prieto) crossed with Muscat of Alexandria in colonial vineyards. Its best home is the high Calchaquí Valleys around Cafayate in Salta, at 1,700 to 3,000 metres, where intense sun and cool nights keep its perfume of rose, jasmine and peach balanced by fresh acidity. It can taste sweet on the nose and bone dry on the palate. Its genetics show how new varieties emerged from the colonial mix of grapes in the Americas.
grapes.trivia: Some Torrontés vineyards in Salta grow above 3,000 metres, among the highest vineyards in the world.

grapes.name: Cereza
grapes.parentage_note: Muscat of Alexandria × Mission (Listán Prieto) per VIVC and Agüero et al.
grapes.hectares: About 25,000 to 30,000 ha (2010s INV), one of Argentina's most planted grapes.
grapes.profile: A pink-skinned Criolla grape, named for its cherry colour, that long supplied Argentina's vast bulk-wine market, sold in cartons and demijohns. It is also used for grape concentrate, table grapes and raisins. It is a full sibling of Torrontés and the Criollas, born from the colonial crossing of Listán Prieto and Muscat of Alexandria. As Argentine consumption has fallen, its plantings have shrunk. Much of its crop now goes into grape juice concentrate, a major export from San Juan and Mendoza, used as a sweetener in juices and soft drinks around the world.
grapes.trivia: Argentina's per-capita wine consumption, once about 90 litres a year in the 1970s, fell below 20 litres by the 2020s, and Cereza plantings fell with it.

grapes.name: Criolla Grande
grapes.parentage_note: Mission (Listán Prieto) × Muscat of Alexandria per VIVC.
grapes.profile: Another of Argentina's Criolla grapes, pink-skinned and high-yielding, once among the country's most planted varieties and used for cheap rosé and white wine, concentrate and brandy. It shares parents with Cereza and Torrontés, and differs from Criolla Chica, which is Listán Prieto itself. Its decline mirrors the shift to Malbec and premium exports from the 1990s. Its high yields and hardiness made it a favourite of growers supplying cheap wine. Today it is often made into grape juice concentrate. A new generation of Argentine natural winemakers has also started bottling Criolla grapes as light, chillable reds, reviving interest in their history.
grapes.trivia: As of 2006, Criolla Grande was Argentina's third most widely planted wine grape.

grapes.name: Quebranta
grapes.parentage_note: Mission (Listán Prieto) × Negra Mole per VIVC.
grapes.hectares: The main pisco grape in Peru (several thousand ha).
grapes.profile: A Peruvian-born grape and the backbone of Peruvian pisco, the brandy distilled from fresh wine in the coastal desert valleys of Ica, Pisco and Moquegua. It is a non-aromatic grape, so Quebranta pisco is earthy and clean, a contrast with aromatic piscos from Italia or Torontel. Its parents are the two Spanish grapes that arrived with the conquistadors, Listán Prieto and Negra Mole, a living record of colonial viticulture. Other pisco grapes include aromatic Italia, Torontel, Moscatel and Albilla.
grapes.trivia: Peruvian law requires pisco to be distilled once from fresh wine and not watered down, so its strength comes straight from the still.

grapes.name: Crouchen
grapes.parentage_note: Parents unknown (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 3,200 ha in South Africa (as Cape Riesling) at its peak; a few hundred ha in Australia.
grapes.profile: A grape from the western Pyrenees, almost extinct in France since oidium and phylloxera, but long important in South Africa and Australia, where it was misidentified as Riesling. South Africans sold it as Cape or Paarl Riesling for decades, and Australians as Clare Riesling, until the French ampelographer Paul Truel identified it as Crouchen in the 1970s. It gives neutral, fresh whites. Its story shows how mislabelled cuttings spread around the world. It is resistant to disease and gives reliable yields, which explains its popularity in the Cape. Its plantings have since declined.
grapes.trivia: After the identification, South Africa required true Riesling to be labelled Weisser Riesling or Rhine Riesling to distinguish it from Cape Riesling.

grapes.name: Douce Noire
grapes.parentage_note: UC Davis DNA work showed Argentina's Bonarda and California's Charbono are Douce Noire from Savoie, not the Italian Bonardas.
grapes.hectares: About 18,000 ha in Argentina (INV, 2010s to 2020s), its second most planted red after Malbec.
grapes.profile: A Savoyard grape that became Argentina's second red. It came to Argentina with immigrants in the 19th century, was grown for bulk wine and later revealed by DNA to be Douce Noire, not the Italian Bonarda its name implied. In warmer eastern Mendoza and San Rafael it gives juicy, soft reds with plum, cherry and fig. In California, as Charbono, it survives in a few old Napa vineyards. Its plush style has found new fans as an easy-drinking Argentine red.
grapes.trivia: Inglenook in Napa bottled Charbono for decades, and a few Calistoga producers still make it.

grapes.name: Heptakilo
grapes.parentage_note: A Greek table grape identified by Crespan and Milani (2001) as a parent of Muscat of Alexandria.
grapes.hectares: Collection vines only.
grapes.profile: A Greek red-berried table grape whose name means 'seven kilos', presumably for its heavy bunches. DNA studies identified it as the second parent, with Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, of Muscat of Alexandria, one of the most widespread grapes in history. Its presence in the family tree supports the idea that Muscat of Alexandria arose in the eastern Mediterranean, probably in Greece or southern Italy, rather than in Egypt as its name suggests. It also shows how table grapes contributed to wine grape genetics.
grapes.trivia: Despite its role in Muscat history, Heptakilo is now known mainly from vine collections.

grapes.name: Norton
grapes.parentage_note: Found around 1820 by Dr Daniel Norton in his Richmond nursery. VIVC gives Vitis aestivalis × ((Bland × V. aestivalis) × V. vinifera). Nuclear and chloroplast DNA studies (Parker et al. 2009; Stover et al.) show it is mostly V. aestivalis with some vinifera ancestry. Genetic studies found Cynthiana indistinguishable from Norton.
