grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares in Missouri, Virginia and neighbouring states (2020s).
grapes.profile: America's oldest native grape still widely made into wine and the official state grape of Missouri (2003). Norton resists the fungal diseases and phylloxera that killed every vinifera planting in 19th-century eastern America, and it gives deep, tart, high-acid reds with black cherry, plum and spice, without the 'foxy' aroma of labrusca grapes. Missouri's German immigrants in Hermann and Augusta built a thriving industry on it before Prohibition: a Norton from Hermann won a gold medal at the 1873 Vienna World's Fair. Producers such as Stone Hill in Missouri and Chrysalis in Virginia revived it after 1970.
grapes.trivia: Missouri was the second-largest wine-producing state in the US before Prohibition, largely thanks to Norton and Catawba.

grapes.name: Concord
grapes.parentage_note: Selected by Ephraim Wales Bull from seedlings of wild Vitis labrusca, first fruiting in 1849 after he evaluated over 22,000 seedlings. SSR analysis later confirmed Catawba as a parent (VIVC: Catawba × V. labrusca).
grapes.hectares: About 10,000 ha in the US, most used for juice and jelly (Welch's).
grapes.profile: The quintessential American grape and the taste of grape juice and grape jelly. Its 'foxy' aroma comes from methyl anthranilate, a compound typical of Vitis labrusca. In 1869 Dr Thomas Welch, a Methodist dentist in Vineland, New Jersey, pasteurised Concord juice to make an 'unfermented sacramental wine' for his church, founding Welch's. Concord is also made into sweet kosher wines (such as Manischewitz) and sweet table wines. Its winter hardiness and disease resistance make it suited to cold continental climates around the Great Lakes.
grapes.trivia: Bull died in 1895 with little reward; his gravestone in Concord reads 'He sowed, others reaped'.

grapes.name: Catawba

origin.place: Buncombe County, North Carolina, USA (Catawba River)

grapes.parentage_note: VIVC gives V. labrusca × Sémillon, with a crossing date of 1802. Discovered growing wild near the Catawba River and propagated by Major John Adlum in Georgetown, DC, by 1823.
grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares in the US; about 1,300 ha in Canada (2006).
grapes.profile: The grape of America's first wine boom. In the 1840s Nicholas Longworth, a Cincinnati lawyer, planted Catawba along the Ohio River and made a sparkling wine that was hailed as America's Champagne; Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote an 'Ode to Catawba Wine' in 1854. By 1859 Ohio was the leading wine state, until black rot and powdery mildew destroyed the vineyards in the 1860s. Catawba has pinkish skins and gives sweet or off-dry pink and sparkling wines with a gentle foxiness. It remains in use around Lake Erie and in the Finger Lakes.
grapes.trivia: Longfellow's poem called Catawba 'Very good in its way / Is the Verzenay / Or the Sillery soft and creamy; / But Catawba wine / Has a taste more divine'.

grapes.name: Scuppernong

origin.place: Scuppernong River, Tyrrell County, North Carolina, USA

grapes.parentage_note: A wild-selected bronze cultivar of Vitis rotundifolia (Muscadinia rotundifolia), a species with 40 chromosomes rather than the 38 of Vitis, which makes crosses with vinifera difficult. Isaac Alexander is said to have found it in 1755.
grapes.hectares: Muscadines cover a few thousand hectares in the US Southeast (2020s).
grapes.profile: The original American wine grape. Giovanni da Verrazzano described large white grapes on the Carolina coast in 1524, and Walter Raleigh's colonists on Roanoke Island in the 1580s found them too. Scuppernong is the bronze form of muscadine, native to the hot, humid Southeast, where it resists Pierce's disease and fungal diseases that kill vinifera. Its thick-skinned berries grow in small clusters and have an intense, musky, grapey flavour. In the 19th century, Virginia Dare, a sweet Scuppernong wine from Garrett & Company, was America's best-selling wine. It is the state fruit of North Carolina.
grapes.trivia: The 'Mother Vine' on Roanoke Island, a Scuppernong, is often claimed to be over 400 years old and one of the oldest cultivated grapevines in North America.

grapes.name: Muscadine
grapes.parentage_note: A distinct species (or subgenus) of grapevine with 40 chromosomes, native from Delaware to Florida and Texas. Hundreds of cultivars have been bred at North Carolina State, the University of Georgia and the University of Florida, including Carlos and Noble.
grapes.hectares: A few thousand hectares in the US Southeast.
grapes.profile: The southern grape of the United States, a separate branch of the grapevine family that evolved alongside Pierce's disease and the humid heat of the Gulf Coast. Muscadines grow in small clusters of large, thick-skinned berries that drop individually when ripe. Cultivars such as the bronze Carlos and the black Noble, bred at North Carolina State University, are made into sweet, fruity wines with a strong musky aroma. Their skins and seeds are extremely high in polyphenols such as ellagic acid, which has made them popular for health supplements. They are also eaten fresh, made into jams and pressed for juice.
grapes.trivia: Because muscadines have 40 chromosomes and Vitis grapes 38, crossing the two was long nearly impossible; breeders only began producing fertile hybrids in the 20th century.

grapes.name: Isabella
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC gives V. labrusca × Meslier Petit; microsatellite work from Jerónimo Rodrigues's laboratory identified Ives (Ives' Seedling) as the labrusca parent. Popularly said to have been discovered by Isabella Gibbs of South Carolina around 1816 and named after her by William Prince.
grapes.hectares: About 30,000 ha (VIVC sum): Moldova about 10,800 ha, Brazil about 10,700 ha, India about 4,500 ha.
grapes.profile: A labrusca hybrid that travelled the world in the 19th century because it resisted oidium, which was then devastating European vineyards. Isabella spread through Brazil, where it remains a major grape for juice and table wine, and across the Black Sea region: Georgia's Isabella is called Odessa or Adesa, and Moldova and Ukraine grow huge amounts. Its foxy, strawberry-like aroma explains the Italian name Fragola. The EU bans wine from Isabella and other direct producer hybrids from being sold as quality wine, but Austria's Uhudler, from Burgenland, won a legal exception in 2016.
grapes.trivia: France banned Isabella and other American direct producer hybrids in 1935, partly over fears about methanol content, and the ban still shapes EU rules.

grapes.name: Vidal Blanc
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Jean-Louis Vidal in the 1930s, Ugni Blanc × Rayon d'Or (Seibel 4986) (VIVC). Vidal aimed to create a hardy grape for Cognac distillation.
grapes.hectares: About 1,900 ha in Canada (VIVC 2008), plus several hundred in US eastern states.
grapes.profile: The grape that built Canadian icewine. Bred in the Charente for Cognac, it found its real calling in Ontario, where its thick skins hang on the vine into January without splitting, while its high acidity balances intense sweetness. Icewine is made from grapes frozen naturally on the vine at minus 8 degrees Celsius or below, pressed while frozen so only a few drops of concentrated juice emerge. Inniskillin's 1989 Vidal Icewine won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in Bordeaux in 1991, putting Canada on the world wine map. It also makes fresh dry and off-dry whites.
grapes.trivia: Ontario's VQA rules require icewine grapes to be picked at minus 8 degrees Celsius or colder, often at night by teams on standby.

grapes.name: Chambourcin
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Joannès Seyve and released in 1963: Joannès Seyve 11369 × Plantet (Seibel 5455) per VIVC. A complex hybrid with V. rupestris, V. riparia, V. lincecumii and V. vinifera in its ancestry. It is a parent of Regent.
grapes.hectares: About 800 ha in France (2008), plus significant US plantings in the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic.
grapes.profile: One of the best French-American hybrids for red wine, with deep colour, fresh acidity, soft tannins and no foxiness. It is the leading red of many eastern US states, from Pennsylvania to Missouri, where humid summers rule out most vinifera. It also grows in Australia's Hastings River region in New South Wales, one of the few hybrid strongholds outside North America. Its resistance to fungal diseases made it a parent of Germany's Regent. It makes everything from rosé to oak-aged reds and sparkling wine.
grapes.trivia: The name probably comes from the hamlet of Chambourcin near the Seyve family's nursery in the Rhône valley.

grapes.name: Seyval Blanc
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Bertille Seyve and his father-in-law Victor Villard around 1919 to 1920: Seibel 5656 × Rayon d'Or (Seibel 4986) (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares in the US and about 100 ha in England (2009).
grapes.profile: A French-American hybrid that made English and New York wine viable. Seyval Blanc ripens early, resists cold and disease, and gives crisp, citrusy whites without foxiness. In 1952 Guy Salisbury-Jones planted it at Hambledon in Hampshire, England's first commercial vineyard since the Middle Ages, and it remained a backbone of English still and sparkling wine until Chardonnay and Pinot took over. In New York's Finger Lakes and Hudson Valley it was the leading white in the 1970s and 1980s. EU rules long barred hybrids from quality wine, so English Seyval was sold as table wine.
grapes.trivia: Hambledon's vineyard, planted in 1952, is often credited as the start of England's modern wine industry, with Seyval Blanc as its first major grape.

grapes.name: Baco Noir
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by François Baco in 1902: Folle Blanche × an unknown V. riparia (Riparia Grand Glabre) (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares in Ontario and the eastern US; nearly extinct in France.
grapes.profile: A Folle Blanche × riparia hybrid created in the Landes after phylloxera, intended to make wine and brandy without grafting. It gives dark, high-acid, low-tannin reds with blackberry and smoky notes. Banned in France with other hybrids, it found a home in Canada and the northeastern US from the 1950s, especially Ontario, where Henry of Pelham's oak-aged Baco Noir became a reference. Its sister, Baco Blanc (Baco 22A), was widely planted in Armagnac and was reauthorised there in 2005 after a long ban.
grapes.trivia: Baco Blanc is the only hybrid grape permitted in a French AOC: Armagnac.

grapes.name: Marquette
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Peter Hemstad and James Luby at the University of Minnesota in 1989: MN 1094 × Ravat 262 (VIVC). Released in 2006. Ravat 262 is a grandchild of Pinot Noir, so Marquette is a cousin of Frontenac with some Pinot ancestry.
grapes.hectares: Several hundred hectares across the Upper Midwest, New England and Quebec.
grapes.profile: The flagship of the University of Minnesota's cold-hardy grape programme, which has made winemaking possible in places where winters fall below minus 30 degrees. Marquette survives temperatures around minus 37 degrees, resists downy and powdery mildew, and gives medium-bodied reds with cherry, blackcurrant and pepper, with less acidity than older hybrids. Its Pinot Noir ancestry gives it more finesse than many hybrids. It is now the most planted red in Minnesota, Vermont and Quebec. It ripens early with high sugar.
grapes.trivia: In 2019 VQA Ontario announced that Marquette would be added to the grapes permitted in its quality-wine system.

grapes.name: Frontenac
grapes.parentage_note: Bred in 1978 by the University of Minnesota (Elmer Swenson, Patrick Pierquet, Peter Hemstad, James Luby): Landot 4511 × a cold-hardy V. riparia (VIVC). Released 1996. Frontenac Gris (2003) and Frontenac Blanc (2012) are colour mutations.
grapes.hectares: Several hundred hectares across the northern US and Quebec.
grapes.profile: The first great success of Minnesota's cold-climate breeding. Frontenac survives winters to about minus 35 degrees and gives very dark, high-acid reds with cherry and plum, often used for rosé, port-style and ice wines. Its high acidity must be managed with malolactic fermentation or blending. Frontenac Gris, a grey mutation, makes aromatic whites with peach and apricot. Together with Marquette and La Crescent, it made winemaking a real industry in the Upper Midwest and Quebec. It ripens early and is usually harvested with very high sugar.
grapes.trivia: The name honours Louis de Buade de Frontenac, governor of New France, a nod to the grape's success in Quebec.

grapes.name: La Crescent
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Peter Hemstad and James Luby in 1988: St. Pepin × Elmer Swenson 6-8-25 (VIVC). Released 2002. Muscat of Hamburg is in its pedigree.
grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares in cold northern states.
grapes.profile: A highly aromatic, cold-hardy white from Minnesota with apricot, citrus and tropical fruit notes, inherited partly from its Muscat ancestry. It survives winters to about minus 36 degrees. Its high acidity suits off-dry and sweet wines, and producers in Vermont, such as La Garagista, have made fresh, natural-style versions that attracted international attention. It is named after the town of La Crescent on the Mississippi. Its early bud break makes it sensitive to late spring frost, so growers favour sites with good air drainage. It is often blended with Frontenac Gris or Brianna.
grapes.trivia: Vermont producer La Garagista helped make cold-hardy hybrids fashionable among natural-wine drinkers in the 2010s.

grapes.name: L'Acadie Blanc
grapes.parentage_note: Bred in 1953 by Ollie A. Bradt at the Vineland Horticultural Research Station in Ontario: Cascade × Seyve-Villard 14-287 (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: About 100 ha in Nova Scotia (2020s), its leading grape.
grapes.profile: Nova Scotia's signature grape. Bred in Ontario, it was tested in Nova Scotia in the 1970s and proved ideal for the province's short, cool seasons and maritime winters. It gives crisp, citrus-and-green-apple whites with good body, and traditional-method sparkling wines that have won international praise, notably from Benjamin Bridge in the Gaspereau Valley. It is the main grape in Tidal Bay, a crisp white appellation-style designation created by Nova Scotia in 2012. It is also made into dessert and icewine styles.
grapes.trivia: Tidal Bay, launched in 2012, was Nova Scotia's first appellation-style wine, named for the Bay of Fundy, which has the highest tides in the world.

grapes.name: Niagara

origin.place: Lockport, Niagara County, New York, USA

grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Claudius L. Hoag and Benjamin W. Clark in Lockport in 1868: Concord × Cassady (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: Several thousand hectares in the US and Brazil, mostly for juice.
grapes.profile: The white counterpart of Concord, with a foxy, sweet grape-candy aroma. It is grown in the eastern US mainly for white grape juice, but also for sweet table wines that remain popular in the Lake Erie area. It is widely planted in Brazil's Serra Gaúcha, where labrusca grapes still dominate juice and table wine, and in Japan. Its parent Cassady is a labrusca seedling. Its fresh aroma makes it popular for sweet sparkling wine and for blending in Concord-based juice. Like Concord, it is winter-hardy and resists fungal diseases.
grapes.trivia: Its breeders tried to control propagation by selling vines only under contract, an early attempt at what would now be plant variety protection.

grapes.name: Delaware
grapes.parentage_note: Parentage unknown; VIVC gives (V. labrusca × V. aestivalis) × V. vinifera. Found in a garden in Frenchtown, New Jersey, in the 1840s and named after Delaware, Ohio, where it was promoted.
grapes.hectares: Several hundred hectares in Japan, a major table grape.
grapes.profile: A small, pink, sweet American hybrid that became one of Japan's most important table grapes after its introduction in the 1870s. Japanese growers learned in the late 1950s to make it seedless with gibberellin treatments, and seedless Delaware remains a summer staple. It is also made into light, fragrant, slightly foxy wines in Yamanashi and Yamagata. In the US it was a 19th-century sparkling-wine grape in New York and Ohio. Its berries are small and sweet with a delicate perfume, and growers in Japan often protect each cluster with a paper bag to keep it clean and prevent disease.
grapes.trivia: Japanese researchers in the late 1950s found that dipping Delaware clusters in gibberellin made the berries seedless, a technique since adopted for other table grapes.

grapes.name: Maréchal Foch
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Eugène Kuhlmann in Colmar in 1911: Millardet et Grasset 101 open-pollinated (riparia × rupestris) × Goldriesling (VIVC). Léon Millot is a sibling.
grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares in Canada and the northern US.
grapes.profile: An early-ripening, cold-hardy red hybrid named after Ferdinand Foch, the French marshal of the First World War. It gives dark, light-bodied reds with dark berries, smoke and an earthy, sometimes gamey note. It is now rare in France but important in Canada and the northern US, where it is often made with carbonic maceration to soften its acidity. Old-vine Foch from Ontario and Nova Scotia has a small cult following. Its small berries and tight clusters ripen in late August or early September, which made it valuable in short-season regions.
grapes.trivia: Kuhlmann named this cross after Marshal Foch, and its sibling after Léon Millot, a Burgundian nurseryman.

grapes.name: Traminette
grapes.parentage_note: Crossed by Herbert C. Barrett at the University of Illinois in 1965: Joannès Seyve 23-416 × Gewürztraminer; evaluated and released by Cornell University in 1996 (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: Several hundred hectares in the eastern US.
grapes.profile: Gewürztraminer's spicy, floral character in a hardier, disease-resistant package. Traminette gives aromatic whites with rose, lychee and honey, slightly fresher than its parent, and is often made off-dry. It is the official signature grape of Indiana (2009) and widely planted in New York, Michigan and Virginia. It survives harder winters than Gewürztraminer and needs fewer sprays. It is often blended with Riesling or Vidal. It is also used for late-harvest and icewine styles in Michigan and Ontario. Its pink-tinged berries and moderate yields make it one of the most planted hybrids in the eastern United States.
grapes.trivia: Indiana adopted Traminette as its signature grape in 2009 to give its wineries a common calling card.

grapes.name: Vignoles
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by J. F. Ravat. The traditional pedigree (Seibel 6905 × Pinot de Corton) was disproved by DNA; the parentage is now unknown, and Vignoles proved unrelated to the Ravat 51 vine imported into the US in 1949 (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares in the eastern US.
grapes.profile: A high-acid, aromatic hybrid with pineapple, apricot and honey flavours that suits late-harvest and icewine styles. Its tight clusters make it prone to botrytis, which can give excellent sweet wines in the Finger Lakes. It is one of Missouri's signature whites. The mix-up over its identity shows how often hybrid names were confused when vines crossed the Atlantic. Its small, compact clusters give low yields and it buds late, avoiding spring frost. It has high acidity, which helps sweet versions stay balanced. Producers in the Finger Lakes and Missouri make dry, off-dry and late-harvest styles.
grapes.trivia: Vignoles is so prone to botrytis that eastern US growers often plan for late-harvest wines rather than fight the rot.

grapes.name: Lenoir

origin.place: Southeastern United States (South Carolina or Georgia)

grapes.parentage_note: VIVC gives V. aestivalis × V. vinifera (prime name Jacquez). Its exact origin is unclear; it was in cultivation by the early 19th century.
grapes.hectares: About 1,400 ha in Brazil (2007); small plantings in Texas.
grapes.profile: One of the American grapes that saved European vineyards. After phylloxera, Jacquez was planted widely in southern France, Portugal and Madeira as a direct producer because it resisted the aphid and mildews. On Madeira it was one of the hybrids that replaced the noble grapes for decades. In Texas, as Black Spanish or Lenoir, it resists Pierce's disease and makes dark, tannic reds and port-style wines. Its use in France was banned in 1935. Its thick skins and deep colour make it useful in blends.
grapes.trivia: Jacquez was one of the six American hybrids banned outright in France in 1935, with Noah, Othello, Isabella, Clinton and Herbemont.

grapes.name: Cayuga White
grapes.parentage_note: Crossed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva in 1945 by John Einset and Willard Robinson: Seyval × Schuyler (VIVC). Released 1972.
grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares.
grapes.profile: A Cornell hybrid named after Cayuga Lake, one of the Finger Lakes. It is productive, hardy and disease-resistant, giving light, fruity whites with citrus and pineapple, made dry, off-dry or sparkling. It played a large role in the growth of Finger Lakes wineries in the 1970s and 1980s, before vinifera such as Riesling took over at the top end. Its large clusters and moderate vigour suit the cold winters of New York, and it is often blended with other hybrids. It is also popular for sparkling and semi-sweet wines in Pennsylvania and Ohio.
grapes.trivia: Cornell's Geneva station, founded in 1882, has bred grapes for well over a century, including Cayuga White, Noiret and Traminette.

grapes.name: Blanc du Bois
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by John A. Mortensen at the University of Florida in 1968: Florida D6-148 × Cardinal (VIVC). Released 1987.
grapes.hectares: A few hundred hectares in the Gulf states.
grapes.profile: A white hybrid bred to resist Pierce's disease, a bacterial disease spread by sharpshooter insects that kills vinifera in the Gulf Coast states. It gives aromatic, off-dry whites with citrus, white flowers and a slightly muscat character. It is especially popular in Texas, where some producers also make fortified, Madeira-style versions. Its name honours Emile Dubois, a 19th-century grape grower in Tallahassee, Florida. It ripens early, which helps it avoid the heaviest hurricane-season rains, and it is often made into off-dry and sparkling wines.
grapes.trivia: Its tolerance of Pierce's disease makes it one of the few white grapes that can be grown commercially on the Gulf Coast.

grapes.name: Herbemont
grapes.parentage_note: VIVC gives Chasselas × unknown (an aestivalis-cinerea type), named after Nicholas Herbemont, a South Carolina grower who promoted it in the early 19th century.
grapes.hectares: About 850 ha in Brazil (2007).
grapes.profile: An old southern American hybrid, popular in the 19th century for its resistance to heat and humidity. It spread to Europe after phylloxera as a direct producer and to Brazil, where it is still used for juice and table wine. In Texas, T. V. Munson praised it, and a few producers still make it. France banned it in 1935. Its thick skins and loose clusters made it suitable for humid climates. It is still grown in Brazil for juice, and a few Texas wineries make it as a curiosity, keeping alive a grape that once represented the best of southern American viticulture.
grapes.trivia: Nicholas Herbemont, the South Carolina grower who promoted it, was one of the first American writers to argue that native grapes, not European ones, were the future of American wine.

grapes.name: Chardonel
grapes.parentage_note: Crossed at Geneva in 1953: Seyval × Chardonnay (VIVC). Released 1990.
grapes.hectares: Several hundred hectares in the Midwest.
grapes.profile: A Cornell hybrid that combines Chardonnay's structure with Seyval Blanc's cold hardiness. It gives full-bodied whites with apple, citrus and a good response to oak and malolactic fermentation, so it is often made in a Chardonnay style. It is especially popular in Missouri and Arkansas. It is late-ripening and needs a long season, so it suits the warm summers of Missouri and Arkansas. It is more cold-hardy than Chardonnay and more resistant to disease, but still needs spraying in humid years. Missouri producers such as Stone Hill have made it a regional favourite. It is also used for sparkling wines.
grapes.trivia: Chardonel took 37 years from crossing (1953) to release (1990), a reminder of how slow grape breeding is.

grapes.name: Rayon d'Or
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Albert Seibel: Seibel 405 × Seibel 867 (VIVC).
grapes.hectares: Negligible today.
grapes.profile: A Seibel hybrid that matters for its children. Albert Seibel, a doctor in Aubenas in the Ardèche, made thousands of crosses after phylloxera to find grapes that could be grown without grafting or spraying. Rayon d'Or was one of his successes, and it became a parent of both Vidal Blanc and Seyval Blanc, two of the most important hybrids in North America and England. Seibel's numbered seedlings underpin a large share of French-American hybrid genealogy. Its sweet, white berries were also popular as a table grape.
grapes.trivia: Albert Seibel numbered his seedlings, and the numbers ran into the thousands; many hybrids are still known only by a Seibel number.

grapes.name: Petite Pearl
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Tom Plocher in 1996: MN 1094 × Elmer Swenson 4-7-26 (VIVC). Released 2010.
grapes.hectares: Small but growing.
grapes.profile: A newer cold-hardy red from independent Minnesota breeder Tom Plocher, valued for lower acidity and finer tannins than older northern hybrids. It survives very cold winters, ripens late and gives dark, structured reds with blackberry, plum and spice, making it popular as a partner for Marquette. It shows how private breeders have joined universities in building a northern wine industry. Its small berries and loose clusters reduce disease pressure. It is also used for rosé and port-style wines. Growers like its ability to ripen sugar without excessive acidity.
grapes.trivia: Tom Plocher co-wrote Northern Winework, a guide to growing and making wine from cold-hardy grapes.

grapes.name: Brianna
grapes.parentage_note: Bred by Elmer Swenson in 1983: Kay Gray × ES 2-12-13 (VIVC). Released 2001.
grapes.hectares: Small plantings across northern states.
grapes.profile: A cold-hardy white from Elmer Swenson, the dairy farmer who became the pioneer of northern grape breeding. Brianna gives fruity whites with pineapple, apricot and citrus, often made off-dry. It survives winters to about minus 35 degrees. Swenson's work, done privately and later with the University of Minnesota, laid the foundation for the Midwest's cold-climate wine industry. It is often used for sweet and dessert wines because of its intense fruit, and it is also grown as a table grape. Its pale green berries develop a golden colour when fully ripe. It is particularly popular in Nebraska.
grapes.trivia: Elmer Swenson began breeding grapes on his family farm in Osceola, Wisconsin, in the 1940s, long before the University of Minnesota took up the work.

grapes.name: Ives
grapes.parentage_note: Raised by Henry Ives in Cincinnati around 1840 from Hartford open-pollinated seed (VIVC). Rodrigues's lab identified it as the labrusca parent of Isabella.
grapes.hectares: Several thousand hectares in Brazil as Bordô.
grapes.profile: A dark labrusca grape raised in Ohio around 1840, once a staple of Ohio and New York wine. In Brazil, where it is called Bordô, it is one of the most important grapes for juice and table wine in the Serra Gaúcha and Santa Catarina. DNA analysis has shown it to be a parent of Isabella, linking two of the most widely planted American grapes. It is cold-hardy and resistant to many diseases, but its foxy aroma limited its use for quality wine in the US. In Brazil it is also bottled as a varietal sweet red.
grapes.trivia: Brazilian growers value Bordô for its very deep colour, which makes it a useful blending grape for juice and table wine.
